items.title: Who is Wetang’ula protecting? Speaker changes tune on missing phone
items.summary:
National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula is facing fresh questions over what he knows about the disappearance of Sabina Chege’s phone after appearing to soften his earlier account of what CCTV footage showed.
Wetang’ula on Tuesday told MPs that cameras had captured a legislator “pocketing” another
items.text:
National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula is facing fresh questions over what he knows about the disappearance of Sabina Chege’s phone after appearing to soften his earlier account of what CCTV footage showed.
Wetang’ula on Tuesday told MPs that cameras had captured a legislator “pocketing” another member’s phone during a heated confrontation in Parliament.
But on Wednesday, after Chege identified herself as the owner of the missing phone, the Speaker offered a different description, saying the footage showed an MP picking up a phone from a seat where it had fallen.
“I also did say yesterday that CCTV showed a member taking a phone. The hansard will bear me. I said CCTV showed after that altercation a member taking the phone from the seat where it fell,” Wetang’ula said.
The change in wording has raised questions about why the Speaker did not identify the MP, particularly after revealing that he had personally watched the footage alongside Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and other lawmakers.
Wetang’ula has not publicly identified the legislator, saying he did not accuse anyone of stealing the phone.
He had earlier said the MP denied taking it even after being shown the CCTV recording.
“I told him to go and wrestle with his conscience for the rest of this term because there are certain things that are not expected of us,” he said on Tuesday.
The controversy gained fresh attention on Wednesday after Chege told the House that the phone which went missing during a confrontation on June 8, 2023, belonged to her.
She said she was caught up in the commotion involving Suba South MP Millie Odhiambo and Kisumu Town West MP Rosa Buyu, after a disagreement over her removal as Deputy Minority Whip.
Chege recounted that she realised her phone was missing after Buyu, who had come to her rescue, picked up her handbag.
She said she later tracked the device from Parliament towards Donholm, but never recovered it.
The nominated MP challenged Wetang’ula to identify the person captured on camera or ensure the phone was returned.
“Before we end this term, please Speaker, either name the person or ask the person to return my phone,” Chege told the House.
Faced with renewed pressure, Wetang’ula announced that he would hand the CCTV recordings to the Powers and Privileges Committee for review.
He also said he would not chair the proceedings, despite being the committee’s substantive chairperson.
“What I will do, as your Speaker, I am the chair of the Powers and Privileges Committee, but I will not chair,” he said.
He will appoint another member to lead the review and present a report to the House.
The committee’s review is expected to establish what the footage actually shows and whether the person can be identified.

items.text:
Super League: London Broncos confirmed as 15th team for 2027 season after clubs voted in favour of motion
Super League clubs voted to expand competition to 15 teams for the 2027 season; London Broncos now confirmed as club to take that place; the league previously voted in favour of two salary cap amendments that allow clubs more flexibility with young players and injuries
Wednesday 25 November 2026 17:01, UK
London Broncos have been confirmed as Super League's 15th team for the 2027 season.
Earlier this month, Super League announced its 14 clubs have voted in favour of a motion to expand to 15 teams for the 2027 season.
Clubs were then invited to apply, with London Broncos - who have made no secret of their desire to be in the top flight - one of those to do so having completed the treble in 2026 during a brilliant season for them in the Championship.
"We are delighted to welcome London Broncos back to Super League for 2027," said chair of Super League Peter Hutton.
"This is an exciting moment for the club and its supporters, and an opportunity to build a lasting presence for our competition in the capital.
"They clearly impressed in the Championship last year, not only winning the League Leaders' Shield but the Grand Final and 1895 Cup in a memorable treble.
"In Grant Wechsel and Darren Lockyer, they have ambitious owners who are intent on making a success of our great sport in London and the surrounding areas.
"On behalf of all Super League clubs, I would like to put on record my thanks to both Grant and Darren for the collaboration they have shown over the last 10 days to enable the RFL to come to this recommendation.
"Expansion is about more than adding another club. We want a compelling, competitive Super League that reaches new audiences while continuing to serve the supporters who are at the heart of our sport.
"With more exciting announcements expected shortly around investment, broadcast deals and new commercial partners for Super League, we look forward to working with the Broncos as they prepare for 2027, and to seeing their supporters enjoy the elite competition in London once again."
After London went back down to the Championship in 2024, they were taken over by an ownership group including NRL and Brisbane Broncos legend Darren Lockyer.
Super League clubs approve salary cap amendments
Also this month, clubs voted in favour of two amendments to the league's salary cap regulations that allow clubs more flexibility with young players and injuries.
The first allows teams to claim salary cap dispensation if a player is injured for over eight cap-relevant matches, allowing clubs to sign a replacement player for the period.
It also forbids teams from claiming further salary cap dispensation should a player who was already exempt from salary cap implications becomes re-injured later in the season, unless he missed a further eight matches which affect the salary cap.
The second allows teams to feature a young player aged 23 and under - who has not previously played in any salary capped games - in two matches without triggering an increase in a club's salary cap spending, with that figure increasing to 50 per cent should they play between three and five matches.
Should the player feature in more than five matches, the full amount of their salary will be applied to the cap.

items.title: 'Triumph over trauma' - new women's boxing promotion begins
items.summary:
Fight Back Promotions, a new venture to support women affected by domestic violence, begins: 'It's triumph over trauma'
Fight Back Promotions will have its inaugural event on Saturday at London's Ladbroke Hall; Fight Back Promotions is a women's boxing venture that supports a charitable programme wh
items.text:
Fight Back Promotions, a new venture to support women affected by domestic violence, begins: 'It's triumph over trauma'
Fight Back Promotions will have its inaugural event on Saturday at London's Ladbroke Hall; Fight Back Promotions is a women's boxing venture that supports a charitable programme which works with women who have been affected by domestic abuse and gender-based violence
Wednesday 25 November 2026 15:34, UK
A new boxing promotion, created to support women who have experienced domestic abuse and gender-based violence, will have its inaugural event on Saturday at Ladbroke Hall in London.
Fight Back Promotions was founded by Lesley Sackey, a former GB boxer, Shelly Sweeney, a champion and coach herself, and Poppy Mason-Watts, who has a background in social impact story-telling.
Sackey told Sky Sports: "Fight Back Promotions is an all-female boxing platform. It started from a CIC [a Community Interest Company or social enterprise] called Fight Forward.
"Fight Back Promotions was born as an answer and response to giving a space for all women to be able to step into the ring with not only safety but community, encouragement and a way to promote themselves and go on their own journey.
"It's about using boxing as a vehicle to support women who'd experienced domestic abuse."
Twenty-five per cent of the promotion's profits will go back to Fight Forward's charitable work.
"Women's sport is having a moment and there's still so much more to do," Sackey said. "It really seems like there's opportunity and potential to be a global platform.
"Women put on excellent fights, I don't think we need to prove that any more, and they can sell tickets as well.
"A percentage of whatever we make will always go back feeding into the not-for-profit Fight Forward to support other women in tough, challenging spaces."
Sackey formed the concept for Fight Forward, which uses boxing training to support its participants, after leaving an abusive relationship.
"The ring is just a destination, it's really about the journey, it's about the process, it's about the discipline of having to show up for yourself which for so many women in these situations, they've not had the choice or even the opportunity to do something for themselves," she explained.
"It's about discipline, it's about showing up, it's about being connected to your body, it's about being present, resilient. These are all the tools that we teach the women who participate in the sessions. Not all of them are contact. It's not just about contact, it's about community, being around other women who get it.
"Just to put on gloves and see another woman in an empowered position, the ripple effect is huge and it reaches so many women just by seeing that.
"It's triumph over trauma. You don't have to remain in this survivor state."

items.title: Kenyan Firms Risk Data Breaches as AI Adoption Outpaces Oversight
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – Kenyan businesses could be exposing themselves to data privacy and security risks through artificial intelligence tools already embedded in their operations, with a new report warning that most organisations lack basic safeguards to manage the technology.
The AI Readiness in
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – Kenyan businesses could be exposing themselves to data privacy and security risks through artificial intelligence tools already embedded in their operations, with a new report warning that most organisations lack basic safeguards to manage the technology.
The AI Readiness in Kenya 2026 report by the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI) and Akili AI reveals that four in five organisations using AI have no designated official responsible for overseeing risks associated with the technology.
The assessment further shows that three-quarters of organisations have no formal AI policy, while seven in ten lack the capacity to detect or respond to AI-related incidents.
The findings raise concerns about how businesses handle sensitive customer and company information as AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday applications and business processes.
According to the report, many organisations are unaware of the extent to which AI is already being used within their operations, with employees independently adopting publicly available tools without clear internal guidelines.
Akili AI Founder and Chief Executive Officer Simon Bransfield-Garth said businesses frequently underestimate the number of applications incorporating AI within their systems.
“Most leaders we speak to guess they have 15 to 20 applications using AI. The answer is usually 50 to 100. You cannot get value from, or manage, what you cannot see,” he said.
The report cautions that the absence of AI inventories, acceptable-use policies and designated accountability structures makes it difficult for organisations to establish where their data is going and whether decisions are being made using unchecked AI-generated information.
It further notes that Kenya’s Data Protection Act already covers AI applications that process personal data, potentially exposing businesses to compliance risks even where AI use is not formally recognised by management.
The assessment, which collected 214 responses in October 2026, found that 99 per cent of organisations surveyed already use AI in some form.
Four in ten have incorporated the technology into core business processes or customer-facing decisions, including credit assessments, insurance claims and customer service.
However, 63 per cent do not provide structured AI training to employees, highlighting a gap in organisational preparedness as adoption accelerates.
The report recommends a four-step approach to strengthening AI governance within the first 90 days.
Organisations are advised to establish an inventory of AI tools in use, appoint responsible officials and introduce clear usage policies, train employees on safe and productive AI adoption, and maintain evidence of compliance.
Akili AI Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Shikoli Makatiani said businesses needed to establish clear rules and accountability structures to maximise the benefits of AI.
“AI is not coming; it is already here, in the tools Kenyan businesses use every day. The question now is how we get real value from it,” he said.
The report notes that despite the governance gaps, three-quarters of organisations intend to increase their AI use over the next year, while more than 90 per cent consider the technology an opportunity.

items.text:
'Best midfielder in the world' - where does Bellingham rank?
- Published
Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?
Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.
"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."
Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.
While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.
"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."
While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?
BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.
Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid)
Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.
He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.
He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.
He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.
When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.
He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.
Vitinha (Paris St-Germain)
While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.
But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.
The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".
He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.
Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.
"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."
Declan Rice (Arsenal)
Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.
He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.
Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.
The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.
He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.
Rodri (Barcelona)
The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.
It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.
The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.
His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.
The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.
- The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top 
  - Published3 October
Pedri (Barcelona)
Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.

items.text:
Why are school shootings continuing to shake the Balkans?
A shooting in Serbia has renewed concerns over firearm access, online warning signs and failures to prevent violence.
A school shooting in central Serbia has renewed concerns about the availability of firearms, social media warning signs, and systemic failures, following a wave of similar violence across the Balkans.
On Tuesday, a 17-year-old suspect shot and wounded two school staff members at the First Technical School in Kragujevac, a city about 145km (90 miles) south of Belgrade.
Local media reported that the suspect, a student at the school, posted a photo posing with a rifle on social media hours before the attack.
Here’s what you should know:
What happened in Kragujevac?
The shooting began at about 8am (07:00 GMT) during the first class of the day.
According to the Kragujevac Police Department, a 17-year-old fourth-year student, identified by his initials V.M., brought a small-caliber rifle into the building and fired a shot towards the security reception desk.
A 50-year-old maintenance worker was struck in the leg, while another employee sustained leg injuries from shattered glass. Both victims were women and sustained lower limb injuries. After being treated in intensive care, they are now in a stable condition and out of danger.
A police patrol stationed nearby responded immediately, disarming and arresting the teenager while students and teachers were safely evacuated.
A juvenile judge at the Higher Court in Kragujevac ordered a 30-day detention for the suspect. The Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has charged him with attempted aggravated murder and illegal possession and carrying of firearms. His father was also arrested on suspicion of keeping the rifle at home without a permit.
The school’s head teacher Nemanja Joksimovic and graduating students described the suspect as quiet, with no history of disciplinary issues.
Following the event, the school shortened class schedules and deployed counsellors and psychologists.
What do we know about the suspect’s social media activity?
The photo of the suspect holding a rifle posted hours prior to the shooting has raised questions about online vigilance.
Nedzad Korajlic, a professor of criminology and safety studies at CEPS Kiseljak, said if other students see posts like this, they should immediately inform a parent, teacher, or trusted adult. In cases of a specific threat or immediate danger, the post should be saved and reported to the police and school leadership immediately, rather than forwarded across group chats, he said.
Korajlic added that adolescents often dismiss such posts as posturing or simply do not know who to contact. For that reason, schools must establish clear, confidential reporting protocols so students know exactly where to turn and what will happen next, he said.
What measures can be taken to prevent further attacks?
In response to previous attacks, governments across the Western Balkans have introduced school police officers, tightened entry controls, and installed security cameras.
However, Korajlic said prevention is key.
Schools should assign a designated safety officer and staff to evaluate reports. Law enforcement should be notified immediately if firearms or explicit threats are involved, with social and health services joining efforts as needed, he said.
The Kragujevac attack highlights the broader issue of widespread civilian firearm ownership in the region due to the availability of legal weapons and unregistered arms remaining from the 1990s Yugoslav wars.
Korajlic stressed that weapon storage regulations must be strictly enforced, meaning firearms must be locked away, ammunition kept separately, and keys or codes strictly inaccessible to minors.
Psychologist Goran Tomin told Serbia’s Beta news agency that shootings traumatise school communities, noting that institutional responses and sentencing policies are often too lenient. There is a high tolerance for violence in public discourse and the media, he said, while school counsellors are frequently overburdened with administrative work.
Following the attack, public officials pointed to digital content.
Zarko Micin, a mayor and politician, promised heightened security in local schools while singling out video games, as he urged parents to monitor media consumption.
But Korajlic cautioned against reducing complex incidents to cases of media consumption, noting that simply playing a violent video game tells us very little about a person’s real-world behaviour without analysing specific motives, context, and explicit threats.
Where else have shootings taken place in the Balkans?
Several shootings have shaken schools in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia over the past three years.
The worst incident occurred in May 2023 at the Vladislav Ribnikar Elementary School in Belgrade. A 13-year-old student used his father’s handgun to kill nine classmates and a security guard, while wounding a teacher and five other students. Because he was under the legal age of criminal responsibility, he was placed in a psychiatric facility, while his father was sentenced to 14-and-a-half years in prison and his mother to three years.
Weeks later, a former student entered Lukavac Grad Elementary School in Bosnia with a firearm, critically wounding an English teacher. The suspect was sentenced to detention in a juvenile correctional facility, while his father was prosecuted for illegal weapon possession and child neglect.
In August 2024, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a school custodian armed with an automatic rifle killed three staff, including the head teacher. He then attempted suicide at the Sanski Most Mixed Secondary School but survived. The 61-year-old suspect was indicted for triple murder and illegal weapons possession.

Let's recap what happened on Sunday.

items.text:
Confusion and anger - Yoro red card rescinded, but row goes on
- Published
Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.
Let's recap what happened on Sunday.
Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.
Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.
It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?
Then came the events of Tuesday.
First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.
Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb said the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.
Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.
But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?
BBC Sport looks at how the system works.
The stand-off between Man Utd and Pro Ref
So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?
"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.
It continued a theme from his post-match news conference.
You can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?
You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.
The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.
As for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.
What about Webb's reaction?
It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.
Would that change his opinion? Almost certainly not.
Webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.
So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?
The VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.
It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.
Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.
It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.
But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.
How can Pro Ref still say it is right?
How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.
An FA regulatory commission has said the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.
Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.
And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.
Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.
The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.
But surely the FA is the higher body? Not quite.
The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.
If the Premier League tells Pro Ref the decision is right or wrong, that counts far more than any vote by an FA commission.
So how did United make their case?
BBC Sport understands the club argued that if Isak had maintained his top recorded speed, he would not have got to the ball first.
The club say that is objectively provable, within minutes, using data. This, they say, was not a subjective decision.
To argue it was not subjective goes completely against the nature of the decision - it required a referee's judgement.
Whatever this data was, it most definitely was not available to the referees. The VAR cannot call upon a 3D animation of each player, detailing their running speed and providing an objective result.
How much stock did the commission place on this evidence? We will not know until the written reasons are published in a few days' time.
But United are not going to let this lie, and Pro Ref is not going to bend.
The unpredictability of FA commissions
Such is the way FA commissions work, you can never be sure who will win.
There are three panel members who are usually former players, but occasionally you might get a retired referee.
The role of the commission is not to "usurp the referee by re-refereeing the incident".
A designated referee delegate is present to answer questions on the laws of the game, but they cannot offer an opinion on the incident.
The only input Pro Ref has is the official's report - a short entry by the referee that says which law was used for the red card. There is no other context.
It will read something like this: "I have to report that I, as the referee, sent off Yoro, Leny of Manchester United FC Under Law 12 section: S5."
The burden is on the club to prove its case by submitting a body of evidence - videos, images and testimony.
There is no right of reply. The evidence is weighed up by the panel, a vote is cast and the majority wins.
It makes predicting the outcome notoriously difficult, as the system is an opinion poll based upon a club trying to persuade at least two p

The Foxes we
items.text:
Leicester no longer for sale as owner refocuses on future
- Published
Leicester City owner Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha has confirmed the one-time Premier League title winners are no longer up for sale and there will be a "refocus" on rebuilding the side after years of decline.
The Foxes were put on the market in the summer after back-to-back relegations saw the side drop from the Premier League and straight through the Championship to land in England's third tier for just the second time in the club's 142-year history.
A sales brochure was produced by US investment bank Citigroup in which an asking price of more than £200m was put on a League One club that a decade ago had defied all expectations by winning the Premier League title at 5,000-1 odds.
Leicester never publicly acknowledged that the club had been put up for sale, with under-fire chief football officer Jon Rudkin going so far as to say he "cannot comment on speculation" when asked about it in a rare interview with BBC Radio Leicester in October.
Khun Top, however, has now said that there were no takers when investment had been sought for a side that the Srivaddhanaprabha family, through its King Power duty free business in Thailand, have owned for 16 years.
"We recently undertook a structured process to explore whether new investment or a change of ownership could actually be the right thing for the club," Khun Top wrote in an open letter to Leicester City supporters on the club's website., external
"Those discussions have not resulted in an agreement, and I have decided to conclude the process to enable us to refocus on the work needed to move the club forward."
Follow Leicester City on BBC Sounds
Pre-match, post-match and topical Foxes content
Subscribe and listen for everything you love about Leicester City
Three relegations in four years, having yo-yoed between the Premier League and Championship before going down to League One, has badly damaged the relationship between the Foxes' owners and their supporter base.
While a golden age of success was bankrolled by King Power, with Premier League glory in 2016 followed up by FA Cup success in 2021, high spending on an underperforming side in recent years has led to an increasing number of supporters calling for Khun Top to sell up.
But the Thai businessman said he has a "deep connection" to Leicester and "its people".
And it is not just euphoric sporting moments that have forged the bond he is talking about, as his father - and predecessor as Foxes chairman - Khun Vichai died in a helicopter crash outside the stadium in 2018.
"For my family and me, Leicester City has been a big part of our lives for many years," he said.
"We have experienced extraordinary moments together, as well as some very difficult ones."
Khun Top added that the struggles of recent years, which included the club being hit with a points penalty last season for breaking spending rules, has got him "thinking a lot about our direction".
Earlier this year he told BBC Radio Leicester that he shoulders the blame for the club's decline.
"Making better decisions" as well as "continuing to learn from our past experiences" are two steps the club "need to take", he said.
Khun Top has insisted that through King Power, a company that has endured difficulties in recent years, the club's "financial position remains secure".
However, he added that there was "work needed to put Leicester City on a more sustainable footing".
"That has been a principle behind the work and decisions of the last year – giving the club the appropriate support for its immediate circumstances, while building the organisational discipline and financial resilience that will underpin a responsible plan for future growth," he said.
As part of Khun Top's missive, he confirmed that chief executive Kevin Davies will be stepping down from the role in December.
Davies had only been in the job since March, and was promoted to the position after a shake-up of a number of leadership roles.

Williams in minor breach of F1 cost cap and take financial and wind tunnel time penalties
watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
Wednesday 25 November 2026 16:33, UK
Williams have reached an "Accepted Breach Agreement" with the FIA in terms of F1's cost cap, receiving financial and wind tunnel time penalties.
"The FIA has determined that the team committed a minor overspend breach and an accompanying procedural breach, unintentionally exceeding the cap by £627,000 - 0.48 per cent over the 2025 cost cap," a Williams statement read.
"The agreed outcome is a financial penalty and a 1.5 per cent reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.
"The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.
"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.
"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future.
"We have always been and will continue to be strong supporters of the cost cap, which naturally requires accurate policing to be effective."

items.title: €561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink
items.summary:
Germany's record budget exposes a coalition on the brink

At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming yea
items.text:
Germany's record budget exposes a coalition on the brink
November 25, 2026
At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming year, and on what. These follow a familiar pattern: The government pats itself on the back, while the opposition voices criticism. But anyone listening more closely will notice that there are doubts even in the ranks of the coalition parties, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), their Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).
"As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.
"If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.
This government has now been in office for about 20 months. Back in early 2025, expectations were enormous. Merz had promised to bring the budget back in line with the debt brake enshrined in the constitution, which stipulates that the government can spend only slightly more than it collects (with exceptions now made for defense and security).
Yet for 2027, spending — at just under €561 billion ($614 billion) — will be higher than ever before, and tax revenues are nowhere near sufficient to cover this, meaning Germany is looking at a record debt totaling €210 billion.
The largest opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) calculated that the government will incur €401,000 in new debt every minute next year. In the Bundestag, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called it a "debt orgy" that will paralyze the country. Merz will "go down in history as the chancellor who led Germany to bankruptcy," he exclaimed.
Record spending and record debt
Germany's debt has only ever been higher in the COVID-19 pandemic. The current pressures are obvious: The economy is struggling, the population aging, and Russia's war against Ukraine is about to enter its sixth year.
The defense budget is now by far the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, with €109 billion allocated for 2027, an increase of €27 billion on last year. Added to this is the multi-year, debt-financed special military fund, intended to modernize the armed forces, bringing the total defense budget to €139 billion.
Defense spending rises to historic levels
The AfD and the socialist Left Party have sharply criticized this. Left Party parliamentary leader Heidi Reichinnek accused the government of pursuing "militarization and boundless rearmament on the one hand, and brutal social cuts and an orgy of budget cuts on the other."
The AfD's Chrupalla said that the temporary reduction in the electricity tax, pushed through at the last minute, would save the average family a mere €100 a year, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "walks out of the chancellery here in Berlin with a check for €200 million after just one afternoon."
"Whose chancellor are you, Mr. Merz?" he asked.
The opposition Greens did not agree. While they also criticized the budget as "unserious," Green Party Bundestag member Britta Haßelmann described the AfD's stance on Ukraine as shameful. She rejected the idea that money was being wasted on Ukraine, saying that supporting Ukraine bolstered security for Germany and Europe.
Aid to Ukraine: Still a central controversy
The chancellor shares this view. "You can't say it often enough, either to the far right or the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than just Ukraine," Merz said.
He added that Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and in space; and that Moscow is also seeking escalation in Germany, even at the cost of lives. "That is why we must show Russia its limits," he said.
But it is becoming increasingly difficult for the government to justify the high spending on Ukraine. Germany's pension and health care costs are only getting bigger: By far the largest single budget item is that of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is rising to over €200 billion, even with cuts to unemployment benefits. 
Social spending growing faster than revenue
Work is currently underway on a reform of the pension system — something that many see as urgent, as the workforce born in the 1960s, when more than a million children were born in Germany every year, is on brink of retiring. Birth rates nearly halved by the mid-1970s and declined even further afterward. For now, so-called "boomers" still make up one-third of the current workforce — but soon they will be drawing pensions.
Even now, Germany's pensions cannot be financed solely with contributions on wages and salaries. In 2025, just over €420 billion in pensions were paid out, with the government contributing €127 billion of that amount. By 2027, the government aims to save €3 billion on this figure, which is likely to further increase pension contributions.
Pension reform becomes a test for the coalition
The coalition parties are stuck in a row over how to reform the pension system. Chancellor Merz insisted in the Bundestag that the coalition was solving the country's fundamental problems, but he warned that in future, tax revenues "will no longer be enough to afford everything we have become all too accustomed to," he said. "All of us here will have to give up some of the ideas we cherish."

items.text:
Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.
Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations.
Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”
As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.
The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

items.text:
Senegal deny Morocco’s allegations of ‘contact’ with CAS amid AFCON row
The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
The president of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF), Abdoulaye Fall, has denied Moroccan allegations that he had “contact” with a Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) arbitrator who ruled that Senegal were the rightful winners of the 2025 African Cup of Nations.
The Moroccan federation (FRMF) alleged after Tuesday’s ruling there had been “contact” between Fall and German arbitrator Ulrich Haas, one of the three CAS panel members, 48 hours before they decided “unanimously” to award the trophy to Senegal.
“That is absolutely false. I have never had any exchange with any member of CAS,” said Fall on private television channel TFM on Wednesday.
“It surprised and astonished me that such accusations could even be made. I have never been in contact with anyone in connection with this procedure.”
In January, Senegal won a chaotic final 1-0 after extra-time.
But two months later, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) sensationally overturned the result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title, after many Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty given to the hosts with the game still goalless.
The CAF Appeals Committee had justified its decision to overturn the result and declare Morocco champions based on Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations.
Those state that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered [loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
However, the Senegal players eventually returned to the pitch and the final carried on.
The three-person CAS panel therefore considered the referee’s decision to restart the final showed “the conditions for resuming the match had been met”, and that articles 82 and 84 were therefore “not applicable in this case”.
The Moroccan federation has the option of lodging an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court, which does not rule on the merits of the case, but intervenes in procedural matters.

Anita Verma-Lallian
items.text:
Nvidia has made clear it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck.
Anita Verma-Lallian has been selling exactly that. Her company, Arizona Land Consulting, assembles data center sites for developers, hyperscalers, AI labs, and neoclouds, giving her a view into who’s buying, what makes a site viable, and where projects are running into trouble. She also partners with investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who has been predicting an industry shakeout.
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Verma-Lallian about who bears the risk when Nvidia gets pickier, why speculative projects could be the first to fall apart, and what a 2027 shakeout might look like.
Listen to the full episode to hear more about:
- What “land, power, shell” means, and why having all three could give some developers a major advantage.
- How community opposition and state-level restrictions are making some markets harder to build in than others.
- Utilities getting major customers like TSMC to help fund the infrastructure needed to deliver more power.
- Who gets stuck with the bill when a data center project stalls, from developers to lenders to customers.
- Why AI labs and hyperscalers might increasingly build their own data centers instead of relying on neoclouds.
- Who could benefit from a 2027 shakeout, including the companies best positioned to acquire distressed projects.
Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify, and all the casts. You can also follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

items.title: Saudi Arabia’s PIF looking to sell 25% of Newcastle through share issue
items.summary:
Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is looking to sell up to 25% of the club by issuing new shares.
The New York-based bank JP Morgan, whose most recent involvement in a major football deal was Fifa’s aborted attempt to sell off 20% of its commercial rights last su
items.text:
Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is looking to sell up to 25% of the club by issuing new shares.
The New York-based bank JP Morgan, whose most recent involvement in a major football deal was Fifa’s aborted attempt to sell off 20% of its commercial rights last summer, has been appointed to handle the sale, as first reported by the Athletic.
PIF is seeking investment partners to help fund major infrastructure projects, such as building a new stadium or redeveloping St James’ Park, and would dilute its shareholding rather than profiting from the proceeds of the share issue.
The state-owned fund owns 84% of Newcastle after the departure of the minority shareholder Amanda Staveley two years ago, with the remaining 16% owned by the London-based Reuben brothers.
Newcastle are the second Premier League club to formally seek investment this season, after Everton’s owners appointed the US bank Moelis & Company to handle their sale process last month. Last summer Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, sold 38% of the club to a consortium which includes the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.
PIF sources insist they retain a long-term commitment to Newcastle, whose value has soared since they bought the club from Mike Ashley for £305m four years ago in a deal that has not proved as transformative for their fortunes as many expected.
Newcastle qualified for the Champions League twice under Eddie Howe, who also led the club to their first domestic trophy for 70 years by winning the Carabao Cup in 2025, but the Premier League’s spending rules have prevented the owners from investing as heavily as the competition’s other state-owned club, Manchester City.
PIF has also cut back its spending on sport generally, with the Newcastle share issue coming months after the fund withdrew its support for LIV Golf, which filed for bankruptcy this month.
PIF has also sold a stake in the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal, is open to selling other clubs, and has withdrawn from a three-year deal to host the Women’s Tennis Association finals 12 months early.
Newcastle has been wrestling for several years with the issue of whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new stadium on an adjacent site, but have made clear a project on that scale would require external funding.
Newcastle declined to comment.

EU must set out a new timeline for cage-free farming, court rules

A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a new timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.
Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge t
items.text:
EU must set out a new timeline for cage-free farming, court rules
November 25, 2026
A European Union (EU) court told the bloc on Wednesday to draw a new timeline for plans to ban cages for farm animals.
Judges at the European General Court ruled that the EU has failed to follow through on a pledge to ban the practice.
In 2021, the European Commission set out the goal to pass a legislation by the end of 2023 to stop farmers from cooping hens, rabbits, sows and other animals in cages. The move came after 1,4 million people signed a petition.
But it failed to follow up on the pledge. This resulted in the campaigners requesting a new timeline and eventually led to a court case when that was also not happening.
The Luxembourg-based General Court, the European Union's second-highest, on Wednesday ruled in favor of the animal rights campaigners.
"The Commission is under an obligation — which is not limited in time — to set out a timeline for all the measures which it intends to take in response to such an initiative," the court said.
According to the "European citizens' initiative" system, the Commission has to receive the petitions that gather over one million signatures across at least seven bloc countries. However, it is not obligated to meet the demands.
The court noted that if the Commission decides to take action, it has to keep the public and the European Parliament posted on a timeline in accordance with the principle of "good administration."
About 143 million chickens are kept in cages in EU
The Commission said it was analyzing the ruling before making a decision. It can still appeal the ruling.
It has previously stated an intention to put forward a proposal for the phased elimination of cage systems for chickens by the end of this year, as well as a separate proposal to transition from farrowing crates to pen-based systems for pigs by 2027.
According to the Albert Schweitzer Foundation, no timetable has been set for calves, rabbits, ducks, geese and quail.
In the EU, about 143 million egg-laying chickens are kept in cages while the majority of female pigs spend at least part of their lives caged.
The use of cage systems in agricultural production accredited as "organic" is already prohibited in the EU.

items.title: South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
items.summary:
South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
The ruling hands the president a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a court bid challenging an independent panel’s report tha
items.text:
South Africa court repeals ‘farmgate’ impeachment threat against Ramaphosa
The ruling hands the president a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has won a court bid challenging an independent panel’s report that had paved the way for his possible impeachment over misconduct allegations linked to a burglary-turned-political scandal called “Farmgate”.
The Western Cape High Court on Wednesday declared unlawful the 2022 findings of an independent parliamentary panel that accused Ramaphosa of a conflict of interest over the origin of large amounts of cash stolen from a sofa at his ranch in 2020.
The ruling hands Ramaphosa a political reprieve by removing a finding that had exposed him to possible impeachment at a vulnerable moment for him and his African National Congress (ANC) party.
“The court found that the panel fundamentally misconstrued its functions,” Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said, reading the court’s unanimous decision.
“The ‌panel went beyond its lawful remit, asked itself wrong questions and made several material errors of law.”
Ramaphosa “notes” and “will study” the court’s judgement relating to his Phala Phala game farm, the president’s office said in a statement.
“In seeking the judicial review, President Ramaphosa exercised a constitutional right,” the statement read. “In line with his respect for the rule of law including judicial independence, President Ramaphosa will study the decision of the court.”
The theft came to light after a former intelligence boss reported to the police that Ramaphosa had allegedly sought to cover up a theft of millions of US dollars in cash at his farm, initially claiming it was about $4m.
Ramaphosa has always denied wrongdoing and said the $580,000 stolen at his farm was money from the sale of buffaloes.
But the episode raised questions about why he had so much cash stuffed in furniture.
The 2022 report said the president failed to report the theft through proper channels, violated the constitution regarding paid work from his farm and directed presidential security to do police work.
The African Transformation Movement party, which is in favour of Ramaphosa’s impeachment, criticised the ruling.
Embarrassing saga
The matter has been embarrassing for a leader who came to power promising to fight corruption and clean up the image of the former liberation movement.
The ANC won about 31 percent of the vote in this month’s local elections, its worst-ever such result, extending a decline that saw it lose its national parliamentary majority in 2024 for the first time since the end of apartheid and beginning of democracy.
The Constitutional Court revived impeachment proceedings against the president in May.
It found that a 2022 parliamentary vote to stop the process was invalid and parliament should set up an impeachment inquiry.
The Western Cape High Court in July temporarily halted the inquiry pending the outcome of Wednesday’s ruling.
Ramaphosa, 74, has been head of state since 2018, and his second presidential ‌term ‌is to end in 2029. The ANC is due to elect its next leader next year when Ramaphosa will step down after two five-year terms as party leader.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia relieved to not be arrested after US court hearing
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national whose wrongful deportation
items.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, wrongfully deported from US, arrives in Spain
The Salvadoran national’s lawyer said in a statement that it was ‘a temporary departure’.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia relieved to not be arrested after US court hearing
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador drew sharp criticism of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has arrived in Spain.
Abrego Garcia did not speak to reporters as he arrived at Madrid’s main international airport on Wednesday, but raised a fist as he climbed into a van.
He voluntarily departed the US a day earlier after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials. A judge had told him to self-deport by Tuesday, The Associated Press news agency reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.
In a post on X, the DHS said: “It’s not surprising this criminal illegal alien would choose to go to Spain, a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens … Good riddance.”
Abrego Garcia’s lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as “a temporary departure”.
“Mr Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration,” he said in a statement.
Sandoval-Moshenberg noted the US government had sought to deport Garcia “in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia”.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, the state where Abrego Garcia lived with his family for around a decade before being deported, said the Trump administration “was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will.”
The departure of Abrego Garcia, 31, brings an end to a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Abrego Garcia in Baltimore in March 2025. He was then transferred to a megaprison in El Salvador despite a prior court order barring him from being sent to the country because of the risk of persecution.
A US official later called the transfer an “administrative error”.
After the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate Garcia’s return, prosecutors secured a criminal indictment charging him with human smuggling in a case stemming from an earlier incident. The Trump administration then brought him back to the US in June 2025. It later tried to deport him to Liberia after a US judge dismissed the human smuggling charge.

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula has ordered a review of CCTV footage capturing a dramatic confrontation in Parliament following the disappearance of a phone belonging to nominated MP Sabina Chege during a 2023 incident.
Wetang’ula said he would appoint another MP t
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula has ordered a review of CCTV footage capturing a dramatic confrontation in Parliament following the disappearance of a phone belonging to nominated MP Sabina Chege during a 2023 incident.
Wetang’ula said he would appoint another MP to chair the committee reviewing the footage, despite being its substantive chairperson, to ensure the process is handled appropriately.
The Speaker announced that he would recuse himself from the review amid renewed attention surrounding the incident, which involved several female MPs confronting him during parliamentary proceedings.
“As your Speaker, I will take the following action. Although I am the Chairperson of the Powers and Privileges Committee, I will recuse myself from chairing this matter. I will forward the CCTV footage to the Committee and appoint another Member to act on my behalf, review the footage and present a report to this House,” Wetangula stated.
Nominated MP Sabina Chege said she realised her phone was missing when her colleague, Rosa Buyu, who had come to her rescue, picked up her handbag.
“That phone was an iPhone 16, Mr Speaker. I had just bought it. It was actually one week old,” Chege said.
The second term legislator narrated how she refused to leave the precincts of Parliament without her phone.
It took assurances by officers from the Sergeant-at-Arms that her phone could not get lost within Parliament Debating Chamber and urged her to seek medical attention first.
“When I got to Nairobi Hospital, we tracked her phone and established that it was still within Parliament. An hour later, its location had changed to an area near Bunge Towers and Protection House,” Chege told the House.
She confirmed that the phone was finally tracked to Nairobi’s Donholm area. Chege stunned her colleagues as she confirmed she is yet recover her phone.
“Please name the person and, at the least, my phone should be returned, Mr Speaker,” Chege appealed.

items.text:
Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
November 25, 2026
Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.
The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.
The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.
To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.
However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.
These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.
Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."
"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.
At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.
"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI
Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."
He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.
Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.
He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.
Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.
Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.
However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

items.title: Football Daily | Manchester City get that empty feeling as they fail to win again
items.summary:
SILENT NIGHT
Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud n
items.text:
SILENT NIGHT
Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners.
At the same time around 420km north of Devon, the players of Manchester City and Napoli were playing out a 2-2 draw in comparative silence, as an eerily quiet home crowd watched their once all-conquering side extend their winless run to five matches and fail to keep a clean sheet for the 10th game in a row. While it is fair to say their performance against the Italian side was significantly better than the shift they put in against Fulham on Saturday, the bar is currently so low that even a snake would struggle to limbo beneath it. “Football is easy and difficult,” sighed Erling Haaland, who looked mightily fed up at having gone three consecutive City games without scoring a goal. “When you win it’s easy and you know what to do. When you don’t you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it’s not so easy.”
His teammate Rayan Cherki, who scored City’s equaliser with one of his trademark soft-shoe shuffles, was considerably less equanimous. “I don’t care about my goal,” he harrumphed at his inquisitor. “I wanted to win the game. Sometimes the game is not like you want and today is like the last game, the last two or three games. We need to work more and come back for a win, just that.” Dressed in what looked like an American prison issue-style orange fourth strip their club introduced as “a special edition kit in collaboration with Puma and CP Company”, the duo cut disconsolate figures before being led away to await whatever sentence is handed down to their club on the back of those guilty verdicts for breaching Premier League rules, though the club is appealing.
With money tight and the weather baltic, it was no surprise there were plenty of midweek no-shows and the sheer volume of unsold tickets did not go unnoticed by gleeful online Etihad Stadium seat scrutineers. Large sections of the stadium’s upper tier were left unopened on a night the fans who did turn up reserved their loudest cheers and a bespoke tifo for their returning hero Kevin De Bruyne. It suggested the Belgium midfielder is more popular at his former club than the one he now plays for. Before the match, De Bruyne said his feelings for City “will never change” even if they end up being stripped of all the Premier League titles he won with them. Given his apparent dissatisfaction at Napoli and rumours of a January exit, the 35-year-old could always re-sign for City and play out his dotage in the noisy surroundings of the North West Counties League.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
The Bigger Cup action continues this evening: Rob Smyth brings you live updates on Sporting 1-1 Manchester United at 8pm GMT, while at the same time Simon Burnton will be following Club Brugge 0-2 Liverpool and the rest of the night’s action at the same in his clockwatch.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“I can see the team is in a difficult moment but I have already watched many of the games over the last few days and I’m very confident about the future” – Edward Iordanescu is the latest man to be given a crack at the Watford job. He’s their sixth head coach in less than 18 months and the 25th since the Pozzo family took control of the Hornets in 2012. That is more than Liverpool have had in their entire history dating back to 1892.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 In this constantly changing world of global disruptions, uncertainties and risks, with social, political and economic disaffection seemingly on the rise everywhere, it’s genuinely heartening to know that some things never change. ‘Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose’, as the late, great French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr famously said, something that I’m sure Big Dunc is well aware of” – Noble Francis.
 May I be the 1,092nd correspondent to demand a review of the Letter o’ the Day award for Monday – and it be awarded to Declan Hackett for his letter foretelling the rescinding of the red card given to Lenny Yoro on Sunday? Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Rollover. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

More than 1.5 tonnes of the highly addictive synthetic drug, commonly known as meth, was seized from the facility in the south-eastern state of Enugu. The haul included both finished drugs and meth still being produced.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) estimates the drugs are worth $2267m (£1723m).
It is the fourth industrial-scale meth laboratory with alleged links to Mexican drug cartels to have been discovered in Nigeria in recent months.
The Nigerian businessman, 63-year-old Chuks Enoch Ezeike, also known as "Over Size", is accused of setting up the laboratory and smuggling the five Mexicans into the country using forged Argentine, Colombian and Chilean passports.
The NDLEA identified the five as Oscar Ramos-Cardenas, who it described as the alleged leader of the group, Juan Antonio Sarabia-Cabrera, Luis Enrique Garcia-Amador, Jose Alejandro Renteria-Reyes and Salomon Cabanillas-Torres.
The laboratory, situated behind an oil company in Enugu, also had accommodation for the Mexican nationals, allowing them to live and work there without attracting attention, the agency said.
Speaking at a news conference in the capital, Abuja, on Wednesday, NDLEA chief Mohamed Buba Marwa said the arrests followed a seven-month investigation involving several countries.
The agency had been monitoring Ezeike since April, when it received intelligence allegedly linking him to Ramos-Cardenas, a Mexican national suspected of specialising in large-scale meth production.
In August, the five Mexicans were refused entry into Nigeria after arriving at Abuja's international airport and were sent back to Mexico.
But less than a month later, they tried again, travelling through Colombia and France before arriving in neighbouring Benin, where they were allegedly given forged passports.
This time, Nigerian authorities deliberately allowed them into the country, Marwa said.
"We wanted the whole network: the meth specialist, the financier, the factory and the product. Sending them home a second time would only have postponed the problem," he said.
The men were allegedly met by Ezeike in Lagos before being taken to Enugu, where they were kept under surveillance.
More than 200 anti-narcotics officers were deployed on 11 November to raid the laboratory and a hotel where Ezeike was staying in simultaneous operations.
The five Mexicans were arrested while producing the drug, the agency said. Ezeike told investigators they had been due to leave Nigeria two days later.
Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth, as well as industrial equipment, were also seized.
The NDLEA said Ezeike had admitted owning the laboratory and bringing the Mexican nationals into Nigeria to produce the drug.
Investigators believe the operation was part of a wider international criminal network in which a Mexican cartel recruited and paid specialists to manufacture meth, while Nigerian collaborators allegedly provided the facilities and resources.
The agency has not identified the Mexican cartel it suspects was involved or said whether the six suspects have been formally charged.
The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa, a region long used as a transit route for illicit drugs.
While some of the meth produced in the region supplies a growing local market, traffickers also target lucrative overseas markets, particularly in Europe and Asia.
Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states.
The latest operation brings to 10 the number of suspected Mexican meth production specialists arrested in Nigeria in recent months, according to the NDLEA. Five others arrested in earlier operations are already in custody awaiting trial.
Issuing a warning to foreign drug cartels, Marwa said: "Nigeria is not your laboratory. It is not your warehouse, and it is not your transit route."
