items.text:
US Army detonates unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa
November 25, 2026
The United States Army detonated about 5 tons of aging lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday, saying the explosive chemical has become too unstable to store.
The controlled blast occurred a little after 9 a.m. local time (1500 GMT) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, and will destroy the country's entire stockpile of the chemical.
The US Army has said residents of a small town and other nearby areas should leave "out of an abundance of caution."
"We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic," said acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling."
What do we know?
The material was moved to Iowa for storage from bases around the country in 2009.
But a March inspection found that it had partly crystallized, which makes it sensitive to friction and cold and could set off a spontaneous explosion.
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Major General Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.
Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, told reporters: "It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."
Is it safe to detonate the chemical?
To limit toxic lead dust, the Army has built barriers around the bunkers holding the material and will use foam and water to trap particles.
Reuters reported that Army projections show dust could settle up to 40 miles (64 km) southwest, reaching northern Missouri.
Officials expect the wind to carry the plume away from Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people.
While residents within 5 miles (8 kilometers) were encouraged to evacuate, the Federal Emergency Management Agency has also advised people 5 to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed.
How have people reacted?
The date of the detonation changed three times after public backlash. A federal appeals court cleared the plan on Monday after environmental groups sued.
Farmer Jill Holler, who organized a protest, told Reuters: "I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option."
"What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying," she added.

items.summary:
St Helens coach Kevin Walters insists he can win a trophy in his first season in charge and wants to restore team's winning DNA
New St Helens coach Kevin Walters has pinpointed where he believes things may have gone wrong for the club in 2026; St Helens missed the Super League play-offs for the firs
items.text:
St Helens coach Kevin Walters insists he can win a trophy in his first season in charge and wants to restore team's winning DNA
New St Helens coach Kevin Walters has pinpointed where he believes things may have gone wrong for the club in 2026; St Helens missed the Super League play-offs for the first time in the club's history; Walters put pen to paper on a three-year deal in August
Wednesday 25 November 2026 15:13, UK
Kevin Walters believes he can win a trophy with St Helens in his first season in charge, as the side's new head coach set out his ambition to restore the team's "winning DNA".
After guiding Australia to their fourth consecutive Rugby League World Cup success earlier this month, the former Brisbane Broncos boss has been tasked with galvanising the Saints following an underwhelming season that saw them slump to seventh in Super League and miss the play-offs for the first time in the club's history.
The 59-year-old, who put pen to paper on a three-year deal with the Saints in August, is confident he can restore the club to where it belongs and added St Helens are "not in as bad a position as some people may think".
Asked by Sky Sports Rugby League's Jenna Brooks whether he can win silverware in his first season, Walters said: "If I say no to that question, I look like a loser. I'm not a loser. I love winning.
"So I'm going to answer that positively and say yeah, I believe we can have great success here.
"It starts early; the pressure is on. I've been at big clubs and I understand the pressure that comes with it. I understand there's a lot of pressure on myself and the club to do well. But I'm confident we can do really well.
"Pressure is a privilege, isn't it? I wouldn't be in the role if I didn't [have that] understanding. There's always pressure in professional sport, particularly in rugby league - in Australia and here in the Super League. It's a big sport in the north.
"Everyone knows about St Helens and their success, and we need to get them back to where they belong."
It was a turbulent season for the 10-time Super League Grand Final winners, who suffered a swathe of injuries to key players, including Matty Lees and Jack Welsby, which contributed to their disappointing form.
St Helens also underwent some major coaching upheavals, with head coach Paul Rowley departing in May, less than a year into his three-year contract, before Eamon O'Carroll took over on an interim basis.
Club chiefs then turned to Walters, one of rugby league's most distinguished coaches. It will mark the first time the 59-year-old has taken up a full-time coaching role since he was sacked by the Brisbane Broncos in September 2024.
Walters reveals why he's the man for the job
Walters, who arrived in the United Kingdom on Monday and has already led a few training sessions with his new team, pinpoints a loss of connection between his players and fans as one of the side's biggest issues.
"It's hard to judge from afar. I've been speaking to people in the club; the connection between the team and the community is one thing that has been lost a little bit," Walters said.
"The Saints fans, from what I've seen and been told, are very passionate about their club. The English fans, across all of the teams, their passion is a little bit different to the Australian fans, who are probably not as vocal in their support, but also in their care for the side.
"I know there were some things that did go wrong; maybe the connection among the players was lost a little bit as well."
Walters, who also spearheaded Melbourne Storm's 2012 NRL Grand Final win, and won back-to-back State of Origin series as Queensland head coach in 2016 and 2017, believes he is the right man to solve that connectivity issue.
"One of my great strengths as a coach is my ability to bring people together for a common cause, and that's what I feel coaching is. Lots of things go into coaching; my ability to bring players and teams together, that's where I feel my big strength is.
"If I can do that here… well, I will do that here and then we'll see where that takes us."
He added: "Without making too many bold predictions, we're going to be hard to beat. That's the mainstay for me. Defensively, we've spoken to our players about getting better in that space.
"The last time Saints won the premiership in 2022, it was based on defence. We have to make sure we have a strong defensive team that's well connected and then when we get the ball, we're going to play some footy.
"The best defensive teams are there where it matters."
'Sailor has a future at St Helens'
Reports have suggested that Tristan Sailor is being eyed up as a potential target for multiple other Super League clubs.
The full-back, who previously played under Walters at the Broncos, joined the Saints in August 2024 and has gone on to make 54 appearances for the club.
While Welsby is favoured to lock down the No 1 jumper for St Helens, Walters insisted Sailor still has a future at the club.
"There's a lot of noise around the whole group and Tristan has been caught up in that," Walters said. "I believe Tristan's got a lot to offer this club still.
"He's been a great player here. I coached him at the Broncos and unfortunately Reece Walsh was parked in front of him in that role at full-back.
"He's come here in a different role, but I feel Tristan... whatever position he plays - he was good playing full-back, centre, five-eighth, he might have played some wing. Mr Versatility but also a very good team person."

items.text:
Ukraine: Poland to create no-fly zone near Ukraine border
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- Poland hopes to establish a no-fly zone near its border with Ukraine by the end of the year
- Russia attacks have halted output at Ukrainian gas facilities as well as a thermal power plant
- Ukraine says it attacked Russian oil facilities in the Samara region
- France's foreign minister defended Ukraine's attacks on Russian shadow fleet ships off the Libyan coast, though Italy's called the attack 'a mistake'
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned against ending Ukraine support, saying 'Russia wants more than Ukraine'
Keep reading for the latest news in Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, November 25:
Poland to create no-fly zone at Ukraine border, urges others to do same
Poland's Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told reporters that Warsaw will set up a no-fly zone inside its border with Ukraine and suggested other regional allies do the same in the wake of repeated Russian incursions into NATO airspace as part of Moscow's war of aggression.
"An ordinance is already being prepared by the government and should enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January," said Tomczyk.
"We will also urge our allies — the entire NATO alliance — to establish such a principle along the eastern flank," he continued, "Poland was a pioneer in this regard, ‌and the Baltic states have since followed our lead."
Poland strictly limits air traffic at its border already.
On Wednesday, Tomczyk said the proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory from the border and provide added support for Poland's armed forces.
Merz defends Ukraine aid, says those opposed are lost or have other aims
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended his government's expenditures on Ukraine aid during a budget debate in the Bundestag on Wednesday.
Merz tackled criticism from opposition parties on the left and right head on, saying "Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine."
"Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea. Russia is escalating ‌in space. And Russia is now escalating massively here, in our own country, too, even at the risk of loss of life," he added.
Merz said, "anyone who doesn't see that, doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims."
The Left Party and Alternative for Germany (AfD) have both called for an end to Ukraine aid and better relations with Moscow.
Among other things, Germany blames Russia for an explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport this summer as well as cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace incursions across the EU and NATO.
Merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself.
"We are learning from Ukraine," said Merz, "technologically for civilian use but of course also in defense technology."
Moscow, Kyiv exchange overnight attacks on energy infrastructure
Kyiv and Moscow both assessed damage to energy infrastructure on Wednesday morning as both sides continued to inflict damage on one another amid Russia's over four-and-a-half-year attempted invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in.
Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations.
Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks.
In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts.
France, Italy offer different takes on Ukraine's actions in Libya
Kyiv's attacks on Russian ships in and off the coast of Libya over the past couple of days have ruffled feathers among Ukraine's allies, with France and Italy, for instance, coming down on entirely different sides of the issue.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday announced that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship.
Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot said, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity."
Barrot said Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?"
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions.
Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on Wednesday, Tajani said, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port."
Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.
Welcome to our coverage
As Russia's invasion of Ukraine creeps toward its fifth year, both sides continue to blast each other's infrastructure.
Overnight attacks targeted gas, oil and thermal energy facilities on both sides of the conflict's front lines.

The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including Chi
items.text:
Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries will they target?
The US is aiming tariffs at 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their factories overproduce.
The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods. China faces the highest rates.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday following an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”.
A senior US official told Reuters that USTR defines this as countries “promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles”, including through subsidies and other industrial policies.
The tariffs are the latest attempt to rebuild Trump’s sweeping import taxes that the US Supreme Court struck down in February.
Here is what we know so far.
What new tariffs are being announced?
The latest tariffs are being imposed under Section 301, part of a 1974 US trade law, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. Trump used it to place large tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, and those tariffs survived challenges in court.
The new tariffs are Trump’s latest attempt to bring back the “Liberation Day” tariffs he announced in April 2025 shortly after he began his second term in the White House. He imposed those under an emergency powers law but, in February this year, the Supreme Court ruled that the law did not allow him to impose trade tariffs.
“It’s supposed to be for international economic emergencies,” Dmitry Grozoubinski, a trade policy expert, said of the emergency law. “Tariffs are like taxes. You can’t really fight emergencies with mild taxes.”
The administration then used another law to put temporary 10 percent tariffs on trading partners in place, which ran out in July. It then replaced those with tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, which together supply almost everything the US imports. This time it used Section 301, arguing that those countries do not do enough to keep out goods made with forced labour.
Grozoubinski said Section 301 was designed to allow a president to hit back quickly at one country over one industry, not to tax almost every import. “The legislation is supposed to be a scalpel, and they used it like a flamethrower,” he said. “It is not meant to set the US tariff code, which is what this effectively did.”
The recent investigation into the “structural excess capacity” of trading partners began in March and covered industries from steel and cars to computer chips and solar panels. It examined government subsidies, wages suppressed by the state and the operations of state-owned companies.
Washington argues that this support enables foreign factories to sell their goods more cheaply around the world, undercutting American manufacturers and discouraging investment in the US. The senior official told Reuters that the new duties would not be added on top of the forced labour tariffs.
Which countries have been targeted
The investigation covered 16 economies, and tariffs have been proposed for 14 of them: China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway, which were also investigated, have been spared.
The Trump administration views China as the biggest offender, pointing to its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries. Beijing rejects the accusation and says its exports are simply competitive. Washington also accuses Chinese companies of investing in Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia to bypass earlier US tariffs.
For the other economies, Washington pointed to the large trade surpluses of Germany and Ireland as evidence against the EU. It also singled out the car industries of China and Japan, Singapore’s computer chips and Norway’s fuel and seafood exports for criticism.
What will the new tariff rates be?
The senior official cited by Reuters did not provide rates for most countries ahead of their publication in the Federal Register. However, China will face the highest charges. The official said its proposed 20 percent excess capacity tariff would come on top of the roughly 25 percent in tariffs set during Trump’s first term. That keeps China above Vietnam, which also faces a proposed rate of 20 percent.
The official said the new duties would not break the tariff limits in trade deals the Trump administration has negotiated. According to earlier Reuters reporting, those include caps of 15 percent for the EU, Japan and South Korea, and 19 percent for Malaysia.
For China, the limit is 20 percent on tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term, under a trade truce with Beijing that expires on January 10.
India has no signed trade deal with the US. The two sides agreed the outline of one in February, but it was never finalised, and talks have dragged on for months. On November 14, Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said a deal could be sealed soon.
Why is Trump doing this now?
Grozoubinski said the timing is significant. The proposal comes just weeks after midterm elections in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered unprecedented electoral losses, in which the cost of living and trade tariffs were major issues. A Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote indicated that 62 percent of respondents would support efforts to scrap trade tariffs.
“One interpretation is, like, OK, they’re going to chill out on these tariffs, because basically every time they say the word tariffs, people remember that their costs are really high and get angrier,” Grozoubinski said. “This shows that at least on some level, they are still prepared despite the headwinds, to go ahead and push that button.”
Hisham Wahby, an independent political analys

items.text:
US plans new tariffs on EU, China and 12 other economies
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
The United States on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on imports from 14 economies, including the European Union and China.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) unveiled the proposed duties after completing an eight-month investigation into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.
Washington accuses the targeted economies of promoting excessive industrial production, allowing cheaper goods to undercut American manufacturers.
The proposed tariffs largely stick to rates set under existing trade agreements, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Wednesday. However, he added that some rates could be "topped up" by a few percentage points.
The duties will be subject to a public comment period and a hearing before taking effect, possibly in January at the earliest.
Which countries would face new US tariffs?
China would face an additional tariff of 20%, the joint-highest rate among the targeted economies.
The proposed duties would respect the 15% tariff cap agreed with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, as well as the 19% cap agreed with Malaysia, a senior US administration official said.
Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam would also be affected.
Mexico and Norway are currently excluded from the proposed measures. Greer said talks with Mexico were continuing as Washington's investigation into its trade practices remained ongoing.
In a separate announcement, the USTR also proposed higher tariffs on Brazilian raw and refined sugar and a new 10% duty on aircraft, which would affect Brazilian manufacturer Embraer.
How would the new US tariffs work?
The senior US official said the proposed duties would not exceed tariff limits negotiated under existing trade agreements.
However, the new tariffs on China would be added to duties of around 25% imposed during Trump's first term, bringing the combined rate for some Chinese goods to 45%.
Around $30 billion worth of Chinese imports that Washington is considering for tariff reductions would be exempt from the new measures.
The proposed duties would not be added to existing sector-specific tariffs on products such as automobiles, steel and aluminum.
Nor would they be combined with tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% imposed in July against 60 trading partners over alleged insufficient action against forced labor. Where both measures apply, the higher rate would prevail.
How have the EU and China responded to the US tariffs?
The European Union said on Wednesday it would examine the proposed US tariffs but rejected Washington's allegations of excessive industrial production.
"We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity," the EU said, adding that it expected Washington to honor the trade agreement reached with Brussels last year.
Beijing also rejected Washington's allegations of excessive industrial production and reiterated its opposition to trade wars, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.
"The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Washington has accused Beijing of flooding global markets with cheap exports, ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products.
Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping last week in Shenzhen and is due to host him at the G20 summit in Miami in December.
An existing trade truce between Washington and Beijing is set to expire on January 10. Access to rare earth minerals and Chinese purchases of US agricultural products could feature in further negotiations.
Why is Trump introducing new tariffs?
The measures are intended in part to replace revenues lost after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping global tariffs in February.
The court ruled that Trump lacked the authority to impose the duties by declaring an economic emergency and bypassing Congress.
The new measures instead rely on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and retaliate against unfair or discriminatory foreign trade practices.
Trump has repeatedly promised that tariffs will bring manufacturing jobs back to the US and reduce the federal deficit.
Could Trump's new tariffs fuel US inflation?
The proposed duties could put further pressure on American businesses, which may pass additional costs on to consumers.
US consumer inflation reached 3.7% year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high. Earlier tariffs, the effects of Trump's war on Iran and a boom in artificial intelligence investment have contributed to rising prices.
High living costs were a key issue in November's midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party lose control of both chambers of Congress.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the elections found that 62% of respondents supported efforts to repeal Trump's tariffs.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that
items.text:
Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
- Published
Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.
Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.
Russia has not commented on the strikes.
The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.
The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.
Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.
"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.
Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.
Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.
"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.
Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.
But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.
Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

items.title: Premier League’s burst of early sendings-off may not last – but red cards are on the rise for a reason
items.summary: Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity (though his suspension was overturned on appeal)
items.text:
Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity (though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford.
This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24.
History suggests the frequency will decrease. It can feel as if referees are keener to exert their authority and clamp down on wrongdoing at the start of a season before calming down.
There have been nine previous Premier League seasons that averaged at least 0.2 red cards per game over the opening 11 matchweeks. The rate dropped between that point and the end of the campaign in every example.
However, only one of those seasons occurred with video assistant referees highlighting indiscretions unseen or underrated by the on-field officials. Six of the 13 straight red cards this season have been thanks to intervention from Stockley Park, with Jean-Philippe Mateta, Igor Thiago and Tarkowski having a booking upgraded after review.
The first two of those three are part of another trend, along with Kevin Danso, Phil Foden and Yoro. They were sent off within the opening quarter of games this season, meaning 2026-27 is one shy of the season-long record of six dismissals before this time bar. Rodrigo Bentancur and Ryan Sessegnon have been shown straight red cards 12 minutes after coming on as substitutes too.
Logic dictates the hot spell of early dismissals will end. The overall rise in red cards stands a greater chance of holding because Premier League football is played at such a frantic pace. Mistakes are common in this environment, with one slightly mistimed challenge potentially all that is required to draw the red from the referee’s pocket. Several other metrics hint at why the chances of a side going down to 10 have increased.
Costly mistakes are occurring more readily. Opta tracks defensive errors that lead to an opposition shot. The average across the past decade was 1.1 per game, yet Premier League clubs are committing 2.1 errors per match in 2026-27, an unprecedented rate. Even though the conversion percentage for this type of chance is below the long-term average this season, the sheer volume of shot-generating blunders means the number of goals from errors (0.56 per game) is higher than ever before.
Players are having to act and react more quickly under the pressure that the preference for man-to-man over zonal marking in open play has brought. Opta’s metric for when a player miscontrols the ball is on the rise as a result. This is reflected in an increase in ball recoveries from last season, as possession is changing sides more frequently. Premier League shots from counterattacking moves have never been as frequent or represented a greater proportion of the total in the data era.
Higher pressure, higher speed football has increased the probability of cards. Which player will be first to be sent off this weekend? It looks inevitable that someone will walk.

items.summary:
Trump announces new tariffs on EU, China despite US midterms defeat
President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday reignited global trade tensions by proposing new tariffs on some of the largest US trading partners, including the EU, Japan and Taiwan. China could be slapped with a 20 percent t
items.text:
Trump announces new tariffs on EU, China despite US midterms defeat
President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday reignited global trade tensions by proposing new tariffs on some of the largest US trading partners, including the EU, Japan and Taiwan. China could be slapped with a 20 percent tariff, a senior official said. The announcement came weeks after a cost-of-living crisis landed the Republicans a sweeping defeat in the US midterms.
The US on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production – the latest move by President Donald Trump to remake Washington's trade relationships.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put US manufacturers at a disadvantage.
The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
Read moreTrump calls Supreme Court decision to strike down his tariffs 'deeply disappointing'
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the US Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The new levies target some of the United States' largest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
The US official made specific mention of China, for whom a 20 percent tariff is being proposed, the joint-highest for any economy.
In a separate announcement, the US Trade Representative's office also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.
Trump's tariffs have targeted Washington's friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in his country.
The latest move offers some relief for partners that earlier signed tariff deals with the Trump administration, but it could still raise temperatures as the US president prepares to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.
"We don't expect this to create tension or rancor" at the G20 summit, the senior US official said. "We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 in the wake of these announcements."
Inflation pressures
Over-capacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement, chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.
The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on costs to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.
Affordability was a key issue in recent midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by Democrats.
Read moreThe economic drivers of US Republicans' rout at polls
US consumer inflation came in at 3.7 percent year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high as prices are pushed up by the effects of Trump's war on Iran, tariffs, and the massive AI investment boom.
US Federal Reserve policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-percent target, say that most price effects of Trump's previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy – but any new levies could push prices up further.
The new tariffs are likely to come into effect in January at the earliest, the senior US official said.
Trump's latest duties come after an investigation the US Trade Representative started in March on excess manufacturing capacity and production.
The concern was whether other countries were taking actions deemed "unreasonable or discriminatory", and if they weighed on US commerce.
Pushback expected
Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among "the most important" actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and "never get turned off, even if there's no demand".
This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a "hollowing out" of US manufacturing, he added.
The US determination is likely to face strong pushback from China and others, with Beijing long rejecting criticism that it relies too much on exports to boost its economy.
While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.
In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.
For economies facing both the forced labor and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said. Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)
Keywords for this article

That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the s
items.text:
German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
November 25, 2026
"Africa is a land of opportunity." "The German-African relationship is a win-win." "The continent is the market of the future."
That's what many business leaders and politicians have to say about Africa at the sixth edition of the German-African Business Summit in Accra, Ghana. While these descriptions aren't new, there's a palpable sense of urgency and seriousness this time.
German firms are increasingly viewing Africa as an attractive destination as they scramble to find new markets amid wars in Ukraine and Iran, high energy prices, punishing US tariffs and slowing growth in traditional markets like China.
"For a long time, many German companies had a secure source of revenue from the major export markets in North America and China, but the geopolitical ruptures of our time have undermined this certainty," German President Frank-Walter Steimeier said during the event.
"One could also say that it is time for new horizons, time to take a closer look at economic opportunities still waiting for us."
Why Africa matters?
Africa is home to some of the fastest growing economies in the world like Ethiopia and Rwanda. Even as European and other advanced economies contend with declining working-age populations, Africa is expected to add hundreds of millions of workers in the next decades, emerging as a key source of future labor.
Germany has already signed a migration pact with Kenya and is working on one with Ghana as it seeks to attract skilled workers to help ease acute labor shortages in certain sectors at home.
Even as Africa remains one of the poorest regions in the world, economic growth in parts of the continent has created a larger and more affluent consumer class over the past three decades. This group is aspirational and a growing source of demand for many of the goods that German firms want to sell, from cars to cosmetics.
The continent, with its mineral wealth and renewable energy potential, is central to European Union efforts to diversify its sources of critical raw materials and reduce reliance on China-dominated supply chains.
It is also playing an increasingly important role in strengthening the EU's energy security after the bloc phased out most energy imports from Russia.
German firms have committed to invest billions of euros in green hydrogen projects in countries such as Mauritania and Namibia.
"We don't have the capital to develop them [natural resources]. So foreign investors are coming to help us develop those resources. Whilst we are getting jobs and industrialization is taking place, they are also making profits," said Amin Amidu Sulemani, energy and infrastructure commissioner at the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).
"It's not a relationship where we send raw materials outside of Africa every time, when we can actually process them here," he told DW.
What is wrong with Germany's Africa strategy?
Despite Africa's growing economic appeal, many obstacles to investment remain, including corruption and governance concerns, unreliable energy supplies, foreign exchange risk and poor infrastructure.
African leaders say they are working to address these challenges and improve the ease of doing business.
Yet while German companies have largely remained on the sidelines, competitors from countries such as the UAE, Turkey and India have made significant inroads across the continent.
German firms enjoy a strong reputation in Africa because of their engineering expertise, vocational training programs and long-term industrial investments, which are more likely to create stable jobs than investments in extractive industries.
However, they have struggled to translate that goodwill into a larger commercial presence. Africa, for instance, accounts for less than 2% of the total foreign investment made by German firms over the past several decades.
Business leaders complain that German firms lack adequate financing and risk protection for projects in Africa. They also criticize excessive bureaucracy and the absence of a coherent German strategy, with engagement fragmented across ministries and agencies.
Industry bodies say German institutions and firms often perceive risks too broadly, treating diverse African markets as if they pose the same level of risk.
"German companies can be a bit more bold and maybe also innovative in the way they approach the continent," Khadi Camara, deputy CEO of the German-African Business Association, told DW. "We see that in the companies that are successful, they don't do business as usual. Every country has its nuances that companies keep in mind and say, okay, this model works here, that model works there."
The 2026 World Investment Report by UN trade body UNCTAD showed that investors from the Gulf and Asia are becoming important sources of investment in Africa, especially in energy, logistics, real estate and infrastructure.
The UAE has been a major investor in greenfield megaprojects in recent years, including the $34 billion (€31 billion) Infinity Power renewable energy project in Mauritania, the $24 billion Ras El Hikma real estate development project in Egypt and the $6 billion H2 Global Energy hydrogen project in Tunisia.
How can German firms seize the African opportunity?
Business leaders are calling for better financing and guarantees and more risk-sharing and easing of bureaucratic hurdles.
Meanwhile, others, including the German president, are urging German businesses to take on more risk and seize opportunities in Africa. Otherwise, they risk being edged out by foreign rivals.
"Be curious, take risks and invest in our common future," Steinmeier said.

items.text:
How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.
"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."
The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.
Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."
Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well
"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."
Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"
This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.
Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

items.text:
Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune. The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue.
Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune.
As reported by Fortune, Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.
Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

items.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
items.summary:
Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.
The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users dis
items.text:
Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.
The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.
Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

items.summary:
Pep Guardiola has said he doesn’t know when he’ll return to football but that his next coaching role will be with a national team.
In an interview with former Barcelona teammate Romario on Tuesday, Guardiola was asked if there was a team he had never coached but would like to. He answered “a nationa
items.text:
Pep Guardiola has said he doesn’t know when he’ll return to football but that his next coaching role will be with a national team.
In an interview with former Barcelona teammate Romario on Tuesday, Guardiola was asked if there was a team he had never coached but would like to. He answered “a national team” and called it “the next step”. Guardiola has been floated as a target for the US national team, who must replace Mauricio Pochettino after his departure for Manchester United.
The 55-year-old left Manchester City at the end of the 2025-26 season after 10 years and said he planned to take a break from football. He has spent 18 years in club management but has never coached at the international level.
He was offered the Italy head coaching position this summer but turned it down, saying the timing was not right.
He confirmed he held talks with the Italian football federation this summer. The federation president, Giovanni Malago, had said in July that financial “exceptions” were in place to allow Guardiola to become Italy’s next coach, but Guardiola declined the offer and Roberto Mancini was appointed.
“I talked with them, and it was an honor,” Guardiola said. “It was ‌one of the ‌greatest honours I’ve had, that they thought of me to ‌coach Italy. But it came at a time when I needed to stop. If it had happened a year or two earlier, I probably would have accepted. But when [technical director Paolo] Maldini and [adviser] Leonardo, whom I love dearly, reached out, it ‌was at a point where I simply had to stop. I needed some time for myself.”
Guardiola has been at the center of conversation around the US vacancy this month, with some reports suggesting he and US Soccer are set for exploratory talks. Earlier this year Guardiola joined Pochettino and several US Soccer staffers at a Major League Soccer game in New York. Before his departure Pochettino was asked what he would tell Guardiola if he sought his opinion on the US job.
“Take it. Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation,” Pochettino said. “Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style.”
The former Barcelona and Bayern Munich manager was noncommittal on the timing of a possible return to coaching.
“I don’t know how long I’ll ‌be away,” Guardiola said. “Right now I feel very well. But if I return to football one day, it will be when my stomach tells me it’s the right time.”

items.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
items.summary:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.
The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the s
items.text:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.
The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.
The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.
Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.
“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”
Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.
One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”
Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.
Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.
Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.
Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

items.title: Do Ferrari need to make Hamilton their No 1 driver?

items.text:
What next for Ferrari after Charles Leclerc, Lewis Hamilton's latest collision with No 1 driver and consequences up for debate
Listen to the latest edition of The F1 Show podcast as Simon Lazenby, David Croft and Jamie Chadwick debate what's next at Ferrari after another driver clash; watch the Qatar GP on Sky Sports F1 this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
Wednesday 25 November 2026 14:16, UK
Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton's latest run-in at the Las Vegas Grand Prix has ramped up scrutiny on Ferrari and what the team will do to try to avoid more costly on-track incidents between their two drivers.
Just two races after a fierce battle when running first and second on the opening lap in Mexico City cost the team victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen and led to clear-the-air discussions, the team-mates collided when battling over sixth place in Las Vegas in an incident Leclerc was found at fault for by the stewards and then received the post-race ire of team boss Frederic Vasseur.
Vasseur has said such incidents "cannot continue" but how does the Frenchman get on top of the situation heading towards 2027, when the team will be hoping to launch a fresh bid to end what stands as an 18-year world title drought?

- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
The Ferrari fallout proved a central topic on the latest edition of Sky Sports' The F1 Show podcast ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, in which host Simon Lazenby was joined by David Croft and Jamie Chadwick.
Asked how big the problems between Hamilton and Leclerc were becoming for Ferrari, Chadwick said: "Significant when you think about what they're going to potentially be going into next year with.
"I think this is the time of the year where you don't want to be having these kinds of conflicts because suddenly it will escalate and it will mean that more serious conversation is going to be had in the background."
So what might Ferrari do next?
Impose a No 1 driver?
Former world champion Damon Hill recently said he believed Ferrari should make Hamilton, the seven-time world champion and F1's most successful driver, their clear No 1 next year if they want to win the world championship.
Speaking on Sky Sports F1 after Sunday's incident in Las Vegas, Jacques Villeneuve, the 1997 title winner, suggested Leclerc - who is in his eighth season with the Scuderia - had "lost" the leadership of the team to Hamilton, who is in his second, and "if there's one of the two drivers knows how to win championships, it's Lewis".
Villeneuve did, however, question whether Ferrari would be able to prioritise Hamilton contractually.
Hamilton said after the race that he has "never asked" for No 1 status at the team, although implied they could have given him more backing when he was second to Kimi Antonelli and around 40 points ahead of Leclerc in the championship earlier this season.
And although Hamilton and Leclerc are both among the sport's biggest names and most-talented drivers, Croft believes events of this season have effectively forced the team's hand and they need to prioritise one over the other in order to achieve better results.
"Whether Lewis Hamilton is asking to be No 1 or not, I don't think matters any more," said Croft.
"I think the way things have panned out this season the matter has been forced.
"Lewis has to be the No 1 because Charles keeps putting himself in a position whereby Ferrari suffer when the two drivers come together.
"He got the penalty on Sunday. Whether you think it's a penalty or not, the move was ambitious and it was ambitious if it was a move on Lando Norris, it was ambitious and a bit foolish if it's a move on your own team-mate.
"So Charles is kind of forcing, albeit not deliberately, Ferrari to make these decisions. He did race Lewis hard in Mexico City, and we saw what happened there, and he raced Lewis hard in Monza, and we saw what happened there."
Long regarded as one of the fastest drivers in the sport, Leclerc, 29, is a graduate of Ferrari's academy and joined their race team in 2019 after a debut season of F1 at Sauber.
He outperformed four-time champion Sebastian Vettel and then Carlos Sainz across their respective seasons as team-mates and was comfortably ahead of Hamilton by over 80 points after the Briton joined from Mercedes last year.
But Leclerc has faced a resurgent force in Hamilton this year, with the 41-year-old holding a 17-point advantage over him in the championship with two races to go.
"Charles is a fine driver, don't get me wrong, but his pole-to-win conversion rate (27 to nine) is not enough," added Croft on Leclerc's Ferrari record so far.
"You can also argue that the team haven't given him the car to make that conversion rate better, but he does make mistakes, we've seen that.
"We've seen in the past when he's been leading a race and he's crashed out all by himself. He's not the finished article and I don't want to be too harsh on Charles because I think he's a truly wonderful human being, but he's no Lewis Hamilton when it comes to his record and his performances and his consistency over the years."
Enforce firmer rules and consequences?
Vasseur said he would hold fresh discussions with his drivers this week.
But do those talks need to now go further in terms of setting out firmly what is and is not acceptable - and establishing consequences for any transgressions?
Chadwick said: "I think the biggest issue [to this point] is the conversations haven't been serious enough.
"I think a clear-the-air talk as in 'okay it's not your fault, it's not your fault' and 'okay this is how things are' versus, actually, what are the rules of engagement? What are the reprimands if you do take your team-mate out and are they severe enough that actually neither driver is g

Chantelle Cameron, the unified super-welterweight champion, signs a multi-fight extension with Most Valuable Promotions; Jake Paul said: "Chantelle Cameron has established herself as one of the true GOATs of women's boxing and what makes her special is that she's still hungry for more"
Wednesday 25 November 2026 13:59, UK
Chantelle Cameron, the unified super-welterweight world champion, has agreed a multi-fight extension with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions.
The reigning WBO, WBA and WBC super-welterweight world titlist is one of the world's top pound-for-pound fighters.
The new agreement extends MVP's partnership with Cameron following a landmark 2026 campaign that saw the English fighter capture world championships in a second weight division - further cementing her position among boxing's elite - and beat American star Mikaela Mayer.
A former undisputed super-lightweight world champion, and the only professional opponent to beat Katie Taylor, Cameron will continue pursuing the biggest fights in women's boxing, starting with her rematch with Mayer on December 24.
Nakisa Bidarian and Paul, founders of Most Valuable Promotions, said: "Chantelle Cameron has established herself as one of the true GOATs of women's boxing and what makes her special is that she's still hungry for more.
"In just over a year with MVP, she's unified three world titles at 154 pounds, headlined a major event in her home country, and is now preparing for another massive championship fight on Christmas Eve in Dubai as part of one of the biggest combat sports events of 2026.
"Chantelle has made it clear that she wants to keep challenging herself against the toughest competition, and we're committed to delivering those fights. This extension is about building on everything we've accomplished together and making sure the next chapter of her career is even bigger."
Cameron said: "I'm delighted to extend my contract with MVP. Since I first signed with Nakisa and Jake they have delivered on every single promise they made to me.
"They have looked after me in and out of the ring and signing a long-term extension was a very easy decision on my part.
"I am boxing on the biggest cards all over the world and I look forward to the rest of my career with MVP."

items.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
items.summary:
Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follo
items.text:
Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.
When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8.30am on Tuesday local time, 30 people including customers and employees were taken hostage, many of whom could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final 20 people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested and one was killed.
In a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year – De la Espriella celebrated the end of the operation.
“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” he said. He appeared with a gun on his waist, as he has on several other occasions in public as part of his populist security rhetoric.
The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
Commenting on what he called an “extraordinary” rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.
In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.
Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

What to know before using AI agents for Black Friday shopping
Artificial intelligence is here to help with Black Friday.
This weekend, 59% of consumers plan on using AI to support their winter shopping, according to the National Retail Federation.
But AI has proven one way it is not unlike humans: It makes mistakes. The stakes of those hallucinations are much higher when your wallet – and holiday unwrapping memories – are on the line. These tools also become better shoppers when you hand over personal data, which also means giving up more information on your private life to massive tech companies.
Here are some tips – and notes of caution – before using AI as your personal holiday shopper.
Treat AI searches like a conversation with a kid
Traditional online shopping is about search terms and the infinite product scroll. AI is meant to be a conversation.
Unlike shopping on a retail website, AI platforms are designed to look more like texting apps. Prompt bars on these platforms sit on the bottom of the page, inviting a back and forth chat between user and bot about what to buy.
After all, it can be hard to know what keyword to plug in to shop for uncle before the Christmas exchange. AI instead allows for search based on a vibe – like describing that uncle's hobbies and personal style. If a shopper wants to buy a suitcase to support their uncle's European travel dreams, this makes it easier to narrow down the options.
"You can say if that bag is overstuffed, will it fit under the seat on JetBlue?" says Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester who advises retailers and brands on digital commerce strategy, including for AI. "Don't give me the dimensions," she advises, "Tell me if it will suit my use case."
Pfeiffer cautions that even though AI is able to think through these nuanced shopping criteria, it works better with more hand holding.
"It's best if you imagine that it's a young child who will probably misinterpret your request," Pfeiffer said. "You want to be as specific and clear as possible."
AI Agents can shop for you. Be careful what you give them
Newer AI models can do more than talk and brainstorm. They can handle shopping tasks.
If shoppers are, for example, worried about holiday shipments arriving on time, AI can monitor an email inbox in order to track packages, even messaging a late shipper on the shopper's behalf. Beyond just suggesting a gift, agents can do the actual buying (with your money).
These are useful features, but require granting access to sensitive personal data, such as an inbox or credit card. One of the first questions Meta's AI agent platform Muse asks is if the user would like to connect their email and calendar.
Meta says its AI is highly secure. Everyone is assigned their own AI agent and the company promises that information shoppers share with it is kept private. Particularly sensitive information like credit card numbers, they say, are held separately and never viewed directly by the AI.
Yet Meta also has long been accused of violating user privacy, as in a 2022 case about improperly sharing user data. Meta did not admit to wrongdoing but settled for about $725 million.
Beyond Meta, there are cases of AI jumping guardrails that programmers set for it. Users have also reported their AI agents acting without their consent, such as sending their home address to a buyer from Facebook Marketplace and booking a hotel.
Philip Bruno, chief strategy and growth officer with ACI Worldwide, says he would share what he's shopping for with AI, but warns to be more careful with personal information.
"I'm cooking for a family of four. That is fine to be able to say," Bruno says. "I would be very careful about payment information."
On that note, experts caution shoppers to be careful with other people's information. It's easy to give most AIs loads of information about your father while brainstorming his gift. Know AI agents can also use this to build profiles of the shopper's friends and family. Being illusive and not specifying who you're shopping for during the brainstorming can help.
Just like for humans, it takes time for AI to find the best deals
One major selling point for using AI agents is that they can check multiple websites and compare prices, bringing them for human review all in one spot. That does not mean the first price it shows you is the best one.
"One of the biggest misconceptions about AI is that it somehow sees everything," Pfeiffer says. "That's just false. It gets you the best answer it can as quickly as possible."
AI agents still need time to hunt for deals. Many will often let shoppers watch along as they browse the web, rather than relying on preset knowledge.
This automating can also mean time savings for the user. Agents often can run in the background 24/7.
If users are in no particular holiday rush, they can leave the AI to continue shopping for weeks or even months, only sending a notice when a price drops into a budget friendly range.
Just know these agents don't always have access to every website. Amazon, for example, blocks Muse, arguing Meta did not alert Amazon of plans and that agents did not identify themselves while browsing.
Check the AI's work
For all the advances since ChatGPT's launch four years ago, AI still hallucinates and makes mistakes.
Visa recently released a report warning buyers to beware of AI shoppers. It tested different AI models and found they failed to recommend a product that met a customer's needs in 42% of test runs – more than half of those still recommended a product that didn't match.
That provides even more reason to click through and read up on whatever potential gift an AI recommends to make sure it's what shoppers want.
Otherwise people may find themselves turning back to that same AI agent for help making a return.

EU plans €50 billion tech equity fund to boost quantum technology

The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete
items.text:
EU plans €50 billion tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
November 25, 2026
The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.
"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.
Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies
Around one-third of the world's quantum companies are based in the European Union, according to the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.
