items.text:
Bayern Munich’s Musiala checked for neurological symptoms in April 2025
Musiala was examined by the German club for neurological dysfunction after the initial onset of symptoms in 2025.
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala was first examined for neurological symptoms in April 2025, more than 16 months before the official announcement of the diagnosis by the player, the club has said.
Bayern said they held talks with Musiala’s management team on Tuesday amid speculation about his contract situation following comments by senior club officials over his future and whether he could ever perform again at the highest level.
The comments from honorary president Uli Hoeness and board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, among others, were strongly criticised by the German players’ union.
Musiala, who signed a contract extension to 2030 in February 2025, was diagnosed with a neurological disorder in August after he collapsed in two games and had to be taken off.
“A constructive discussion took place yesterday, Tuesday, between FC Bayern Munich and Jamal Musiala’s management,” the club said in a statement.
“For both parties, the player’s health is the absolute priority. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throughout his recovery process.”
“In light of various rumours circulating over the past few days, FC Bayern and 11WINS — the agency representing Jamal — wish to clarify the following: Jamal Musiala was first examined for absence-like symptoms on April 22, 2025,” Bayern said.
“This examination took place in consultation with FC Bayern and the club’s medical department, immediately following the initial onset of these neurological symptoms.”
Musiala said in August that he had been diagnosed with “temporary, brief, but easily treatable absences caused by a neurological dysfunction”.
Musiala missed much of last season after breaking his leg during the 2025 Club World Cup. In September, he was sidelined with a hamstring injury, returning to action last week in a 1-1 draw with Cologne in the Bundesliga.

items.title: Senegal regaining Afcon title is the right end to embarrassing farrago but issues do not stop here
items.summary: A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon fin
items.text:
A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history.
As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday, was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute.
“Correcting one injustice with another cannot be considered an acceptable response, either from a sporting or an ethical standpoint,” Sobha said. “Football is founded on core values: fairness, merit and the truth of what happens on the field. Awarding a title outside these principles, even when supported by regulatory provisions, undermines the credibility of the competition and damages the integrity of the game.
“Rather than restoring balance, such a choice risks intensifying frustrations and calls for a deeper reflection on how to safeguard fairness and uphold the honour of African football.”
Managing the huge reputational damage from the crisis over the past 10 months has been arguably the biggest governance test for the five-year Caf presidency of the South African billionaire Patrice Motsepe.
In a frustrated, exasperated moment, he admitted he was “sick and tired” of it all, navigating the treacherous diplomatic minefield of wounded Moroccan and Senegalese feelings, while reiterating his neutrality and belief in the integrity of the judicial process to bring the dispute to a just end.
The Cas resolution of the dispute compels Caf to carry out a desperately needed and long overdue task: the root-and-branch reform of its justice system, particularly the appeals board chaired by the Nigerian judge Roli Harriman.
The Cape Verdean Faustino Varela Monteiro, the board’s vice-chair, is a notable, honourable exception, standing for the correct legal position in his dissenting judgment.
The appeals board needlessly overturned the verdict of Caf’s disciplinary committee, which struck the right balance of upholding the result of the final while imposing fines and bans on the Senegal team for the egregious act of disrupting the match, and in so doing exposed its acute lack of understanding of the critical role it is duty-bound to play in the dispensation of football justice.
“You are right,” says a Caf executive committee member about the need to dissolve the appeals board and reconstitute it with jurists possessing the knowledge needed to restore confidence in the African football justice system.
Ensuring that politically exposed people are no longer members of a reconstituted appeals board is also imperative, if confidence in the impartiality of its verdicts is to be restored. No federation president should have a place on it. The presence of Moez Nasri, the president of the Tunisian Football Federation, strips it of credibility, as Motsepe acknowledged when I pointed this out to him in March.
But the poor quality of Jean-Jacques Ndala Ngambo’s refereeing of the Afcon final and Safari Olivier Kabene’s equally bad chairing of Caf’s referees committee – whose selection of match officials was responsible for the inadequate quality of game management throughout the last tournament – remain the proverbial elephants in the governance room.
When I asked a high-ranking Caf official why Ngambo has not faced a disciplinary hearing for his management of the final, he claimed its hands were tied by the Cas judicial process. That excuse expired on Tuesday.
Ngambo’s decision to allow a restart of the game, after Senegal illegally walked out for about 15 minutes in protest against a penalty awarded to Morocco, was a deeply questionable, some would say unacceptable, use of his discretionary powers, which should have leaned towards a declaration of match abandonment, with Morocco being declared the winners.
That said, the referee’s earlier failure to award Senegal what appeared to be a clear goal, subsequently giving a penalty to Morocco in second-half stoppage time, was the trigger for the chaos.
Ngambo’s lack of fortitude and experience, to cope with the demands of an Afcon final, is an indictment of the committee that picked the wrong man to handle it. And Kabene is responsible for that. “We have to do a clearout of the referees committee,” says a member of the Caf executive committee.
It is a situation in sharp and sad contrast to the world-class officiating at the 2024 Afcon in Côte d’Ivoire, under the competent general management of the Ivorian Noumandiez Doué, who would be the ideal person to restore sanity.
But after the shabby way he was treated, losing his job while on assignment at the last Championship of African Nations, for domestic-based players, in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania – the countries staging the 2027 Afcon – it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than it would be to convince him to return to his old job.
With just over eight months to the next Afcon and 20 months to the 2028 tournament, yet to have a designated host, Caf’s governance and organisational challenges are far from over.
The last two Afcons of Motsepe’s presidency, which ends in March 2029, will be decisive in shaping his legacy.

items.text:
Ukraine: Industrial attacks and anger at Russia among Ukraine's allies
November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- Russia attacks have halted output at Ukrainian gas facilities as well as a thermal power plant
- Ukraine says it attacked Russian oil facilities in the Samara region
- France's foreign minister defended Ukraine's attacks on Russian shadow fleet ships off the Libyan coast, though Italy's called the attack 'a mistake'
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned against ending Ukraine support, saying 'Russia wants more than Ukraine'
Keep reading for the latest news in Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, November 25:
Moscow, Kyiv exchange overnight attacks on energy infrastructure
Kyiv and Moscow both assessed damage to energy infrastructure on Wednesday morning as both sides continued to inflict damage on one another amid Russia's over four-and-a-half-year attempted invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in.
Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations.
Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks.
In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts.
France, Italy offer different takes on Ukraine's actions in Libya
Kyiv's attacks on Russian ships in and off the coast of Libya over the past couple of days have ruffled feathers among Ukraine's allies, with France and Italy, for instance, coming down on entirely different sides of the issue.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday announced that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship.
Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot said, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity."
Barrot said Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?"
Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions.
Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on Wednesday, Tajani said, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port."
Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.
Welcome to our coverage
As Russia's invasion of Ukraine creeps toward its fifth year, both sides continue to blast each other's infrastructure.
Overnight attacks targeted gas, oil and thermal energy facilities on both sides of the conflict's front lines.
While Moscow chided former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson's calls for a contingent of Western soldiers to be stationed in Ukraine, France's foreign minister defended Kyiv's recent attacks on Russian maritime vessels in far away Libya — something Italy's foreign minister criticized.
In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended German support for Ukraine as opposition parties with sympathies for Moscow complain it's too expensive.
Merz called out those wanting to curtail support as either "failing to grasp" the fact that "Russia wants more than Ukraine" or "pursuing entirely different aims with regard to our country's freedom, openness and liberalism."
Lastly, Poland's defense minister on Wednesday expressed astonishment over the fact that the US has not yet condemned or even reacted to repeated Russian drone and missile incursions into Polish airspace in recent days.
Stay tuned to DW for these stories and all the latest news on the conflict in Ukraine….

items.text:
In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
November 25, 2026
In many parts of Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, male doctors are no longer allowed to treat women. The consequences have been highlighted in a recent United Nations report, which offers disturbing insight into the harsh reality many women face.
In one case, a woman from Kunar province described how she suffered several miscarriages without being able to access medical care.
Her case highlights the increasing number of pregnant women who urgently need medical assistance and are unable to receive it because of restrictions imposed by the Taliban.
And overall, women in Afghanistan are increasingly losing access to essential healthcare. This is due both to the Taliban's restrictions and to cuts in international aid funding.
Taliban remove women from public life in Afghanistan
"If a pregnant woman dies because male doctors are not allowed to treat her, her husband can marry another, younger woman. That is how the Taliban think," said 28-year-old Tamana Zaryab Paryani.
Paryani is an Afghan women's rights activist and one of the best-known voices of resistance against the Taliban.
A trained lawyer, she worked as a newspaper journalist before the Taliban returned to power. Following their takeover in August 2021, she took part in protests against restrictions on the rights of women and girls. In January 2022, she was detained by the Taliban in Kabul alongside her sisters. After her release, she managed to reach Europe.
Since then, she has continued to advocate internationally for the rights of Afghan women. At the end of October, she addressed the UN Security Council, describing the repression of women in Afghanistan and urging the international community not to normalise their systematic disenfranchisement.
"This is gender apartheid. We expect the international community to recognise it and stand with the women of Afghanistan," Paryani told DW.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees severely restricting the lives of women and girls. Girls are barred from secondary education, while women are denied access to universities. Women's opportunities to work outside the home are also severely restricted.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), which monitors and regularly documents the human rights situation in the country, reported in September 2025 that inspectors from the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice were further restricting women's access to healthcare through the enforcement of regulations and decrees.
According to the UN, around 2.6 million girls are excluded from secondary education. This is likely to lead to more girls being married off at an early age and to an increase in maternal mortality, UN Women warns.
Afghanistan has a population of around 45 million. With a median age of approximately 17, it has one of the youngest populations in the world. Around 42% of its population is under the age of 15.
The world's 'worst women's rights crisis'
"What is happening in Afghanistan goes beyond gender-based persecution, as already defined under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court," Haroon Mutasem, professor of International Criminal Law at the American University of Afghanistan and research fellow at Berlin's Humboldt University, told DW.
The Afghan legal scholar examines how the systematic oppression of women in Afghanistan can be classified and prosecuted under international law.
"This is not just about individual acts of persecution, but about an institutionalised system of oppression and domination of one gender group by another. They have established a system that considers women as secondary and defines a life for them as raising kids, working at home, and also actually satisfying the sexual desires of their men."
Mutasem argues that failure to respond to the systematic oppression of Afghan women could undermine the universal validity of human and women's rights. He warns that other authoritarian regimes and extremist movements could adopt similar practices.
According to UN estimates, in 2027 more than 4 million children under the age of five, as well as around 1.27 million pregnant and breastfeeding women, will require treatment for acute malnutrition.
Susan Ferguson, the UN's Special Representative in Afghanistan, described the situation in her latest report as "the world's worst women's rights crisis." Afghan women, she said, are now "fighting for their very survival."
Cuts in aid funding have forced humanitarian organisations to make "impossible decisions about which women and girls can receive support and which have to be turned away," Ferguson said.
This article was originally written in German.

items.text:
Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain on December 12
Former regional leader says he will unveil his proposal for a renewed Catalan independence push on December 17.
Catalan separatist and former regional leader Carles Puigdemont has said he will return to Spain on December 12, ending nearly a decade of self-imposed exile.
Speaking at a televised news conference from Brussels on Wednesday, Puigdemont said he would unveil his proposal for a renewed Catalan independence push on December 17.
Puigdemont’s return to Spain comes after the Supreme Court applied an amnesty law and shelved the criminal case against him.
“I left as president of the government of Catalonia, and I will return to the place where Catalan democracy elects or dismisses its presidents: the Parliament of Catalonia,” the former leader said.
He added: “I will do so on Saturday, 12 December, at midday, and that very night I will be able to sleep at home, with my family,” Puigdemont told the Brussels news conference.
In exile since 2017
Puigdemont fled to Belgium in October 2017 after organising an independence referendum that Spanish courts deemed illegal.
The vote triggered Spain’s worst political crisis in decades and deepened tensions between Madrid and Catalonia, a wealthy northeastern region with its own language, culture and a strong separatist movement.
Puigdemont briefly returned to Spain in August 2024, delivering a defiant speech in Catalan capital Barcelona, advocating for Catalonia’s right to self-determination before disappearing and prompting a police operation.
The amnesty, approved by parliament in 2024, was part of a deal between Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s Socialist Party and Catalan separatist groups, including Puigdemont’s Junts party, after an inconclusive election in 2023.
Spain’s conservative opposition unsuccessfully challenged the measure in the courts and parliament.
Puigdemont will return to Spain after this Sunday’s snap general election. Opinion polls suggest a potential coalition of the conservative People’s Party ‌and far-right Vox – both strong supporters of a unified Spain – winning an absolute majority of parliamentary seats.

items.title: ‘It threw me off my bowling a bit’: Isobel Goodwin living dream after England callup
items.summary:
Not many phone calls are important enough to justify Isobel Goodwin missing her turn in a game of tenpin bowling. The England head coach ringing to give her a first senior international call-up qualified as an exception for the overjoyed London City Lionesses striker.
After scoring with a pin-point
items.text:
Not many phone calls are important enough to justify Isobel Goodwin missing her turn in a game of tenpin bowling. The England head coach ringing to give her a first senior international call-up qualified as an exception for the overjoyed London City Lionesses striker.
After scoring with a pin-point finish at the Emirates this month under the gaze of Sarina Wiegman, Goodwin had been hotly tipped to be given a chance with the Lionesses and she is now eager to impress as the squad prepare to face Ukraine in their World Cup qualifying playoff.
The 23-year-old has been a key part of the forward line for England’s youth sides and therefore is familiar with her surroundings as she speaks to the media for the first time at St George’s Park, but was still clearly somewhat bowled over by Wiegman’s call.
“I actually missed the call [initially],” Goodwin says. “I must have been taking my go when she called and then I looked at my phone a couple of minutes later and it said: ‘This is Sarina, please can you call me back?’ So I went outside and rang her and she congratulated me. Normally I’m really good at bowling – it kind of threw me off a little bit.
“I rang my mum straight away and she was crying on the phone. She was just so happy for me. I’m so delighted to be here. So it was such a nice moment.”
The former Aston Villa, Coventry United and Sheffield United forward has had to bide her time to reach this point in her career, spending three seasons in the second tier a period on the London City bench at the start of this campaign. But with four WSL goals this term, including one in each of the past two matches, and four in the League Cup, three of which came against Crystal Palace, her recent improvements have been undeniable.
“It has been one of probably the best weeks in my life,” Goodwin says of scoring against Arsenal and Palace in the WSL either side of Wiegman’s call. “It’s quite surreal to be here, to be honest. But I’m really enjoying it so far.
“It’s been a long journey but this is obviously something that you dream of as a little kid. So, yeah, it’s been hard to get here. But I’m just obviously just so happy.”
Rangy, lean and aerially strong, yet possessing a good first touch, Goodwin is adept at running the channels or being the target player, resembling a throwback to a stereotypical, old-style English centre-forward. This has made her stand out in a club side dominated by continental stars known for their poise and style. Nevertheless she has combined well with London City’s former Barcelona players.
Goodwin, who won the WSL2 Golden Boot in 2024-25 as she helped London City win promotion, said: “Everyone [at London City] has just said: ‘Just be yourself. You deserve to be here, so just showcase yourself.’ So that’s what I’m going to try and do. Hopefully I can show to the world what I’m like. Everyone wants to be the best they can be, so that’s what I want to try and become.”
The Arsenal striker Alessia Russo has been England’s established No 9 since Ellen White’s retirement in 2022 but the competition for the spot of backup or support striker looks wide open. Goodwin says she is eager to learn from Russo: “She’s such a great player, someone that I really look up to as a No 9. To be training with her is going to be a really nice feeling, and to obviously try and learn as much as I can from her.”
Goodwin is joined by two club-mates in this camp, in Freya Godfrey and Poppy Pattinson. Godfrey and Goodwin may spend their downtime in the camp playing the video game Fortnite together – “I’ve actually brought my iPad and my PlayStation remote to hopefully play and I think Freya brought hers as well” – but they have far more serious ambitions with London City third in the table. “It’s quite clear that we want to aim for [the] Champions League this season,” Goodwin says. “We’re really enjoying ourselves.”
That domestic quest will now be put to one side for a fortnight, as the serious business of trying to help England qualify for the World Cup rolls into view, starting with Tuesday’s away leg in Spain.

items.summary:
Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
- Published
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion
items.text:
Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
- Published
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
How we came to a figure near half a million
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.
Additional reporting by Ilya Barabanov

items.text:
Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.
Army Explosives Detonation In Iowa, Abrego Garcia Leaves The US, Congress And Nvidia
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.
- 🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.
- 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.
Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.
- 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.
Today's listen
NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.
There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.
Life advice
If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.
- 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"
- 🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.
- 🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.
- 🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has dismissed reports claiming it has cleared former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua to contest the 2027 Presidential Election.
In a statement issued on Tuesday, November 25, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said the commission had made no determination on Gachagua’s eligibility, warning that reports suggesting otherwise were misleading.
“For the avoidance of doubt, the Commission has neither cleared nor made any determination regarding Hon. Rigathi Gachagua’s eligibility to contest the 2027 Presidential Election,” Ethekon stated.
The clarification follows reports arising from remarks made by IEBC Director of Legal Services Chrispine Owiye during an engagement with political reporters in Nairobi on Monday.
IEBC explained that Owiye was only discussing constitutional provisions on election qualifications and disqualifications, particularly Articles 99 and 193, which provide that a person is not disqualified until all avenues of appeal or review have been exhausted.
The commission said his presentation did not address impeachment, removal from office under Article 75 or whether an impeached person can contest an election.
It further noted that the constitutional requirements for presidential candidates are outlined under Article 137, alongside other applicable electoral laws.
“Any determination of a prospective candidate’s eligibility will be made at the appropriate stage of the electoral process, in accordance with the Constitution and applicable laws,” Ethekon said.
IEBC also clarified that registration of candidates for the 2027 General Election has not started and will take place within timelines prescribed by law.
The commission urged media houses to exercise accuracy and due diligence when reporting on sensitive electoral and constitutional matters, warning against information that could mislead the public.
The clarification puts to rest reports suggesting Gachagua had already received the electoral body’s approval to enter the 2027 presidential race, although his eligibility remains an issue to be addressed at the appropriate stage.

items.title: Will Hajime Moriyasu get a high-profile job in Europe after his eight years in charge of Japan?
items.summary: A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from Jan
items.text:
A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early.
The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered.
It is easy to forget that in the eight years before his 2018 appointment, there were six different coaches on the national team bench. Javier Aguirre lasted just 10 games before leaving in 2015 after being named in a Spanish anti-corruption investigation. Then came Vahid Halilhodzic, stock high after leading Algeria to the knockout stages of the 2014 World Cup, but the Bosnian’s more pragmatic and direct style never seemed suited to that of his employers. Shinji Kagawa was dropped, Keisuke Honda benched and the rest seemed shocked.
A 4-1 loss against South Korea in December 2017 led to an emergency Japan FA meeting and then, in April, Halilhodzic was fired, just weeks away from the World Cup – not quite the scene of serenity and stability that many associate with the Samurai Blue, especially as he threatened to sue the JFA chief executive, Kozo Tashima, now challenging Gianni Infantino to be Fifa president, claiming an illegal dismissal. Under Akira Nishino at the 2018 World Cup, Japan squeezed into the knockout stages by receiving fewer yellow cards than Senegal.
Things have been much more settled since. Under Moriyasu Japan have become, by some distance, the best team in Asia. Fans do not have to look far for a glimpse of how things can go wrong. South Korea have talented players and went to the World Cup with Son Heung-min, a Paris Saint-Germain midfielder in Lee Kang-in and Bayern Munich’s centre-back Kim Min-jae, but they were awful and have been in meltdown ever since. Iran fans are desperate to see the back of their coach, Amir Ghalenoei; Saudi Arabia fired theirs just before a World Cup that went badly; and Qatar, back-to-back continental champions, are about to say goodbye to Julen Lopetegui after an underwhelming period.
It wasn’t just about rivals going backward, though. Clear progress has been made, standards have risen and so has confidence. After Japan became the first team to qualify for the last World Cup in March 2025, the captain, Wataru Endo, told fans it was no longer enough to be content with a place in the tournament but to look to win it. That may have been a tad optimistic and Moriyasu later talked of the last eight.
Japan eased through their group to set up a last-32 clash with Brazil. In the first half in Houston, the South Americans were very much second best. However, the Asian team sat back after the break and ended up losing in stoppage time. What made it worse was that it was a fifth failure to get past the first knockout game. Back in 2022, perhaps too much respect was paid to Croatia and the result was a penalty shootout defeat. It reinforced the claims that Moriyasu was overly conservative and cautious when it really mattered, especially given the talent that has increasingly been at his disposal. Not being able to quite deliver in tournaments was the case in Asia too. The failures at the Asian Cup in 2019 can’t be put at the door of a new man but the quarter-final exit in 2023 was a genuine disappointment.
Now, though, the four-time champions, confident in their continental status, judge their progress against the best in the world. The fact there was disappointment at not beating Brazil is a clear indication of the improvement made over the years and unthinkable for any who watched Neymar score all four in a 4-0 win over Japan in 2014.
The 3-2 win over Brazil this month was the second over the South Americans in the space of 13 months, during which Japan also became the first team from Asia to beat England. Moriyasu was able to knock on the door marked “world elite”, perhaps even unlock it, but couldn’t quite make it through. That is the job of his successor.
There are other doors to open, however, with Moriyasu reportedly interested in a move to Europe. However, he is not European, nor South American, so he is not going to get the size of job or level of league that his experience and CV – which also includes three J.League titles – deserve. But there has to be a first one, then the next and then the next. There may be a debate over just how successful Moriyasu’s national-team time was but there is now hope that he can create a legacy as a pioneer for Japanese and Asian tacticians in Europe.

items.text:
Patrick Mahomes vs Josh Allen: Who will win the NFL's biggest game of the season? Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills headline blockbuster Thanksgiving
Watch the NFL's Thanksgiving triple-header live on Sky Sports from 5pm on Thursday, starting with Chicago Bears at Detroit Lions, followed by the Philadelphia Eagles against the Dallas Cowboys and Patrick Mahomes' Kansas City Chiefs vs Josh Allen's Buffalo Bills from 1.20am on Friday
Wednesday 25 November 2026 10:51, UK
It has become an era-defining rivalry in the NFL, and now the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills will meet yet again in the biggest game of the regular season on one of football's most-watched stages.
Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen will face off for the 11th time when they headline the NFL's Thanksgiving schedule on Thursday night, live on Sky Sports from 1.20am in the early hours of Friday.
Once more they are positioned neck and neck at the forefront of the NFL's playoff race, once more they will trade the greatness that has governed football for the best part of a decade.
Together they have forged modern football's answer to Tom Brady vs Peyton Manning. Two generational quarterbacks, dictating one another's story, time and time again, although Allen would prefer if the outcome had been a little more even by now.
Mahomes, the driver of a Chiefs dynasty and so often the AFC's Super Bowl gateway; and Allen, the starved nearly man banging down on the Championship door only to see dominant talent blunted by his Kansas City counterpart.
Last season's Thanksgiving Day match-up between the Chiefs and the Dallas Cowboys became the most-viewed regular-season NFL game in history with an audience of 57.230 million. This might well shatter that.
- Latest NFL fixtures, results and UK kick-off times
- Get latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Allen arrives 5-1 in their regular-season head-to-head record, while Mahomes leads the rivalry 4-0 where it matters most - in the playoffs. Five of their last six match-ups have also been decided by one score, their most recent seeing the Bills win 28-21 in November 2025.
Mahomes and the Chiefs defeated Allen's Bills in the postseason four times from 2020-2024, including two AFC Championship Games and two Divisional Round match-ups. And when the Chiefs missed out on the playoffs for the first time since 2014 last season, Buffalo failed to capitalise.
Football swings in waves by way of a league that craves parity and a system structured for the purpose of emerging contenders, new storylines, fresh obstacles, unpredictable risers and fallers.
But every once in a while sport throws in a notion of consistency, an unwavering narrative that shall assert itself as the spine of an entire chapter in its history; Mahomes and Allen remain that constant at the forefront of league discussion and debate.
Who is the best? Who is No 1? Mahomes boasts the resume with three Super Bowl rings, five Super Bowl appearances, seven straight AFC Championship Game appearances from 2018-2024 and the angle-defiant, off-script absurdity to arm talent challenging every boundary in the game during that period.
But while Allen lacks the same accolades, the frequency at which he has carried his Bills outfit through the air and on the ground in critical moments as football's most obvious decider, equaliser and game-wrecker has tossed him into perennial MVP status; there may be no team who struggles as dearly were they to lose their quarterback than the Bills with Allen.
Their rivalry is perhaps best epitomised by January 2022's iconic 13-second miracle. With 1.54 remaining Mahomes connected with Tyreek Hill for a 64-yard touchdown, before Allen hit back with a scoring strike to Gabriel Davis that would see Buffalo lead 36-33 with... 13 seconds left.
The game was over. Until it wasn't. Until teams across the NFL were frightened into ever believing they had beaten Mahomes and his Chiefs until the clock hit zero. It was the greatest lesson in the importance of aggression against a team that, at its peak, thrived in the face of shoot-outs.
Mahomes connected on passes to both Hill and Travis Kelce to put the Chiefs in field goal range, where Harrison Butker broke Bills hearts with a 49-yard kick to send the game to overtime. Kansas City would win the toss and then the game as Mahomes returned to Kelce for the deciding touchdown. Allen had been 13 seconds from the AFC Championship Game, but for those pesky Chiefs.
The Bills are 9-1 as they prepare to host the first game between the two teams at Buffalo's new Highmark Stadium, where the Chiefs will arrive 8-2 in their bounce-back season after last January's playoff omission.
Mahomes and the Chiefs have rediscovered the offensive spark absent for the last two or three years, their quarterback feasting on the back of last December's season-ending surgery-requiring knee injury and Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III having ignited Andy Reid's attack since signing in free agency.
The Chiefs offense ranks No 1 in yards per game through 10 weeks, while sitting fourth in passing, fifth in rushing and seventh in scoring following Sunday's 34-7 win over the Arizona Cardinals.
Mahomes has thrown for a sixth-most 2,709 yards for 22 touchdowns to just four interceptions with a third-ranked passer rating of 108.3. With Sunday's performance he has now gone four straight games without throwing a pick, while combining for 1,235 yards and 13 touchdown passes.
He has looked a scary reminder of his former self with tight-window aggression, off-platform invention and out-of-structure magic to enter the Comeback Player of the Year race.
Allen is, meanwhile, riding a six-game winning streak without, in his eyes, playing his best football. He has gone 194 of 302 passing (64.2 per cent) for 2,527 yards and 14 touchdowns to nine interceptions with a passer rating of 93.5, having thrown two picks in Sunday's 26-9 win over the Miami Dolphins.

items.title: Study: Persons with disabilities hold only 1.28pc of jobs in public institutions
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – Persons with disabilities account for just 1.28 per cent of employees in seven public institutions in Kenya, falling short of the statutory requirement that at least 5 per cent of positions be reserved for them.
A new gap analysis found that only 371 of approximately 29,011 e
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – Persons with disabilities account for just 1.28 per cent of employees in seven public institutions in Kenya, falling short of the statutory requirement that at least 5 per cent of positions be reserved for them.
A new gap analysis found that only 371 of approximately 29,011 employees in the institutions that provided workforce data were persons with disabilities, highlighting persistent challenges in implementing disability-inclusive employment policies.
The findings were presented in Nairobi on Wednesday during a meeting convened by the Unlocking Opportunities Programme in partnership with the Mastercard Foundation.
The assessment covered 42 institutions across Embu, Kilifi, Kisumu, Nairobi, Nakuru and Turkana, examining institutional policies, systems and practices relating to employment and government procurement opportunities for persons with disabilities.
Under the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025, employers with 20 or more employees are required to reserve at least 5 per cent of positions for persons with disabilities and provide reasonable accommodation.
However, the study found that of 10 public institutions assessed, only three reported meeting the requirement.
Four did not meet the threshold, while three could not confirm their compliance because the necessary workforce data was unavailable.
The report cautioned that the employment figures were based on institutional submissions and had not been independently verified against complete human resource records.
Beyond recruitment numbers, the assessment identified shortcomings in workplace accessibility, reasonable accommodation and career progression.
Budgetary provision for reasonable accommodation scored 36.7 per cent, while accessibility of digital systems and communication scored 33.3 per cent.
The findings indicate that meeting the employment target requires more than recruiting persons with disabilities, with institutions also needing to invest in assistive technologies, accessible workplaces and opportunities for retention, promotion and leadership.
The study also examined disability participation in government procurement and found some improvement in the share of contracts awarded to businesses owned by persons with disabilities.
Nationally, their share of government procurement awards increased from 9.84 per cent to 14.38 percent.
In the six counties covered by the assessment, the value of contracts awarded to these businesses rose from Sh46.37 million in the 2024/25 financial year to Sh95.46 million in 2025/26. Their share of AGPO awards in the counties increased from 4 per cent to 15.1 per cent.
Despite the gains, the report identified barriers including inaccessible tender information, complex procurement requirements, limited access to finance and delayed payments.
Timely payment scored only 40 percent in the institutional assessment, with the report warning that delays could affect the ability of small businesses to fulfil contracts and compete for further opportunities.
Speaking during the meeting, Senator Isaac Mwaura, Head of the Office of Diversity, Inclusion and Disability Rights in the Executive Office of the President, urged public institutions and employers to turn inclusion commitments into measurable outcomes.
He said businesses owned by persons with disabilities could deliver quality, innovation and value, while employees with disabilities contributed unique perspectives to workplaces.
Charles Warria, Programmes Director at inABLE, speaking on behalf of the Unlocking Opportunities Programme, said the assessment would help identify areas where implementation was falling short and guide practical interventions.
The Public Procurement Regulatory Authority, represented by Deputy Director for Resource Mobilisation and Partnerships Eannes Ongus, said public institutions were making procurement reservations under AGPO, but translating those reservations into actual contract awards remained a challenge.
The report recommends that institutions strengthen disability-inclusive recruitment, improve access to procurement information and digital platforms, ensure timely payments and allocate resources for reasonable accommodation.

items.text:
Overnight RSF drone attacks kill 19 in Sudan
The attacks also injured at least 20 people – the latest casualties in a drone war that is quickly escalating.
At least 19 people have been killed in drone attacks in Sudan’s Blue Nile state.
A Sudanese military source told Al Jazeera that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted the city of Damazin in a series of attacks late on Tuesday that also injured at least 20 people.
The attacks targeted multiple sites across Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile, and the neighbouring town of Roseires.
Three families were killed in the bombing of a residential area in Damazin, the military source said.
According to Emergency Lawyers, a rights group based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, drone attacks also targeted electricity facilities in Damazin and a big dam in Roseires.
Emergency Lawyers said six women were among the dead.
Sudan is currently in the grip of a large-scale civil war between the Khartoum-based Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary group RSF.
The southeastern Blue Nile state is strategically significant because it neighbours some of Sudan’s most unstable regions and is home to some of the SAF’s most experienced fighters, Al Jazeera correspondent Almigdad Alruhaid explained.
Reporting from Omdurman in Sudan, Alruhaid said, “The attacks come amid a sharp escalation in the use of drone attacks between the RSF and the SAF in the last days.”
On November 22, drone attacks in Sudan’s capital area around Khartoum and Omdurman killed at least four people and damaged a United Nations building while staff were inside.
Between January and June this year, at least 1,390 civilians were killed in Sudan – 80 percent of them by drones. In the following four months, another 840 civilians were killed, including about 520 in drone attacks.
“Civilians right now are paying the price. There is no safe zone for civilians, whether in Damazin or in Khartoum,” Alruhaid said.
Three years of war
Civil war broke out in Sudan in 2023 after a power-sharing agreement between two rival camps fell apart following the protest-led ousting of then-President Omar al-Bashir in 2019.
Two rival military leaders emerged in al-Bashir’s wake: Sudan’s de facto ruler Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who now heads the SAF, and his deputy-turned-rival Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as “Hemedti”, who heads the RSF.
Each accuses the other of attacking first and starting the war that is now in its fourth year.
Reports say the war in Sudan has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced about 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine.

items.text:
Spain: Catalan separatist Puigdemont sets date for return
November 25, 2026
Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont said he would return to Spain on December 12, nearly a decade after fleeing the country following a failed independence bid.
The announcement comes just days after Spain's Supreme Court closed criminal proceedings against him under a controversial amnesty law, removing the last legal obstacle to his return.
Speaking at a televised news conference in Brussels, Puigdemont said he would return to the Catalan parliament in Barcelona.
"I left as President of the Government of Catalonia, and I will return to the place where Catalan democracy elects or dismisses its presidents: the Parliament of Catalonia. I will do so on Saturday, 12 December, at midday, and that very night I will be able to sleep at home, with my family," he said.
Puigdemont also announced plans to present a proposal for a renewed push for independence of Catalonia on December 17.
Who is Carles Puigdemont?
Puigdemont is a former president of Catalonia, a wealthy region in northeastern Spain with its own language, culture and a strong independence movement.
He led Catalonia's regional government in October 2017 when it organized a referendum on independence from Spain that Spanish courts had declared illegal.
The vote and the subsequent failed attempt to break away from Spain triggered the country's worst political crisis in decades, deepening tensions between the central government in Madrid and Catalan separatists.
Puigdemont fled to Belgium that same month to avoid arrest and has lived in self-imposed exile ever since.
His "Junts per Catalunya" party remains an important force in Spanish politics and played a key role in securing the parliamentary support needed for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to remain in power in 2023.
Why has Puigdemont now been cleared to return to Spain?
Spain's Supreme Court on Monday shelved the criminal case against Puigdemont after applying an amnesty law passed by parliament in 2024.
In a ruling dated November 20, the court determined that the amnesty had extinguished any potential criminal liability for Puigdemont and two other separatist figures.
The decision followed a Constitutional Court ruling in October that extended the amnesty to cover embezzlement allegations linked to Catalonia's independence bid.
The Supreme Court had initially ruled that the law did not apply to those investigated for embezzlement, including Puigdemont.
Following the Constitutional Court's intervention, the Supreme Court lifted the arrest warrant against him. Monday's decision to close the criminal proceedings completed the legal process, allowing him to return without facing detention over the 2017 case.
Why is Spain's Catalan amnesty law controversial?
The amnesty was a key concession by Sanchez to Catalan separatist parties, including Puigdemont's Junts, in exchange for their support following Spain's inconclusive 2023 general election.
The agreement allowed Sanchez to secure another term as prime minister but sparked strong opposition from conservative parties and critics who accused him of putting his political survival ahead of Spain's interests.
The conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox opposed the legislation and unsuccessfully challenged it in parliament and the courts.
The controversy intensified after Puigdemont said in a recent interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo that his party had exploited Sanchez's ambition to secure concessions for Catalonia.
"We had to test how far we could go," Puigdemont said, calling Sanchez "an amoral person with an excessive thirst for power".
"We have exploited this excessive ambition for power to inflict certain defeats on Spain that we would otherwise not have been able to bring about."
His remarks became a flashpoint in the campaign ahead of Spain's snap general election on November 29.
Polls suggest the Popular Party is likely to win the most seats but fall short of an outright majority, potentially leaving it dependent on Vox to form a government.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – The Mwananchi Party has rescheduled its National Aspirant Forum from November 30 to December 1, 2026, with party leader Babu Owino expected to engage prospective candidates seeking to contest on its ticket in the 2027 General Election.
In a statement, the party said the forum will be held at its headquarters along Mukinduri Road in Karen, Nairobi, between 10am and 2pm.
The meeting will bring together registered aspirants from across the country to familiarise themselves with the party’s nomination procedures, campaign strategy and expectations for candidates seeking elective positions.
The forum will also provide an opportunity for aspirants to engage directly with the party leadership as the movement prepares for the next election cycle.
The programme will feature training on nomination rules, a joint campaign strategy session and a dedicated engagement with party leader Babu Owino and patron Kavutia Kirana.
During the nomination training, aspirants will receive guidance on eligibility requirements, nomination procedures, timelines and the standards expected of candidates seeking the Mwananchi Party ticket.
The campaign strategy session will focus on coordinated messaging, grassroots mobilisation and collaboration across constituencies and counties.
The party said attendance will be restricted to individuals already registered on its aspirant platform to ensure an orderly and productive engagement.

items.text:
Ex England star Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
Raheem Sterling admitted inhaling ‘laughing gas’ and driving erratically before crashing his car.
Former England winger Raheem Sterling has been spared an immediate jail sentence after he admitted dangerous driving by inhaling “laughing gas” while behind the wheel before crashing his Lamborghini.
Sterling, 31, was reported driving erratically on the M25 and M3 motorways in southern England during the morning rush hour on May 28, with witnesses saying ‌he was inhaling from a balloon and weaving between lanes.
Police later found Sterling sitting in the passenger seat of his crashed car holding two canisters of nitrous oxide. No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.
Sterling, who most recently played for Dutch side Feyenoord, pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide and failing to provide a blood specimen.
He appeared for sentencing on Wednesday at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court where Judge Kirsty Allman said Sterling had acted with “conscious disregard for the safety of other ‌road users”.
She sentenced Sterling to 12 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, and ‌ordered ‌him to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are
items.text:
Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.
U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.
There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.
Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.
Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.
For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.
"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.
Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.
"The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.
Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.
"Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."
The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.
In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.
Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer.

items.text:
Sinner uncertain for Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery
The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon in July.
Jannik Sinner risks missing the Australian Open in January after confirming that he has undergone surgery on his troublesome right knee.
The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon for the second time in July, with less than two months until the start of the first major tournament of the season in Melbourne.
“Over the past few months, together with my team we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery,” Sinner said in a statement on Tuesday.
“After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we had all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band.”
The procedure, which had been reported earlier in the day by broadcasters RAI and Sky Sport, and sports daily La Gazzetta dello Sport, was performed by knee injury specialist Lasse Lempainen at a clinic in Finland.
Another knee specialist, Fabrizio Terrone at the Isokinetic centre in Turin, told Sky Sport that Sinner’s absence could last “at least three to four months”.
That means the earliest Sinner might be back on court with a racket in hand would be during the American hard-court swing, at Indian Wells and Miami Masters.
The 25-year-old admitted recently that the worst injury of his career left him barely able to move.
“The worst part for me about this injury is that I cannot compete, I cannot play tennis,” said Sinner in a recent video.
“Also, my life outside of tennis is a bit more limited because of a simple fact that I cannot do things that I really like, because I want to protect my knee.”
Sinner, a two-time champion at the Australian Open which begins on January 17, recently said that he will make his comeback at the “Six Kings Slam” tournament in Saudi Arabia, which has been rescheduled for late December due to the conflict with Yemen’s Houthis.
But that now looks impossible and a difficult start to 2027 seems in store for the man who has in recent years risen to be, alongside Spanish star Carlos Alcaraz, the pre-eminent force in men’s tennis.
Sinner was having a brilliant campaign before being stopped by his knee problem, with five Masters 1000 titles going alongside his triumph at Wimbledon.
The Italian’s 94 percent winning record in 2026 is the best of his career, even beating his figures from the previous two seasons in each of which he won two Grand Slams and the ATP Finals.
He suffered a major disappointment at the French Open when, leading Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerundolo by two sets and 5-1 ahead in the third, he succumbed to heatstroke and was eliminated in the second round.
Sinner recently lost top spot in the men’s world rankings to losing Wimbledon finalist Alexander Zverev, who has taken advantage of injury problems for both Sinner and Alcaraz to win Roland Garros and the US Open.

Counting the Cost
After Brexit, is Britain heading back to the EU?
Ten years after Britain voted to leave the European Union, London and Brussels have struck a deal to bring their economies closer.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Brexit “has not worked” and would like to see Britain rejoin in his lifetime.
But not in this parliament, and he is sticking to the Labour Party’s red lines on the single market, the customs union and free movement.
Critics say he has no mandate to reopen the debate. Burnham says it is up to voters.
United States President Donald Trump welcomed the Brexit vote. Now his tariffs are one reason Britain and the EU see more to gain together.

items.title: Raheem Sterling avoids jail over reckless driving while using nitrous oxide
items.summary:
Raheem Sterling has avoided jail for dangerous driving while inhaling nitrous oxide, receiving a 12-month sentence suspended for 18 months at Basingstoke magistrates court on Wednesday.
The former England international was also ordered to do 100 hours of community service. His MBE and charitable and
items.text:
Raheem Sterling has avoided jail for dangerous driving while inhaling nitrous oxide, receiving a 12-month sentence suspended for 18 months at Basingstoke magistrates court on Wednesday.
The former England international was also ordered to do 100 hours of community service. His MBE and charitable and foundation work was accepted in mitigation, together with his decision to voluntarily submit to addiction treatment.
Sterling pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving after driving his Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide in May.
The court heard in September that the former Chelsea and Manchester City forward embarked on a prolonged period of reckless driving on the M25 and M3, inhaling nitrous oxide balloons, before crashing his £270,000 car.
Sterling also admitted possession of nitrous oxide and refusing to provide a specimen and was disqualified from driving.
Simon Jones, prosecuting, told the court one witness had “genuine concerns the driver might kill someone” and described Sterling’s driving as “absolutely horrendous”.
The 31-year-old Sterling has been without a club since he his short-term contract with Feyenoord expired at the end of last season.

items.text:
US Army to detonate unstable lead-based explosives in Iowa
November 25, 2026
The United States Army plans to detonate about 5 tons of aging lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant on Wednesday, saying the explosive chemical has become too unstable to store.
The controlled blast is set for 9 am local time (1500 GMT) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, and will destroy the country's entire stockpile of the chemical.
The US army has said residents of a small town and other nearby areas should leave "out of an abundance of caution."
"We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic," said acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling."
What do we know?
The material was moved to Iowa for storage from bases around the country in 2009.
But a March inspection found that it had partly crystallized, which makes it sensitive to friction and cold and could set off a spontaneous explosion.
"Inaction is no longer an option," said Major General Eric Shirley, who leads the operation.
Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, told reporters: "It's not a matter of if, it's a matter of when, and that would not be a great place for us to be in."
Is it safe to detonate the chemical?
To limit toxic lead dust, the Army has built barriers around the bunkers holding the material and will use foam and water to trap particles.
Reuters reported that Army projections show dust could settle up to 40 miles (64 km) southwest, reaching northern Missouri.
Officials expect the wind to carry the plume away from Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people.
While residents within 5 miles (8 km) were encouraged to evacuate, the Federal Emergency Management Agency has also advised people 5 to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed.
How have people reacted?
The date of the detonation changed three times after public backlash. A federal appeals court cleared the plan on Monday after environmental groups sued.
Farmer Jill Holler, who organised a protest, told Reuters: "I'm not opposed if this is the only safe option."
"What I'm saying is that it's been so mishandled that people are confused and don't trust anything they're saying," she added.

items.title: Sterling given suspended jail sentence for dangerous driving
items.summary:
Raheem Sterling: Former England international given suspended 12-month jail sentence for dangerous driving
Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in September and admitted possession of six nitrous oxide cannisters for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen.
items.text:
Raheem Sterling: Former England international given suspended 12-month jail sentence for dangerous driving
Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in September and admitted possession of six nitrous oxide cannisters for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen.
Wednesday 25 November 2026 11:37, UK
Former England player Raheem Sterling has been given a suspended 12-month jail sentence for dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after a crash involving a Lamborghini on the motorway.
Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in September to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed on May 28. The sentence is suspended for 18 months.
He has also been handed a two-year driving ban and must undertake 100 hours of unpaid community work. Sterling will have to re-take a driving test to hold a licence.
The 31-year-old admitted possession of six nitrous oxide cannisters for wrongful inhalation, a class C drug, and failing to provide a specimen.
Sterling scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate's side reach the 2018 World Cup semi-finals and the final of Euro 2020. He came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut.
Sterling, who was born in Kingston, Jamaica, moved to Manchester City in 2015 and won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the FA Cup in 2019. He left for Chelsea in 2022 but after falling out of favour spent the 2024/25 season on loan at Arsenal.
Sterling joined Dutch club Feyenoord on a short-term deal until the end of the 2025/26 season. He is currently without a club.
In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport after fronting anti-racism and discrimination campaigns and speaking out strongly against racism on and off the pitch for several years.
It came amid controversy over England fans booing players taking the knee at matches as a gesture against intolerance.

items.summary:
Zidane was much better than me: Bellingham after Real Madrid wonder goal

Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham has brushed aside comparisons with football great Zinedine Zidane followin
items.text:
Zidane was much better than me: Bellingham after Real Madrid wonder goal
Jude Bellingham admits he had ‘no idea’ what he’d done after scoring a goal that drew comparisons with Zinadine Zidane.
Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham has brushed aside comparisons with football great Zinedine Zidane following his sensational goal against PSV in the Champions League.
The England international came on at half-time with Los Blancos trailing and inspired a sensational second-half display, including a magnificent effort from distance, at the Santiago Bernabeu on Tuesday.
Bellingham said he “did not know” how he scored his brilliant goal, flicking the ball up on the edge of the box and slicing a stunning effort inside the far post.
Having seen an acrobatic volley blocked minutes earlier, the England midfielder controlled Kylian Mbappe’s pass with two touches in the air and curled a superb shot into the far corner from well outside the area.
“I have no idea what I did,” Bellingham told RMTV. “I had the ball in a good position and thought about shooting.”
The 23-year-old, upon joining Real Madrid, took Zidane’s number five shirt in “homage” to the Frenchman, whom he admired, and some have compared his goal to a Zidane-style strike.
“I do things that you guys think are similar to Zidane, but he was much better than me,” Bellingham told reporters.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho hailed Bellingham’s game-changing display as the midfielder gave Mourinho credit for helping him find arguably the best form he has enjoyed at Madrid in recent weeks, with Los Blancos winning a 10th straight match, but the coach said the midfielder only had himself to thank.
“I think the main figure responsible for what Jude is today is Jude, and his teammates. I try to help a little,” said the Portuguese coach.
“He’s an absolutely extraordinary player who has everything – he has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything and today, obviously not by himself, but he changed the direction of the match.”
“He’s an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world,” Mourinho said.
Madrid’s victory over the Dutch champions maintained their 100 percent start to the league phase, in which they are provisional leaders.
Mourinho reiterated his view that it was a “scandal” that Bellingham was not ranked in the top 10 players in the world at this year’s Ballon d’Or ceremony.
Mbappe netted twice to put Real out of sight before Vinicius Jr got in on the act with a late goal, having struck the post twice earlier in the game.

items.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
items.summary:
