Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat w
items.text:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.
Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.
In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.
Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.
A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.
The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”
She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.
Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”
A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”
Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.
Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”
She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.
Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.
Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

Israeli strike kills Hamas official, his wife and children

An Israeli air attack on Gaza has killed a senior Palestinian security official and his wife and daughters, according to a statement from the enc
items.text:
Israeli strike kills Hamas official, his wife and children
The air strike hit their Gaza apartment amid escalated Israeli attacks, Interior Ministry says.
An Israeli air attack on Gaza has killed a senior Palestinian security official and his wife and daughters, according to a statement from the enclave’s Ministry of Interior.
In a statement posted on its Telegram channel on Wednesday, the ministry identified the official as Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47, director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza.
Noura Ezzat Abual-Awf, his wife, aged 41, and his children, Yusra Mohammed Abu al-Awf, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Awf, 13, were also killed in the strike, the statement added.
The ministry described the killings as a “horrific massacre perpetrated by the Israeli occupation forces when they bombed [the family’s] residence in the Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, at dawn today”.
The attack is part of “ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society”, it added.
The strike comes less than 24 hours after the killing of the Internal Security Service’s director general, Brigadier-General Naim Abu Nahal.
Israeli attacks continue
Israeli strikes reported overnight killed several people, according to medical sources.
A source at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed to Al Jazeera that four people from the same family were killed and several others were wounded in an Israeli attack on a residential apartment in the Shati refugee camp.
Separately, medical sources at the Nasser Medical Complex reported that a Palestinian girl was shot by Israeli forces in areas outside their control in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip.
Daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza have been recorded since October 2025, with Israeli air attacks regularly targeting the enclave and at least 1,680 people killed and more than 6,000 injured as Israel’s genocidal war continues.
Hamas called on the guarantor states of the “ceasefire” deal to intervene immediately “to rein in the occupation, impose a halt to its crimes, and obligate it to adhere to the agreement’s path”.

The 48-year-old replaces Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge following a run of seven defeats in their p
items.text:
Watford appoint Iordanescu as head coach
- Published
Watford have appointed former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu as the Championship club's new head coach.
The 48-year-old replaces Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge following a run of seven defeats in their past 10 league games, culminating in Saturday's 4-0 loss to Sheffield United.
"I am very proud and happy to be at this football club," Iordanescu told the club website., external
"I can see the team is in a difficult moment but I have already watched many of the games over the last few days and I'm very confident about the future."
He becomes Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.
- Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford 
  - Published1 day ago
The former CFR Cluj and Legia Warsaw manager will be joined at Watford by backroom staff Alexandru Radu, Grzegorz Mokry and Michele Iannucci, but will watch Wednesday's Championship match at home to Blackburn Rovers from the stands before taking charge for Saturday's game at Derby.
Adrian Mariappa will oversee Wednesday's match at Vicarage Road (19:45 GMT), alongside Paul Furlong and Lloyd Doyley.
The Watford job is Iordanescu's first since leaving Legia Warsaw in October 2025, where he won the Super Cup last season.
It is the 10th managerial post of his 15-year coaching career, which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj - who he guided to the Romanian title and two domestic cups after joining midway through the 2020-21 season.
He also spent two-and-a-half years in charge of Romania, guiding them to the last 16 of Euro 2024, where they were beaten by the Netherlands.
Iordanescu takes over a Watford side currently three points above the relegation zone, having won only four of their 16 games so far.
Who is Iordanescu and what is he facing?
Although untried in English football, Watford are getting a trophy-winning head coach with a wide-ranging CV spanning spells in his homeland, Bulgaria and Poland, as well as elite-level international experience with Romania.
His connections with his national side run deep as the son of his country's legendary former head coach Anghel Iordanescu, who famously took them to the quarter-finals of the 1994 World Cup during a reign of more than 100 games.
It is likely he will need every bit of that nous and inspiration as he becomes the latest boss to try to revive a club which continues to plough through managers at an alarming rate.
Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, with Iordanescu becoming the sixth permanent boss since Tom Cleverley was sacked in May 2025.
The Hornets' slow start to the season - with only four home wins and one point out of 24 away - has played out against the backdrop of uncertainty and unrest off the pitch.
Watford's owner, Gino Pozzo, is currently standing trial in Spain as one of a number of defendants accused of tax offences relating to Spanish team Granada, a club he used to be associated with.
He denies the allegations, which are related to player trading at Granada.
The case continues a tumultuous period for the club, with supporter and former owner Elton John voicing his frustration after a 4-0 home defeat by Burnley last month.
Fans have also questioned the running of the club, with one supporters' group declaring a loss of confidence in the ownership.
Iordanescu's immediate concern will be improving results, particularly Watford's form on the road, where they have yet to win and have conceded 18 goals in eight matches - with only Burnley letting in more.
He arrives with a reputation for defensive organisation and stability, which the Hornets are in deseprate need of.
Iordanescu 'thrown in at deep end' - analysis
Geoff Doyle, BBC Three Counties Radio sports editor
So Watford try again with a new head coach - it is a regular occurrence at Vicarage Road.
Iordanescu has a decent CV with his work overseas in Romania, Bulgaria and Poland and is well thought of as a coach and manager.
But a lack of Championship experience is a concern and he is thrown in at the deep end with his new team hovering just above the relegation zone and confidence and morale low.
Iordanescu needs to hit the ground running in a critical week with the Hornets up against mid-table Blackburn and then Derby who are in the relegation zone.

items.text:
Arthur Rinderknech denies refusing to take anti-doping test after charge confirmed for French tennis player
French newspaper L'Equipe reported Arthur Rinderknech's alleged refusal to take doping test; International ‌Tennis Integrity Agency has since confirmed charge; former Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova handed four-year ban in June after tribunal found she refused test
Wednesday 25 November 2026 11:15, UK
France's Arthur Rinderknech is confident he will be cleared of an alleged refusal to undergo a doping test.
The International ‌Tennis Integrity Agency [ITIA] confirmed on Wednesday that the 31-year-old had been charged for refusing a test in Brittany in June after French newspaper L'Equipe initially reported in their story that he was facing a four-year ban.
Rinderknech denied the allegation on Instagram, while stressing that he has never taken a banned substance and revealing he has asked for the matter to be heard by an independent tribunal.
- Keep track of the full tennis schedule live on Sky Sports
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW
The ITIA said in a statement: "Following media reports and the player's social media post, we can confirm that Arthur Rinderknech has been charged with refusing a test.
"We go to great lengths to keep cases confidential, and we are disappointed that the details have become public in this way.
"The case will be heard by an independent tribunal early next year and we will not be commenting further on the specifics of the investigation."
The ITIA also explained that the maximum length ban Rinderknech could face if found to have refused a test is four years, but could be up to two years if the panel determines there is no significant fault.
Rinderknech: I have never taken any banned substance
Rinderknech had earlier written: "I am aware of the reports regarding my alleged test refusal case with the ITIA which according to the ITIA, was supposed to be kept strictly confidential.
"I have already advised the ITIA that I deny the allegation, and I have ‌already requested that the matter be heard and determined by an independent tribunal as is my right.
"It is my belief that when the matter is presented to the independent tribunal I will be exonerated of the test refusal allegation.
"I have never taken any banned substance and I am proud of my accomplishments in professional tennis, all of which have been achieved through hard work and with integrity always."
Former Wimbledon women's champion Marketa Vondrousova received a four-year ban in June after an independent tribunal found she refused an anti-doping test in December 2025, with the Czech since appealing to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
Rinderknech has a highest career ranking of 24 and reached the final of the Shanghai Masters 1000 event in 2025 before losing in straight sets to cousin ‌Valentin Vacherot of Monaco.
Rinderknech's best Grand Slam result is reaching the fourth round of the US Open last year, while he beat current world No 1 Alexander Zverev in the first round of Wimbledon in 2025.

items.text:
Lincoln sack head coach duo Cohen and Shaw
- Published
Lincoln City have sacked their head coaches Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw just six months after they took joint charge of the Championship side.
The pair departed a little over 12 hours after they oversaw a 4-0 defeat at fellow strugglers Charlton Athletic on Tuesday.
The loss leaves the Imps just three points above the relegation places in what is the club's first season back in the second tier for 65 years.
Cohen and Shaw were assistant coaches under Michael Skubala when Lincoln were promoted as League One title winners last season.
They were surprisingly promoted to replace their boss as a joint managerial double act.

The expanded programme will take effect in the current finan
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – The government is expanding the Public Service Internship Programme (PSIP) from 8,000 to 50,000 internship opportunities annually in a move aimed at improving youth employability and practical workplace experience.
The expanded programme will take effect in the current financial year, providing young people with opportunities to acquire on-the-job skills and experience to enhance their prospects in both the public and private sectors.
The expansion was discussed on Wednesday during a Public Service Internship Programme stakeholders’ consultative meeting at the Kenya School of Government in Nairobi.
The meeting was led by Head of Public Service Felix Koskei and brought together senior government officials and representatives of public institutions to deliberate on the implementation of the expanded internship programme.
In a statement following the meeting, Rûkû GK said the initiative was intended to equip young people with practical skills and workplace experience that would improve their employability locally and internationally.
The meeting was attended by Principal Secretary for Public Service and Human Capital Development Professor Jane Kere Imbunya, other principal secretaries, chairpersons and commissioners of constitutional commissions, and holders of independent offices.
Also in attendance were chairpersons and chief executives of state corporations and government agencies, vice-chancellors of public universities and other senior government officials.
The consultations focused on the implementation of the expanded internship interventions and coordination among government institutions expected to support the programme.

items.title: Search for next USMNT head coach needs to prioritize competence over fame

items.text:
First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it.
But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work. Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players.
The federation has already begun its search for a successor to Pochettino. The Argentine oversaw just over two years at the head of the USMNT, a successful if hardly transformative period, but has now set off on a bold quest to cure Manchester United of their misery. “Our guide for the types of managers that we would consider is not based on the level of fame or celebrity,” the federation’s chief operating office, Dan Helfrich, told the Athletic. “But it is based on a very high standard of excellence, and ambition, and talent, and experience, and belief”. There was more such word-salad pabulum about moving “at the pace that the situation dictates”, but the long and short of it is that US Soccer is apparently willing to consider any candidate at all.
The federation expects to have the same type of billionaire donor backing that underwrote Pochettino’s $6m annual salary – which was about double that of Jürgen Klinsmann, the previous highest-earning USMNT manager. Much of it came from hedge-funder Ken Griffin, who got better value out of the last-16 World Cup performance posted by Pochettino than the $40m he set on fire supporting Republicans in the midterm election.
Helfrich is right in surmising that it makes little sense to prioritize resume over compatibility in the new man, assuming that it is a man and dismissing, with great prejudice, TNT analyst Kyle Martino’s half-cocked idea of putting Emma Hayes in charge of both senior national team programs, as if coaching the women’s team somehow isn’t a full-time job on its own.
It’s nice that the federation can afford just about anyone these days, and a stark departure from previous coaching searches. In 1991, Bora Milutinović got the gig in part because he was far cheaper than any of the other seasoned international coaches, although the Serb seems to have compensated for this by having his salary sent to some kind of offshore holding company. But at this stage of the cycle, and without a seminal World Cup looming on a home soil, nevermind a slumping core of key players to kickstart, the job is different.
Presently this isn’t a sales job in the way it was before this summer. And even if it were, it’s debatable whether having even a manager with Pochettino’s stature moved the needle in the American mainstream. Pochettino was rarely seen on any of the remaining TV shows of influence, or, but for a single hit on the Pat McAfee Show, on the podcasts that now set the agenda. He didn’t go on the late-night talk shows, the sort of thing even his affectless predecessor, Bob Bradley, managed to do. No amount of soccer coaching fame, it seems, suffices to gain traction in the today’s fractured media landscape … short of, perhaps, Guardiola’s.
Which begs the question of whether paying for Pochettino’s fame premium yielded a return off the field. Mind you, the 54-year-old was, and presumably remains, a good coach. His appointment made sense for the stage the USMNT was in. But his successor will stare down three-and-a-half years of Concacaf tournaments and World Cup qualifiers, with a Copa América in the summer of 2028. That’s a lot of trips to San Pedro Sula and Port of Spain and the Azteca.
The work of refreshing a golden generation that will be at the tail end of their primes by 2030 and integrating the latest wave of tantalizingly talented teenagers is presently more urgent than proselytizing. Right now, the program doesn’t need an exciting figurehead; it needs a competent bureaucrat who will quietly do the finnicky work of fine-tuning a team that’s trending upwards.
And so Steve Cherundolo and BJ Callaghan may not excite in the way that a name with a fun pronunciation that you recall seeing in the Premier League might, but generating buzz isn’t in the job description just now; ensuring continuity and parlaying momentum from six straight post-World Cup wins is. Better to do it with a coach who already knows the player pool and the path through all the unexciting bits of the World Cup cycle.
- Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Holders Northamptonshire Steelbacks begin their defence away at Hampshire Hawks on the opening day of the tournament, in a repeat of the 2026 final.
The 18 counties have again been split into three groups of six, with each team playing 12 matches, six at home and six away. Counties will play the other five sides in their group home and away, then two matches - one home and one away - against two different sides from outside of their group.
Gloucestershire have changed their name for the T20 Blast and are now known as Bristol Lions going forward.
The top two teams in each group will qualify for the quarter-finals, in addition to two best third-placed teams, with all quarter-finals currently scheduled to take place on Wednesday July 15 ahead of Men's Finals Day at Edgbaston on Saturday July 17.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Three fishermen have died after their fishing boat collided with a ship travelling from Kisumu to Tanzania at Kibuogi Beach in Suba South Constituency, Homa Bay County.
The accident occurred at around 9pm on Tuesday while the fishermen were out on a fishing expedition.
The deceased have been identified as Erick Ouma, 40, Joseph Ogolla, 38, and Pasaka Kanonge, 42.
Sindo Sub-Location Assistant Chief Caroline Ngere said the ship rammed into the fishermen’s boat, leaving three people missing.
One fisherman survived the accident, while a search operation is underway to retrieve the bodies of the deceased.
Ngere appealed to emergency response teams to expedite the search and recovery operation to enable the families to accord the victims a decent burial.
She also urged fishermen operating on Lake Victoria to prioritise their safety by wearing life jackets whenever they venture into the lake.
The administrator noted that the use of the safety equipment could help prevent fatalities in similar accidents.
“Fishermen should make wearing life jackets a routine whenever they go out fishing,” Ngere urged.

items.title: COP31’s setback underscores the importance of China’s climate leadership
items.summary:

items.text:
The failure of COP31 to reach a comprehensive agreement was a disappointment for the global climate community. But amid the frustration, one message stood out. The fight against climate change must continue through cooperation, practical action and a shared commitment to a greener future.
China’s response to the conference’s outcome reflected that conviction.
As COP31 ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact, China’s Vice Minister of Ecology and Environment, Li Gao, expressed disappointment but urged countries not to lose faith in multilateralism. His message was that climate change is too pressing a challenge for nations to retreat into blame or abandon cooperation.
It was a reminder that progress on climate action is not always determined by the outcome of a single conference. It is also built through sustained investment, technological innovation, national commitments and the practical solutions countries bring to the global effort.
China has increasingly demonstrated that commitment through its green transformation.
The country’s expanding renewable energy capacity, investments in clean technology and growing role in the global supply chain for solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are helping reshape the energy landscape. These developments are not only transforming China’s economy but also creating opportunities for countries around the world to accelerate their own transitions to cleaner energy.
A recent opinion article in the Financial Times highlighted the scale of China’s contribution, pointing to growth in renewable electricity generation and developments in its emissions trajectory. It argued that the global climate conversation should pay greater attention to the country’s progress in clean energy.
China’s expansion of solar power has been particularly remarkable. Its investments have helped drive down the cost of renewable technologies, making solar energy increasingly accessible to countries seeking alternatives to traditional energy sources.
The impact extends beyond electricity generation. Chinese innovation and manufacturing in batteries, electric vehicles, wind energy and other green technologies are helping accelerate the global transition towards lower-carbon economies.
For developing countries, this contribution is especially significant. The transition to cleaner energy requires technology that is affordable, scalable and capable of meeting growing demand. China’s manufacturing capacity and technological advances are helping make that possible.
Africa stands to benefit considerably.
The continent faces the twin challenges of expanding energy access and building resilience against the effects of climate change. Millions of people still lack reliable electricity, while droughts, floods and changing weather patterns continue to affect communities, agriculture and livelihoods.
The transition to a greener economy must therefore go hand in hand with development, industrialisation, job creation and improved living standards.
China’s growing role in renewable energy offers Africa an opportunity to pursue these objectives. Affordable solar technology can help expand electricity access in underserved communities. Battery storage can improve reliability. Electric mobility can support cleaner transport systems, while investments in green manufacturing could create jobs and strengthen local economies.
The opportunity goes beyond importing technology. African countries can use partnerships with China to develop skills, strengthen industrial capacity, attract investment and build their own renewable-energy ecosystems.
Kenya, with its strong renewable-energy base and ambitions to expand clean power, is particularly well positioned to benefit from global advances in green technology. Greater access to affordable solar equipment, battery storage and electric mobility solutions could complement existing investments and help accelerate the country’s transition.
The wider lesson is that climate action must deliver tangible benefits to people. It should lower energy costs, improve access, create opportunities and strengthen economies while protecting the environment.
China’s approach has increasingly connected environmental objectives with economic transformation. Its investment in clean-energy industries demonstrates how climate action can become a driver of innovation, manufacturing, employment and new economic opportunities.
That experience offers valuable lessons for countries seeking to pursue development while building more sustainable economies.
The outcome of COP31 also reinforces the importance of international cooperation. Climate change does not respect borders, and no country can address it alone. Differences over climate finance, energy pathways and development priorities remain, but they should strengthen the case for dialogue rather than weaken the commitment to collective action.
China has reaffirmed its commitment to advancing its climate goals, accelerating green transformation and working with other countries towards a shared future. Its engagement in the negotiations and its investments at home demonstrate the importance it attaches to both international cooperation and practical climate action.
The global transition will require contributions from governments, businesses, scientists, communities and international partners. It will also require countries to learn from one another and recognise that progress can take different forms depending on national circumstances.
COP31 may have ended without the agreement many hoped for. But the momentum behind renewable energy, green technology and sustainable development continues.

items.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals
items.summary: Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. items.text:
Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio.
Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer.
The next day, the small group of Argentines went to Alfredo Saad’s apartment in Copacabana, where Maradona and Pelé sat for an hour discussing football and life. ‘It was all great, they chatted, Pelé got out his guitar, he sang some songs, it was really nice,’ Blanco recalled. ‘Then there was a moment when it got a bit deep when Pelé started to give Diego some advice. He took Diego’s hand and he started giving him counsel. “Look after your body. Remember to always train. There’s a lot of responsibility on your shoulders.” It was like a premonition. Everything that would happen to Diego, Pelé, with all his experience, was telling him would happen.’ Before they left, Pelé hugged Maradona’s father and gave his son a signed ball, a Brazil shirt and a Pelé watch. The friendship between the players appeared to be sealed. ‘I knew Pelé was a God as a player,’ Maradona said. ‘Now that I’ve met him, I know he is as a person, too.’
Those present that sunny afternoon in Rio could never have imagined how the paths of the two men would diverge, overlap and collide, like wingers and full-backs determined to get the better of each other. Their mutual admiration survived for a few more years but when it soured, it soured royally and the fallout made headlines around the world. They were often described as rivals but what they really had was a love-hate relationship fuelled by South American nationalism and grandiose egos. Adding even more spice were the moralistic subtexts of good vs evil, the establishment vs the people, and the conformist vs the rebel. They were two completely different people and everyone took a side. Maradona summed it up perfectly: ‘We’re oil and water.’
The first cracks in their friendship appeared three years after their Rio meeting, when Pelé criticised Maradona’s performance at the 1982 World Cup. The Brazilian agreed to write a syndicated column during the tournament, and before it even kicked off he predicted that Zico would make more of an impact than Maradona. In a sentence that would drive the first wedge between them, he questioned not just Maradona’s ability but his character. ‘My biggest doubt,’ Pelé wrote, ‘lies in knowing if Diego has sufficient greatness in his person to justify the honours that the world audience pays him.’
Pelé’s scepticism turned out to be entirely justified. Maradona lost the plot in Argentina’s second-round match against Brazil and was sent off after stamping on Batista in the dying minutes of their 3-1 loss. The defeat meant the champions were out and Maradona, as Pelé predicted, had failed to live up to the hype. In his column the next day, Pelé piled on the misery, calling Maradona ‘an immature young man, who almost hasn’t had the time to transform himself into the great player that many people blindly state that he is’.
To Maradona, the words were a betrayal. He had considered Pelé a friend and an ally, and he never forgot how the Brazilian became one of the first major figures to cast aspersions on his talent and character. Maradona was hardly a paragon of loyalty – he fought with just about everyone who ever loved him – but he demanded fealty from everyone else and Pelé’s slight wounded him deeply. And yet it took a while for his anger to show. Maradona was just 21 and a long way from becoming the all-conquering superstar who would wow the world. He had opinions but he was still shy about speaking out, not yet sure how good he would really be. It was only after leading Argentina to victory in 1986 that his ego exploded and he started reacting to his critics. It was then, after the world united in appointing him as the successor to Pelé’s throne, that he began assailing everyone who questioned his greatness.
It took a while, but Pelé saw what was happening and he realised he had to react. He began defending his legacy and the rivalry between the two men was up and running. For almost his entire career, Pelé was recognised as the greatest footballer of all time. Rivals had come and gone but none posed a lasting threat to the coveted title. Peers such as Alfredo Di Stéfano, Eusébio and Johan Cruyff all had the talent to threaten his supremacy but they and their supporting casts were either not good enough or not consistent enough to keep their teams at the top for extended periods, especially at international level.
Maradona was different and Pelé knew it. He wasn’t just brilliant, he also played for a nation that produced enough quality players to help him win the titles he needed to be considered extra-special. Crucially, like few players before or since, he had both an aura about him as well as a gift for making the players around him better. He never won anything single-handedly, as many people liked to say, but when he was on form his teammates grew in stature and together they became more than just the sum of their parts.
His performances in leading Argentina to the World Cup in 1986 were so remarkable that Pelé started playing up his own achievements and subtly questioning those of his rival. While the rest of the world marvelled at football’s new messiah, Pelé would grumpily ask how anyone could

items.title: Has a footballer had a longer career hiatus than Ronaldinho’s 11 year-gap? | The Knowledge
items.summary:
“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”
Ronaldinho’s last professional appearance
items.text:
“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”
Ronaldinho’s last professional appearance before his return for Ravenna came on 26 September 2015 for Fluminense, who won 2-0 at home against Goiás. He was withdrawn after 45 minutes. Fans of symmetry will be pleased to see that 11 years and 50 days later, the Brazilian returned for Ravenna in a 2-0 home win against another team with five letters and an accent in their name, Forlì, and was withdrawn after 45 minutes.
Considering he is now 46 and was playing against a team containing a couple of players 26 years his junior, his 25 touches, one key pass (in the buildup to the opening goal) and 81% passing accuracy in a single half is better than respectable. And nope, stats weren’t available for tracking back and we don’t imagine he ranked too highly on that metric … but he’s 46! Only time will tell if the World Cup winner plays again. “It was amazing,” he beamed after the match. “I got more than 30 minutes under my belt and feel good. I didn’t really want to come off. It was all over in a flash. I’m still not sure if this will be my only appearance, but if the president comes calling, I’ll be back.”
But back to the question. There have been a few high-profile returns following a player’s initial “retirement”. In 2012 Paul Scholes jumped back into Manchester United’s midfield seven months after hanging up his boots to help out amid an injury crisis and played for another 18 months, helping United to seal their 20th league title in May 2013. Arjen Robben resumed his career at his boyhood club, Groningen, a year after calling time at Bayern Munich.
A more curious example is that of the former Argentina goalkeeper Carlos Roa, who at his peak and aged 30, took a retreat from football to focus on his faith with reports suggesting he anticipated the year 2000 being the end of the world. A devout Christian, Roa went to live with his family in a secluded area of Argentina to prepare for the apocalypse. When it didn’t come, he resumed his career at Mallorca a year after his last appearance but never played for the national team again.
But these tales get us nowhere near to Ronaldinho. Gareth Barry had a four-and-a-half-year hiatus between his retirement as a professional at West Brom in 2020 and his return to playing again at Hurstpierpoint in the Mid Sussex League Championship in February 2025 – not at professional level but still pretty competitive. Jürgen Klinsmann made a similar return to playing at amateur level five years after “retiring”. Klinsmann scored on his farewell appearance for Tottenham in a 1-1 draw with Southampton on the last day of the 1997-98 Premier League season. However, aged 39, he came back under the pseudonym “Jay Göppingen” and scored five goals in eight appearances for Orange County Blue Star, a team in the Premier Development League (then the fourth tier of the US pyramid).
Maybe Ronaldinho was inspired by his former World Cup-winning teammate Denílson signing for Íbis Sport Club in 2022, 12 years after his retirement. However, the then 44-year-old never made an appearance for the lower-league Brazilian club, with the signing seemingly a publicity stunt for a club often dubbed the “worst in the world” after going three years, 11 months and 26 days without a win in the 1980s.
Which takes us to another brilliant Brazilian. The late, great Sócrates came out of retirement on 20 November 2004 aged 50, 15 years after his last appearance for Botafogo on 12 November 1989. He signed a one-month player-coach deal with Garforth Town, on the outskirts of Leeds, in the Northern Counties East Football League and played 12 minutes at the end of a 2-2 draw with Tadcaster Albion. “It was far too cold; the second I got out there I had an incredible headache. I’m just not used to it,” he gasped after the match. “But I really enjoyed it and it was an interesting experience.” His appearance drew huge crowds to tiny Wheatley Park and came about because of a shared interest in football coaching schools for children which the owner, Simon Clifford, was trying to promote.
The hiatus for Sócrates stands at 15 years and eight days, four years greater than that of Ronaldinho, though perhaps Ronaldinho’s ability to step back into the third tier of a professional league and more than hold his own is a more impressive achievement. What is unarguable, though, is their status as two Brazil greats.
The former Scotland defender Neil McBain had a playing hiatus longer than the two legends above, however. “McBain started his career as a half-back for Ayr United in 1915,” writes Robin Horton. “He retired in 1931, as player-manager for Watford, by which time he was playing centre-half, his last game being an FA Cup tie at Birmingham on 14 February. By 1946 he was in charge of New Brighton.”
“On 15 March 1947, with the club suffering a goalkeeping crisis, and with four players – including chosen keeper Corbett – failing to turn up for a match at Hartlepool United, McBain himself donned the green jersey. The Rakers duly lost 3–0, although the first goal was a shot ‘which might easily have caused Frank Swift’s eyes to boggle’. At 51 years old, he was the oldest player ever to play in the Football League – 16 years, one month and one day from his previous appearance.”
Drawing down
“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.
Leicester won the FA Cup in 2021, when Youri Tielemans scored a spectacular winner against Chelsea at Wembley in front of a post-Covid crowd of 20,000. As any fule kno, they’re now in League One after back-to-back relegations. That meant an early start in the FA Cup: on 6 November, to be precise, when Leicester won 4-2 at Oxford City.

Aaron Rodgers has been benched by the Pittsburgh Steelers for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos with Mason Rudolph to start in the four-time NFL MVP's place.
Rodgers, who turns 43 next week, has struggled during the Steelers' back-to-back defeats to the Cincinnati Bengals and the Philadelphia Eagles.
Pittsburgh confirmed in a statement that the veteran quarterback will be "inactive", despite head coach Mike McCarthy saying on Monday that he remained the starter.

Rodgers is amid his 22nd and final NFL season, having reunited with McCarthy after the two previously won the Super Bowl together at the Green Bay Packers in 2010.
He was key in McCarthy being hired to take over from Mike Tomlin.
Rudolph has started only 19 games in seven seasons with the Steelers and the Tennessee Titans, so this is a big call from Pittsburgh, even considering Rodger's flagging numbers.
Rodgers has completed under 61 per cent of pass attempts this season, marking one of his worst campaigns since he became a full-time starter with Green Bay in 2008.
The quarterback has been sacked 31 times, surpassing last year's total of 21 already, and leads the league with 257 yards lost in those sacks.
Earlier this week, McCarthy said of Rodgers when discussing Pittsburgh's successive defeats: "When you talk about the quarterback position, I think there's things offensively we need to do better and that always benefits and leads into quarterback play.
"I just need him to just keep ploughing away. We got a lot of work to do."

Mugabe was arrested ear
items.text:
Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
- Published
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.
The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.
They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.
Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.
The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.
His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.
Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.
In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.
In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.
He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.

items.text:
How to unearth young stars, the Bayern Munich way
- Published
Bayern Munich are one of the elite powers in European football and current home of Ballon d'Or winner and England captain Harry Kane.
But, while Kane is the latest hugely successful foreign import at Bayern, the German giants also put a particular focus on producing their own elite young talent.
In 2013, Bayern had four homegrown players in the starting line-up as they won the Champions League.
Repeating that victory, and continuing the club's history of nurturing young players, is what director of youth development and campus Jochen Sauer says Bayern are aiming for.
Sauer joined from Red Bull Salzburg in 2017 when the academy campus opened in another part of Munich, away from the first-team training complex.
The club's motto "Mia San Mia" translates to "we are who we are" and Sauer says it has always been the club's goal to have a local homegrown element in its senior side.
"It was always our identity and philosophy to be a regional club, but at the same time to be competitive internationally and on Champions League level," Sauer tells BBC Sport.
"But always having a core of our team coming from the Munich area and the Bavarian region with a deep identification with the club and the city.
"Our recruitment guidelines, especially for the under-11 to the under-15 teams, is trying to recruit as much talent as possible from the Munich area and the region of Bavaria."
Munich-born Croatia international Josip Stanisic is a good example. The midfielder, 26, signed as an under-17 player from local outfit SC Furstenfeldbruck, while 22-year-old Aleksandar Pavlovic joined the academy aged eight and has worked his way up to the first team and is a Germany international.
But perhaps the biggest name to come out of the academy in recent times is Jamal Musiala. The former Chelsea youth player, who joined aged 16, is a star for Bayern and Germany and has already won six Bundesliga titles at just 23 years old.
It was part of the club's strategy to bring in the best young foreign players, and those with German passports, to the club, but they also enjoyed a bit of luck.
The move came around the time Bayern Munich were interested in then-Chelsea winger Callum Hudson-Odoi, who shared the same agent as Musiala, who moved from Germany to England when he was seven.
Bayern were already aware of Musiala because he was born in Germany, but the timing was right to make a deal happen.
"There were for sure some pieces that came together at that time," Sauer says.
"I think one reason why we fought for the player at that time was the reason we had the feeling that Chelsea is not really seeing his full potential to be a top player for their first team.
"Because, otherwise, if they would have seen him as a future prospect, then it would been hard, even for Bayern Munich, to get a player out of the Chelsea environment."
Other young players in the first-team squad include 18-year-old Bara Sapoko Ndiaye, signed from Gambinos Stars Africa in The Gambia, and 18-year-old Lennart Karl, who joined the academy four years ago and has been capped by Germany.
How Bayern recruit
The Bayern Campus can house up to 43 players in accommodation, predominantly local players before they widen the search overseas.
"I think there is basically kind of a guideline that we want to have a minimum 60% of the players coming from the region and reaching the level of the under-19 age group," Sauer says.
"This automatically means that the other 40% of the team has to be recruited from other regions nationwide.
"Coming to an age group of under-17, we are also reaching out to the main European football markets to recruit the most talented players internationally.
"Jamal Musiala is one perfect example. As soon as we're coming to an age of 16 and the regulations allow us to do international transfers, we want to recruit the best talents in Europe. That's for sure part of our recruitment philosophy."
Another piece that fell into place for Musiala was the Bayern under-17 team at that time was coached by Miroslav Klose, the former Bayern forward who is the record goalscorer for Germany.
Klose is credited with pushing Musiala to work on the defensive side of his game. He also knew what a player needed to get to the highest level, with the former striker becoming an assistant to Hansi Flick when Musiala joined the first team.
That idea of having former players in charge of the next generation continues.
Ex-Bayern centre-back Dante, who also played for Nice for more than 10 years, is the current under-19 head coach.
"They can inject a little bit of the Bayern Munich DNA into the players," Sauer explains. "More from a personality side, not necessarily from a playing style.
"He also has some different ideas on the playing style but you know playing for Bayern Munich and being in the first team of Bayern Munich, at least they can tell our players what they have to be from a character, from a personality to make it up to the first team."
With so many players coming into the system and a difficult first-team set-up to break into, the Bayern style remains consistent throughout age groups.
Coaches are given guidelines to work towards but it does not stop them from having their own ideas as they aim for a style of "dominance and intensity".
"But football is always a process of evaluation," Sauer says.
"Opening the campus in 2017, we have put a very clear idea of football in place, but always kept the openness to add in ideas from coaches like [Jupp] Heynckes, [Julian] Nagelsmann, [Thomas] Tuchel, Hansi Flick, and, for sure, [current Bayern manager Vincent] Kompany. The football is always developing.
"So we have to be open enough always to amend little things. But I would say that the overall strategy is still what it was in the times of Heynckes, Pep Guardiola or Louis van Gaal."

items.text:
Max Verstappen showed 'race craft' edge over George Russell and Kimi Antonelli during Las Vegas GP, says Jacques Villeneuve
Max Verstappen withstood pressure from Mercedes' George Russell and Kimi Antonelli on his way to winning a thrilling Las Vegas GP for Red Bull; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
Tuesday 24 November 2026 21:25, UK
Former Formula 1 world champion Jacques Villeneuve says Max Verstappen's Las Vegas Grand Prix victory showed that Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell will not be able to beat the Red Bull driver in next year's championship unless they have a superior car.
Verstappen retained the lead from pole position at the start but was challenged by Russell and then later Antonelli for almost the entire 50-lap race amid near constant changes of position throughout the field, but the Red Bull driver expertly saw off their best efforts before both made late errors to drop down the order.
Antonelli has already been crowned 2026 world champion after Mercedes' dominance early in the season helped him build a significant advantage, but Verstappen is putting together an ominous finish to the year, with the four-time world champion having won four of the last six races and claimed nine successive podiums.
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Sky Sports F1 pundit and 1997 F1 world champion Villeneuve said after the race: "It was exciting. People will say there was a battery involved [in all the passes], but it doesn't matter.
"We saw some race craft. Max was above and the two Mercedes drivers were lacking in that respect.
"And what it is telling us is that unless next year Mercedes have a car that's superior, they can't win because there's something missing."
A combination of factors, most notably the extreme power of the slipstream effect, meant there were more than 350 overtakes during a breathless race at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.
The lead changed hands 34 times, but every time Verstappen was overtaken, which on almost every occasion was by a Mercedes, the four-time world champion retook his position within a few corners.
Russell locked up and hit a barrier as he tried to pass Antonelli for second in the closing stages, before the Italian suffered a loss of power at the start of the final lap after incorrectly lifting off the throttle as he was preparing to mount a final challenge to Verstappen.
Villeneuve was also impressed by the drives of seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and last year's title winner Lando Norris, who took advantage of the Mercedes errors to finish second ahead of his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri.
Hamilton could have also ended up on the podium had it not been for him spinning in a contentious collision with his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.
"You could see that Lewis had good race craft as well as Lando," Villeneuve added.
"It was really fun to see. We saw today a race where you don't need pit stops, you don't need tyres that degrade.
"We had a race where drivers could push like qualifying laps all the time and that allowed them to race. It was great fun."

In 2022, an indepe
items.text:
Court to rule on South African president's bid to set aside 'Farmgate' report
- Published
A South African court is due to rule on President Cyril Ramaphosa's attempt to overturn a report that found he has a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The ruling could either exonerate the president or clear the way for him to possibly face impeachment.
Wednesday's ruling will be handed down by the Western Cape high court - the same court that blocked a parliamentary committee from proceeding with the impeachment process while a review challenge of the report is under way.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
If the Western Cape High Court rules in his favour, it could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
A ruling against him would allow the parliamentary committee to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

items.title: Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?
items.summary:
Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?

Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it begs the question: are United
items.text:
Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?
- Published
Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it begs the question: are United this season's Spurs?
Well while Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points, they actually started the season better than United have. After 11 games last season, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.
But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.
While the table was prompting talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.
United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.
But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.
While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.
Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.
But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.
And it's not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.
As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.
By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the % chance of each club finishing in each position in the League.
While the above means it's more likely United will survive, it's worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.
There's a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.
History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.
Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.
A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has ever finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.
Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.
Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there wouldn't be entirely unprecedented.
It's a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they've played than they did last season.
Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last season
Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.
While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals
So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

items.text:
UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal
- Published
The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community.
The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini.
The BBC has obtained a copy of the draft deal between the two governments, in which the UK pledges to cover the costs of his resettlement for up to three years.
The UK government was finalising plans for 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya to live there permanently when he died.
Migration experts told the BBC this was the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling in such a manner a refugee permanently overseas.
In 2024, the Labour government scrapped a controversial plan to send asylum seekers with pending claims to Rwanda. Now it wants to send failed asylum seekers overseas to third countries when they cannot be sent to their home countries, but is yet to announce any deals. Last week, five EU countries reached a deal to send people whose claims have been refused to Rwanda.
The Eswatini deal raises questions about how much the UK government should disclose about such arrangements, and how it protects both the people it sends overseas and the communities that receive them.
The UK government told the BBC that protecting the British public was its priority and that it "continue[s] to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case".
Peramalya's family is demanding answers about his treatment, while critics in Eswatini have accused Britain of using their country as a "dumping ground".
Royal Navy rescue
In 2021, the Royal Navy rescued Peramalya in the Indian Ocean, along with dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers, as they tried to sail from India to Canada.
They were then detained in a camp on Diego Garcia, an island in the British Indian Ocean Territory, run exclusively as a UK-US military base.
The island's authorities, who answer to London, recognised that Peramalya and others could not safely return to Sri Lanka, and awarded them refugee protections. But the group remained in the camp for three years while British officials debated their future. A court later ruled their detention had been unlawful.
As a teenager, Peramalya had been tortured and sexually abused by officers in the Sri Lankan military and was later diagnosed with PTSD. During his detention on Diego Garcia, his mental health deteriorated, according to court papers. He suffered from depression and anxiety, and repeatedly attempted suicide. UN inspectors who came to the island raised concerns over the conditions he was being kept in.
While there, he committed a series of crimes, including assault and arson, during two suicide attempts, and spent 24 weeks in prison. He was also convicted of four counts of sexual assault for which he received a suspended prison sentence.
In December 2024, most of the Sri Lankan asylum seekers were allowed to enter the UK but ministers refused to let Peramalya join them because of his crimes. He remained on Diego Garcia.
The High Court upheld the UK's refusal to admit him, in part because of the risk he posed and because ministers were making genuine efforts to find somewhere else safe for him to live. Court documents, seen by the BBC, show the UK approached more than 20 countries and could not secure an agreement.
Undisclosed British deal
Then, in February 2026, the US began using its military base on Diego Garcia in its war with Iran. The island authorities began withdrawing non-essential personnel.
At the end of March, the Maldives offered to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was transferred there before being sent on to Eswatini, formerly known as Swaziland.
At the time of his death, the British and Eswatini governments had been finalising the agreement for Peramalya to live there permanently, with the UK to pay for the "reasonable costs" of his accommodation, healthcare, and other support for up to three years.
The document does not specify a total cost or explain how the two governments would manage the risks Peramalya posed to himself and others. But it explicitly acknowledged he required support that would meet his basic needs and protect his physical and mental health, and wellbeing.
Peramalya's family has told the BBC he was initially placed in an isolated guesthouse on his own.
Speaking from India, his sister said the family had not been aware of the plan to make his transfer permanent, and that his mental health had worsened while in the country.
She said he would call her four times a day. "My brother did not want to go there at all," she said. "He couldn't manage being there alone, he was very lonely." The family also said it had been unaware of sexual offences committed by him.
He initially saw a psychiatrist weekly, she said. Later, after his mental health declined, he had daily appointments, and an attendant was brought in to prepare his food.
On 13 September, he took his own life.
The UN's refugee agency, which had previously raised concerns about Peramalya's condition on Diego Garcia, said it was "deeply saddened" by his death and stressed that refugees being transferred to other different countries must be protected.
"UNHCR recognises that asylum seekers and refugees may, in certain circumstances, be lawfully transferred to a third country. However, this requires that specific safeguards are in place and those conditions are fulfilled in practice."
'Highly unusual' arrangement
Peter Walsh, of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, described the case as "highly unusual".
"In most cases, people with criminal convictions who cannot be returned to their home country would simply remain in the UK. Third countries are generally quite reluctant to accept foreign national offenders," he said.

items.summary:
Nelson Hysa aims to beat Agit Kabayel, win WBC world title and take on Tyson Fury, his 'favourite fighter'
Nelson Hysa challenges Agit Kabayel for the WBC title on Saturday in Dusseldorf; Hard-punching Hysa hopes to upset popular German Kabayel and then look to take on his 'favourite fighter' Tyson
items.text:
Nelson Hysa aims to beat Agit Kabayel, win WBC world title and take on Tyson Fury, his 'favourite fighter'
Nelson Hysa challenges Agit Kabayel for the WBC title on Saturday in Dusseldorf; Hard-punching Hysa hopes to upset popular German Kabayel and then look to take on his 'favourite fighter' Tyson Fury; Hysa says Moses Itauma is still the best in the division - 'I don't want to fight him!'
Tuesday 24 November 2026 19:23, UK
Nelson Hysa has a vision. He wants to dethrone Agit Kabayel, win the WBC heavyweight world title and then take on his favourite fighter – Tyson Fury.
Hysa, unbeaten in 25 professional fights, challenges Kabayel on Saturday for the WBC heavyweight world championship.
The Albanian has taken 23 of those wins inside the distance and is looking to upset the popular German when they fight in Dusseldorf this weekend.
A power-puncher, Hysa told Sky Sports: "The knockout was with me from the first day that I started boxing.
"In this match [against Kabayel] I am preparing to do more good rounds because I know the opponent is a very good boxer, he's a tough boxer, a serious boxer.
"But we are planning, we are trying to do our best. We have our strategy to win the match and I think we will win the match earlier than the 12th round.
"I need to move up the ratio of knockouts!"
With Oleksandr Usyk vacating his championships, there are now new belt-holders in the division, but Hysa does not consider Kabayel the best of the current heavyweight titlists.
"For me No 1 now of the guys that have the belts, No 1 is Filip Hrgovic, [then Daniel] Dubois and for me the special one is Tyson Fury.
"Hrgovic will do very good because he's a good boxer," Hysa added. "Hrgovic beat the best guy in the heavyweight division. He beat Moses [Itauma]. I don't want to do a fight with Moses, he's a good guy! He will be the best heavyweight in the world. He is the best heavyweight in the world but he needs more time."
Fury will fight Anthony Joshua for the WBA 'super' heavyweight title when they meet on December 11. Hysa tips Fury to win and is eager to box him in a unification if he comes through his own fight.
"Who doesn't want to fight Tyson Fury? He's a legend," Hysa said. "The No 1 man at heavyweight.
"He's my No 1 favourite boxer, I love him, I love everything he does. His style, everything.
"Who doesn't want to fight Tyson Fury?"

items.text:
Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
- Published
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.
Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu.
The family did not disclose the cause of his death, although local media reported that the Nollywood star had been in poor health in recent months.
Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.
"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.
