items.title: Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
items.summary:
Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth int
items.text:
Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.
More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.
Why the iOS Safari Experience Sucks
What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.
How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.
Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.
High Refresh Rate Interactions
Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.
If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.
In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.
- Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed.
- Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region.
- Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container.
- Want a dial with notches? Snap points!
The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.
Creating “The Controller”
I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.
Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.
First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.
Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.
What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.
Each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.
Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering update queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.
This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.
I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.
Squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.
Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.
If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.
Just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.
One issue remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.

items.title: Pep 'embarrassed' to turn down Italy job, says national team 'next step'
items.summary:
Pep Guardiola said he felt "embarrassed" to turn down the head coaching position with Italy, but added he could return to coaching in the future and, if he did, would like to do it with a national team.
In the end, Guardiola said in an interview on Romario TV on Tuesday that he passed on the Italy j
items.text:
Pep Guardiola said he felt "embarrassed" to turn down the head coaching position with Italy, but added he could return to coaching in the future and, if he did, would like to do it with a national team.
In the end, Guardiola said in an interview on Romario TV on Tuesday that he passed on the Italy job because he needed to take a break following his departure from Manchester City after 10 years.
A trophy-laden decade in the dugout from 2016 to 2026 at City that included six Premier League titles, three FA Cups and a Champions League crown, left Guardiola exhausted and forced him to take a self-imposed sabbatical of at least one year.
Soon after, though, Guardiola was approached by Paolo Maldini and Leonardo, who were working on behalf of the Italian federation in its search for a new coach, to gauge his interest in taking over the top spot for the Azzurri after they had missed out on the World Cup for a third consecutive time.
"This is the first time I speak about this, but yes, I did talk to them," Guardiola told Brazil legend and former Barcelona teammate Romario on his show. "I felt embarrassed to say 'no' to Italy, a country like Italy, it would have been one of the greatest honors of my career to coach the Italian national team. But I realized I needed to stop. If they had called two years earlier, I probably would have accepted. But when Paolo Maldini and Leonardo, whom I love dearly, reached out, it was at a point where I simply had to stop.
"I needed some time for myself. After 18 years as a coach, with matches every three days, week in and week out, there comes a moment when you just have to say 'phew.'"
Italy ultimately hired Roberto Mancini, who had already managed the team from 2018 to 2023 and led it to the 2020 European Championship.
The former Barcelona and Bayern Munich manager did not rule out a return to coaching, saying that when he does it will be because "someone wants me."
As to where that might be, Guardiola said he didn't know, but that if there was one team he never coached but would have liked to it was "a national team," adding "and that is the next step."
Guardiola was rumored to be a target for U.S. Soccer as it looked for a new manager to replace Mauricio Pochettino after the Argentine left the United States for Manchester United.
Around the time of Pochettino's departure, ESPN sources said U.S. Soccer's search was "expected to include former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola," though a federation source cautioned that it was premature to call Guardiola the top target.
On his way out, Pochettino was asked about a possible succession plan centered on Guardiola and he said it was "the perfect moment to arrive" at the USMNT.
"Everything is in the right direction. I think, of course, take [it]," Pochettino said in his last news conference as U.S. coach. "Take it because [Guardiola is] going to find really good people, good players. The player can fit for his style; the National Training Center that wasn't [there] before."
During Italy's pursuit of Guardiola in July, an ESPN source also confirmed Guardiola's interest in coaching a national team but could not confirm the countries. The source added that the Netherlands, who recently hired Xavi, and England, managed by Thomas Tuchel, have both been credited with an interest in the Catalan coach.
For now, Guardiola says he is content on the sidelines.
"The truth is, I don't know, I really don't know. But for now, I'm doing fine," Guardiola said Tuesday. "If I ever return, it will be because my gut tells me to, and because someone wants me, then I we'll go back. But it's been many years, so many matches."
ESPN Brazil contributed to this report.

items.title: Bellingham credits Mourinho 'full stop' for stellar form after Madrid stunner
items.summary:
Jude Bellingham praised José Mourinho for helping him reach career-best form after the midfielder scored a stunning goal in Real Madrid's 5-1 comeback win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
Madrid trailed 1-0 at halftime before Mourinho made a triple substitution -- including the introduction of Belling
items.text:
Jude Bellingham praised José Mourinho for helping him reach career-best form after the midfielder scored a stunning goal in Real Madrid's 5-1 comeback win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
Madrid trailed 1-0 at halftime before Mourinho made a triple substitution -- including the introduction of Bellingham -- and the home side then dominated, with Kylian Mbappé netting a brace, and Vinícius Júnior scoring his first Champions League goal this season.
Madrid are now top of the league phase table with 15 points after winning all five UCL matches so far, with a visit to Arsenal in their next European game on Dec. 9.
"Mourinho. Full stop," Bellingham told journalists at the Bernabéu, when asked to explain his outstanding form, with four goals in his last five club games. "I'm enjoying my football a lot. I love the coach, his staff, and my teammates help me a lot.
"That's why I'm playing well, because I have a lot of help."
Bellingham's goal in the 60th minute was a beauty, coming after he lifted the ball with his left foot, kept it up in the air with his right and used the outside of the same foot to curl a shot into the far corner.
Bellingham spoke to TNT Sports too. If we wanted to add a bit more on his goal, we could:
"I think so," Bellingham told TNT Sports, when asked if his goal was among the best of his career. "They're normally a lot closer, aren't they!? That one was a nice one.
"It looped up nicely and I thought I'd go with the outside of my boot. I'm not one for smashing the ball too hard. It was a nice moment."
JUDE BELLINGHAM, THAT IS FILTHY 🤯 Two juggles, then a finish with the outside of his boot 💥 Stream the #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 https://t.co/8OOMUS4izI
— CBS Sports Golazo ⚽️ (@CBSSportsGolazo) November 24, 2026
Bellingham was also asked if his displays with England at the World Cup -- where he scored seven goals playing behind Harry Kane -- had been the catalyst for his renewed goal threat.
"I don't know if it's because I'm playing as a number 10, it's having freedom," Bellingham said. " Freedom to move, to drop deep, to help build up, and to play higher up to finish.
"I think Mourinho has given me a lot of confidence. That's why I'm playing well, because I'm happy."
Madrid have now beaten Inter Milan, Roma, RB Leipzig, AEK Athens and PSV in the Champions League this season, despite some inconsistent performances.
"The second half was a question of mentality," Mourinho told Movistar. "We made changes, and Jude is a different player. He gives us what we didn't have in the first [half].
"It was a mental 'click.' In the first half we didn't find our rhythm, we didn't press, we didn't win duels."
Mourinho refused to reveal if he'd been angry with his players in the dressing room at halftime.
"The dressing room is like Vegas," the coach said. "What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas.
"We spoke. We're friends, and we spoke."
"Once again, the first half wasn't good," goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois said. "In modern football, if we don't all run and do what the manager asks of us, it's impossible, especially against a team that presses you man-to-man.
"With the clips [Mourinho] showed us on the screen at halftime, you could see we weren't doing things right. That changed our attitude."
Madrid, who are three points behind LaLiga leaders Barcelona, next play Alaves at the Bernabeu on Nov. 28.

items.title: Arteta questions 'how in hell' Arsenal didn't score more in Dortmund draw
items.summary:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta rued his side's failure to put Borussia Dortmund away as "unbelievable" after watching the Premier League champions create 30 shots before drawing 1-1 at the Emirates Stadium.
Viktor Gyökeres crashed in Arsenal's opener after 10 minutes of Tuesday's Champions League cont
items.text:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta rued his side's failure to put Borussia Dortmund away as "unbelievable" after watching the Premier League champions create 30 shots before drawing 1-1 at the Emirates Stadium.
Viktor Gyökeres crashed in Arsenal's opener after 10 minutes of Tuesday's Champions League contest, but for the second time in as many games, following their 2-2 draw at Newcastle, Arteta's men were unable to see out the victory after Maximilian Beier's second-half equalizer.
Olley: Dortmund draw shows that the jury is still out on Gyökeres
Arsenal hit a post three times in response, while Gyökeres also wasted a golden opportunity to restore his side's advantage when he headed wide from six yards with 15 minutes left. In all, Arsenal found the target just four times.
Although Arteta was pleased with his side's dominant display, against a team that occupies top spot in the Bundesliga, he was left to reflect on what might have been.
"It was a brilliant performance," he said. "The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition, is something I can be very, very pleased about because there is very little more that you can demand from the team.
"But obviously, the feeling is we should reward ourselves much more when you put in that kind of performance and get those amount of chances.
"There is an element of luck, and an element of us finishing the actions better. There's no question how superior, how dominant, and how much of a threat we were. It was great to watch, but it was unbelievable that sometimes the ball didn't end up in the back of the net.
"I don't know if it is our mentality. As I said, there was an element of luck, because how in hell have some of the goals not gone in?"
The draw extended last season's finalists' unbeaten streak in the Champions League to 20 games but ended their 12-game home winning streak in league phase.
Arsenal now sit in fifth position ahead of the completion of the fifth round of matches on Wednesday. The top eight qualify automatically for the round of 16.
Tuesday saw goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga handed a rare appearance in place of David Raya.
Arteta is uncertain if his number one -- injured against Newcastle on Saturday -- will be fit to face Manchester City in the Premier League this weekend.
"I have nothing to add to that unfortunately," he said. "We need to know first how bad it is and whether he has a chance or not to make it."
Arsenal might have had the lion's share of shots, but Jobe Bellingham had a goal ruled out for offside for Dortmund. Gyökeres could also count himself fortunate not to give away a penalty when a Dortmund corner struck him on the arm in the second half.
"I thought VAR should have looked at the handball. It would have been worth a check," Dortmund coach Niko Kovac said.
"They are trying to intervene less with the on-field decisions, but it doesn't mean you should not intervene when you should do.
"I am not crying about it. It is what it is. We got a point. It is a big point away to Arsenal, a big one for all of us -- our fans, our team and the club."
Information from PA contributed to this report.

items.text:
Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
- Published
Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.
She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.
Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.
Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.
He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.
"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.
That decision would have devastating consequences.
She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.
They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.
"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.
Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.
Median initially thought she was dreaming.
"To my surprise, it was reality."
The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.
Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.
Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.
She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.
For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.
A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.
The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.
They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.
Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.
But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.
By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.
Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.
Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.
Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.
Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.
The violence has devastated communities and forced half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.
At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.
Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.
The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.
Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.
The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.
For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.
Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.
But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.
She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.
"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.
"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."
Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.
Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.
The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.
Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.
Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.
"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.
Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.
The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.

items.text:
PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches
A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson.
The text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude. I plan to rewrite it in my own words over Thanksgiving Break but needed to get the project out. So apologies for this move - all of my other posts were written by me, and all future posts will be as well. Even if you find Claude more comprehensible than my meandering thoughts, meander nonetheless I shall.
Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad.
So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt.
Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected.
How it works
That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture.
The data
Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive.
The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them.
Training a model
I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Here are the rows I found most interesting; the paper has the rest.
Data and how you show it. Those are the big rows. Cut the data and everything gets worse. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0.
The clever parts barely register. Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly worse; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing.
Even the transformer is optional, sort of. An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up new hands. On drawings, where sequences are several times longer, it falls well behind.
Samples
Enough tables. Here’s what the two models make.
The drawing model takes a few controls besides the prompt. One of them is how much ink to use.
It can also draw some things it was never shown as long as a blend of two familiar ideas will do.
Picking up a new hand
The trick is almost embarrassingly simple. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. No style encoder, no fine-tuning. That’s how the 21 hands at the top of this post were written.
It also works from a photo. There are no strokes in a photo so I trace a few of its words with InkSight and fit one new writer vector to the traces, with the rest of the model frozen.
Reading the letters
One head in layer 4 puts 81% of its attention on the letter being written. I looked for heads that specialize in cursive or print and found none; every head reads the same positions in both.
Do you need captions?
Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?
You can’t. The picture-only model has the best likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).
What it can’t do
The drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.
Closing thoughts
If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in The Bitter Lesson. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.
I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My pr

items.title: Yale’s Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a ‘detriment’ to U.S. industrial might — not a champion
items.summary: What the market celebrated Monday could prove to be a giant mistake, and not just for Nvidia’s board. Renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale says the directors who reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and also returned him to the board — even as the board says it is investigating whether fo
items.text:
What the market celebrated Monday could prove to be a giant mistake, and not just for Nvidia’s board. Renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale says the directors who reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and also returned him to the board — even as the board says it is investigating whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted him — face a “historic level of individual liability.”
Nvidia’s chairman had effectively ruled out a reinstatement just last week. Then, in a torrent of private weekend calls led by Vice President JD Vance, top administration officials leaned on the board to bring Huang back, with President Trump calling the board directly to vouch for him. “I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC on Monday.
In an interview Tuesday morning, Sonnenfeld wondered whether the market is feting a company that’s largely responsible for putting sophisticated technology in the hands of the country’s adversaries, at a moment when the risks couldn’t be higher.
He pointed to research suggesting Nvidia’s most advanced chips have reached China despite U.S. export controls, and to sinking shares of Anthropic, which he links to the realization that China’s seemingly miraculous open-source AI models are in a sense copies of top U.S. labs’ work. Indeed, Huang’s return was greeted with relief in Asia, The Washington Post reported. “The king is back!” read one headline from China’s state-affiliated Star Market Daily.
The legal deluge has already begun. As we noted a couple of weeks ago, a potential class-action lawsuit was filed almost immediately. Days later, a shareholder derivative suit followed. Filed on Nvidia’s behalf against the directors themselves, the suit alleges the board ignored red flags about Huang’s relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.
The class action is very much aimed at making Nvidia and Huang compensate investors for their losses, while the derivative suit puts the directors’ own behavior on trial, with any recovery going to Nvidia. Three more suits followed on Nov. 18, the day after Nvidia’s most recent earnings call; all five were filed in Northern California, where Nvidia is based.
Huang and Nvidia are also juggling a Justice Department antitrust investigation, a reported SEC probe into Nvidia’s accounting, a possible FBI review, a California subpoena, an export-control case that landed partner Megaspeed on the U.S. trade blacklist on Monday, and congressional inquiries, including a Senate Banking hearing next week at which Huang has agreed to testify.
Here’s some of what Sonnenfeld had to say, in a Q&A that’s been edited for length and clarity.
TC: So much has happened since we last talked. Huang was ousted, he’s come back. Do you think the board’s reliance on government assurances here is defensible or an abdication of its own duties?
JS: They failed to rely on experts. That’s one of the reasons this board is going to be sued and lose, and these directors are likely to face a historic level of individual liability. They have a very inadequate directors and officers liability policy. They have also just failed in their diligence. They hired the Wachtell [law] firm. The Wachtell firm barely got off the blocks to do an investigation. And then they have already reversed themselves, so they didn’t use the expertise needed.
It’s wild that they also put Huang right back on the board of directors.
The board showed, in addition to incompetence and collaboration, just cowardice in their capitulation because Trump has nothing to wave over them. If this was SpaceX, where 46% of its business comes from the government [you could maybe see the case for Trump’s involvement].For Nvidia, it’s not even 1% of its business that comes from the U.S. government, so [the board] didn’t have that threat. [Trump] can call off [federal] investigations, but he can’t call off the shareholder litigation. Some are already filed, and the estimates are there’ll probably be 30 of them, and they’re going to be extremely costly.
And this is not, by the way, just a blue or red state issue. We already have 14 GOP senators who’ve already come out against this, and very prominent conservatives, like Pete Ricketts and Josh Hawley and Tom Cotton and John Cornyn. Those are some issues that may help explain why Nvidia’s stock is tumbling today.
Might the board say, ‘We saw the classified intelligence findings, and they assure us Jensen will be absolved of wrongdoing’?
They haven’t seen those findings, and we also haven’t seen what will be the result of the Senate Intelligence Committee, the Senate Special Committee on Investigations, the Senate Banking Committee, and all their House counterparts. The board hasn’t seen any of that, and even if they saw it, which they have not yet, that still wouldn’t matter.
Do you think the Commerce Department will continue to tighten its chip export controls to keep China from accessing so much compute or walk back some of those recent moves?
We already see that Megaspeed has finally been put on the sanctions list, as it should have been before. And we have documentation now that Nvidia, rather than a champion of U.S. global industrial might, is actually a detriment to U.S. global industrial might, because their chips have now turned out to be in the hands and in the systems of not just the Chinese military, as they got channeled to Northwestern Polytechnical University, which is a military institution — this is going into weapons that will, of course, be funneled to Iran and Russia, and they didn’t have access to that a year ago. [Editor’s note: China has long denied supplying weapons to either country. Nvidia chips have been found in Russian drones, however, and the U.S. ambassador to China said in September that President Trump had discussed selling arms to China, an account Trump has denied.]

items.title: Bellingham plays down Zidane comparison after wonder goal
items.summary:
Bellingham plays down Zidane comparison after wonder goal
- Published
Manager Jose Mourinho described Jude Bellingham as "without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world" following a wonder goal which inspired a brilliant second-half performance for Real Madrid in a 5-1 win against PSV.
Mourinho
items.text:
Bellingham plays down Zidane comparison after wonder goal
- Published
Manager Jose Mourinho described Jude Bellingham as "without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world" following a wonder goal which inspired a brilliant second-half performance for Real Madrid in a 5-1 win against PSV.
Mourinho opted to leave the England midfielder out of the starting line-up for Tuesday's Champions League game at the Bernabeu - an understandable decision given the demands of Madrid's fixture schedule and the strength in depth at his disposal.
But after watching his side trail 1-0 at half-time against the Dutch side, Mourinho knew changes were needed.
On came Bellingham.
"He is an amazing player that has everything," the Portuguese manager said. "He has physicality, he understands the game, he has absolutely everything. Today, he has changed how the game was evolving."
Captain Fede Valverde equalised in the 50th minute and 10 minutes later Bellingham produced his moment of magic.
Receiving the ball just outside the penalty area, he took two touches to lift it into position before unleashing a magnificent volley with the outside of his right footr, leaving PSV keeper Matej Kovar with no chance.
It was a sensational finish, executed with extraordinary precision.
"I was a bit surprised, honestly," Bellingham said about the goal. "I knew that I could control the ball well and get it into my grasp. But normally from there, I'm looking to see who's on as an option to play through.
"It popped up nicely and I thought I'm just going to hit it. So yeah, it was a nice goal and important for the team, being the second goal, and gave us control."
The 23-year-old celebrated in trademark fashion, standing with his arms outstretched in front of the home supporters as thousands serenaded him with chants of 'Hey Jude'.
It was his fourth goal in his past five appearances for Real.
Asked whether he should be compared to Real and France legend Zinedine Zidane, who won the Ballon d'Or and World Cup in 1998, Bellingham maintained his humility.
"I think Zidane is much better than me. He's much more elegant and he's my idol," he said.
'I don't care about the Ballon d'Or'
Kylian Mbappe scored two more goals and Vinicius Junior put away the fifth to complete a super turnaround from a team that had looked short of ideas in the first half.
At the suggestion that he is currently in the form of his life, Bellingham said: "I think you're only as good as your next one [game]. Your last one doesn't really matter.
"But my focus has to change now to preparing for the next game. Thinking about my best form or being the best player in the world doesn't mean anything to me."
For Bellingham, the ability to respond when things are not going according to plan is what separates the best teams from the rest.
"We're managing to show that mentality that good teams do, that even if you're not playing well, you can raise the level at any point," he said.
His adaptation to life in Spain has also been an important part of that journey.
Asked about his increasingly impressive Spanish, Bellingham admitted he still gets nervous when speaking the language in public.
"It's getting a little bit better. I get a little bit nervous speaking to you guys. It's much easier in the changing room," he joked to journalists.
"I'm loving living in Spain. I'm loving the club. I think for English players it's such an important thing to go and move abroad and learn new things and I've obviously benefited massively from that."
And while his performances have inevitably brought renewed attention to individual awards, Bellingham said that personal recognition is not what motivates him.
Asked about the Ballon d'Or, he said his focus was only on the team.
"I don't care about the Ballon d'Or, honestly. I want to win a lot of titles with the team, the Champions League, the League."
"The Ballon d'Or is something for you, journalists, to vote and create a bit of tension. But for me it's more important that the team win."

items.title: Dortmund draw shows that the jury is still out on Gyökeres
items.summary:

For starters, the 28-year-old produced the most devastating moment of his time in north London, smashing in a stunning 28-
items.text:
LONDON -- Anyone who has somehow missed the first 16 months of Viktor Gyökeres' Arsenal career needs to only watch Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund to catch up in full.
For starters, the 28-year-old produced the most devastating moment of his time in north London, smashing in a stunning 28-yard strike to break the deadlock at Emirates Stadium in the 10th minute.
And then, with the game in the balance following Maximilian Beier's 55th-minute equalizer, Gyökeres somehow managed to head wide 6 yards out with the goal gaping. He looked so certain to score that Mikel Arteta began celebrating on the touchline only to stop abruptly when reality struck.
It would be unfair to pin this failure to win solely on Gyökeres. Arsenal ended with 29 shots on goal, hit the woodwork three times and racked up an xG of 2.20 compared with Dortmund's 0.92. The hosts, and reigning Premier League champions, should have won this game.
It follows a familiar pattern of the Gunners failing to press home their advantage seen at Slavia Prague -- when racing into a 2-0 lead and clinging on to a 2-1 win -- and Newcastle United, where they were so absurdly superior for 45 minutes only to score once, then concede twice and scramble a 2-2 draw.
But Gyökeres was the player Arsenal acquired to solve this problem. A €73 million signing from Sporting CP, the Sweden international scored 97 goals in 102 games for the Portuguese side and his arrival was heralded as the No. 9 Arsenal have long needed to take them to the next level.
They won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years, and Gyökeres scored 21 times, but doubts remained over his ability to settle the biggest games. Arteta's team selection toward the end of the previous campaign suggested as much -- using Kai Havertz ahead of Gyökeres -- as did the summer pursuit of an elite attacker which ended in disappointment. And so far this season, Gyökeres has sat behind Havertz in the pecking order, reduced to proving himself in games where Arteta rotated as he did against Dortmund, making six changes with Sunday's Premier League visit of Manchester City in mind.
Since joining the club, Gyökeres has scored more Champions League goals than any other Arsenal player. And this season, he has five goals and four assists in his last 10 games for club and country.
But scratch the surface of that statistic and you realize those interventions have come against Dortmund, Slavia Prague, Fleetwood Town, Poland, Bosnia-Herzegovina (twice) and Romania (twice).
Dortmund are unbeaten in the Bundesliga, sitting two points clear of Bayern Munich and SC Freiburg at the top. They are clearly a talented side -- Beier's equalizer alone was evidence of that -- but ultimately Gyökeres was unable to break a cycle which is in danger of becoming a deeper issue, as much as Arteta continues to suggest otherwise.
"I love the way the team played," Arteta said. "I think there's no question how superior, how dominant, how much of a threat we were, how connected everybody was to the game, between the relationships.
"It was great to watch. It was unbelievable that sometimes the ball hasn't ended up in the back of the net. That's my feeling."
Although the broad pattern of dominating the first half and dipping for a spell after halftime continued, Arteta rejected any comparison to their draw at Newcastle.
"I think it was nothing similar to what happened to Newcastle," Arteta said. "In that sense, it was a different game.
"I think the margins today were even bigger. There were a few of those against Newcastle, two top opponents. There's a lot to like, but obviously we want to win every game. Today we didn't manage to make that difference in the scoreline, unfortunately."
There was a similar defense of Gyökeres, whose night ended at 87 minutes with seven shots and 15 passes completed out of 24 attempted.
"I think he had a brilliant performance today," Arteta said. "He scored an unbelievable goal. He has the technique and the quality to do that. What I love the most is how connected he was to the team.
"We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch. There was a lot to like in that performance, and that's the Viktor that we needed."
Everything they needed except the goal that secured the win. Arteta remains confident that the only challenge Arsenal have is to "sustain that momentum [in] the way we are playing and the win will come."
He might well be right. Man City's porous defense might struggle to cope with Arsenal peppering their goal like this. But they need to find a clinical touch to end their current wastefulness before it starts severely undermining their efforts.
It remains uncertain whether Gyökeres can ever provide the answer.

items.title: Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games
items.summary:
Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games

In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game
items.text:
Arteta says Arsenal need more luck to kill off games
- Published
It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.
In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game by more than a single goal.
The latest frustration came in Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund, though perspective is needed. Arsenal might consider it as two points dropped having gone into half-time ahead, but they remain unbeaten in the current Champions League league phase and have not lost at this stage of the competition for more than two years.
But of late, despite dominating large parts of matches, Arsenal have had periods where they have dropped off and allowed opponents back into the game.
Against Slavia Prague away in the Champions League, after scoring twice in the first half, Arsenal's standards dropped. The same happened against Newcastle in the Premier League last weekend where they found themselves 2-1 behind in the second half having led at the break, before recovering to eventually draw 2-2.
They are producing periods of high-level football, but the struggles to consistently turn that into more goals can lead to nervy finishes.
In the draw with Bundesliga leaders Dortmund, Arsenal had 30 shots but just four of those attempts were on target.
Boss Mikel Arteta mentioned the failure to capitalise post match, though was keen to praise his side's "brilliant performance".
"The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition that we played today and what we've done out there, is just something to be very, very pleased [about] because there is very little more that you can demand from the team," Arteta said.
"But obviously, the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance in the amount of chances (and) situations.
"There is an element of luck; there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist because I think what the team has done and shown today, I think it's the right direction."
Missing chances or need more luck?
Arteta made six changes to the side that drew with Newcastle, with one of the biggest calls to rest striker Kai Havertz and bring in Viktor Gyokeres.
The striker has had a difficult season so far, with four of his seven starts coming in the Champions League against opposition where Arsenal have been favourites.
However, Gyokeres scored a powerful effort from outside the area to give Arsenal the lead against Dortmund.
Overall though, it ended up being a mixed night for the 28-year-old as he missed a header from inside the six-yard-box that would have surely won the game for the Gunners late on.
Arteta was asked if the chances his side are missing were down to mentality, misfortune or composure.
"Mentality, I don't know," he said.
"There is an element of luck here because how some of the goals they haven't gone inside, I don't know.
"The execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think it was really, really good."
Arteta was also full of praise for Gyokeres, with particular emphasis on the striker's link-up play; an element of his game at times criticised.
"What I love the most is how connected he was to the team," Arteta said.
"We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch.
"There was a lot to like in that performance and that's the Viktor that we needed."
City up next for the Gunners
Noni Madueke has been Arsenal's best attacker in recent weeks.
The winger, who was left out of the last England squad, is enjoying a run in the Arsenal starting XI with Bukayo Saka out injured and is taking his opportunity.
Madueke has registered a goal and two assists in his past three games and was again the best Arsenal forward against Dortmund.
The Gunners host Manchester City on Sunday and are currently six points clear at the top of the Premier League table.
Madueke, who was frustrated with the performance against Dortmund, said the clash with third-placed City is a great chance to get back to winning ways and shake off any frustration.
"I think these are the best games. I'm really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same," Madueke told Amazon Prime.
"We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We're champions, we're at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates.
"There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction."

items.text:
'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt
- Published
Manchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.
The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.
It started flawlessly under the Italian with the side winning their first eight games, but that smooth operation is beginning to turn into a turgid and pedestrian showing.
Similar to Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham, moans and groans filled a rather flat Etihad Stadium as the home faithful watched their side labour to a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli.
City's recent defensive issues also continued, now conceding in 10 successive games and letting in the first goal in seven of those matches.
Maresca said: "We are always looking for three points but when you are not able to win it is important you that don't lose. We take the point, five games [played],10 points and overall I think it is a good result in the end.
"Today, off the ball, once again we didn't concede a lot, the problem is that in this moment they are clinical when we concede a chance, almost every time it is finishing with a goal. We created many chances but in this moment it is like this and move on.
"The first 10 games we always scored first and then in this moment it is exactly in the opposite way, we just need to find a way to avoid that, but I don't think it affects the players in terms of their confidence. We fought until the end."
'Dull and predictable'
City were strong favourites for this game and should have had few issues in collecting all three points against a Napoli side that are languishing in eighth place in Serie A.
Their injury issues mean they were able to name only seven substitutes, two of those being goalkeepers, while they had suffered defeat in their past three meetings with City.
They threatened a shock result after twice going ahead through well-taken goals from Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang, but Rayan Cherki managed to salvage a late draw for the hosts.
Maresca's side had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, which largely lacked incisiveness, and of that figure 303 were in the final third compared to Napoli's 77.
The latest disappointing result means City's perfect start is quickly unravelling, now having won only one of their past seven games in all competitions inside 90 minutes.
"It was really surprising to see Manchester City so dull in the first half and so predictable," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"If you play a team that takes their time, you get yourself set. It is 100% easier to defend.
"You sit and watch City pass, pass, pass, slow, slow. You can get a cigar out."
Is Haaland lacking service?
Star striker Erling Haaland has been in prolific form again this season, scoring 20 goals for club and country, but the 26-year-old has drawn a blank in his past two games.
The Norwegian had chances but failed to score against Fulham on Saturday and though he was handed the captain's armband against Napoli, Haaland was on the periphery for much of the game.
The frontman managed only 14 touches of the ball against the Serie A side on Tuesday, the lowest figure of any player that started the match.
It raises the question whether he is receiving the service to try and find the back of the net.
"I feel I am getting more than enough chances to score," Haaland told TNT Sports. "We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn't. Not good enough and we let them in too easy.
"Football is easy and difficult; when you win it's easy and you know what to do, when you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy."
City are sixth in the Champions League table, before Wednesday's games, but in the Premier League they have failed to win their past four.
It does not get any easier this weekend, facing a daunting trip to leaders Arsenal on Sunday as they aim to find some form.
Haaland added: "It's the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away.
"We need a top performance from every single player."

items.title: Arsenal showing bluntless in attack - but Man City have problems too
items.summary:
Arsenal and Manchester City's problems analysed as both set to meet in bumper Premier League clash this weekend
Arsenal and Man City both slipped up in the Champions League in midweek ahead of their big Premier League meeting this weekend; watch Arsenal vs Man City live on Sky Sports Premier League
items.text:
Arsenal and Manchester City's problems analysed as both set to meet in bumper Premier League clash this weekend
Arsenal and Man City both slipped up in the Champions League in midweek ahead of their big Premier League meeting this weekend; watch Arsenal vs Man City live on Sky Sports Premier League this Sunday, kick-off 4.30pm
Tuesday 24 November 2026 23:57, UK
Arsenal face Manchester City in a blockbuster Premier League contest this weekend, but in recent days and months, both teams have issues to overcome.
Arsenal have drawn back-to-back games against Newcastle and Borussia Dortmund, with Mikel Arteta's side throwing away comfortable half-time leads in both matches.
City, meanwhile, come into the game on a run of just one win in their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Latest on YOUR PL club!
- Premier League fixtures & scores | FREE PL highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
The game could have a huge impact on the Premier League title race, with Arsenal hoping to open up a nine-point lead over Enzo Maresca's side, who in turn could close the gap to the reigning champions to just three points with a win.
Sky Sports reporters Sam Blitz and Adam Bate were at Arsenal and City's draws in midweek and analyse their respective issues...
Arsenal showing bluntness in attack again
Sky Sports' Sam Blitz at the Emirates Stadium:
Arsenal have the most 1-0 wins out of any Premier League team since Mikel Arteta took over the club in December 2019. It's all well and good - until teams start making it 1-1.
And in the last two games, they have. And Arsenal only have themselves to blame.
After the Gunners' 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund, Arteta was convinced that their recent draws against Newcastle and the Bundesliga leaders are not comparable.
He claims Arsenal played well in this Champions League stalemate - and repeated on several occasions that Dortmund benefited from an "element of luck". There's an element of truth to that - the woodwork was struck three times in the second half.
But Arsenal had thirty shots against Dortmund - the most they've ever had in a Champions League game. Just four of those shots were on target. Seven shots came from within the six-yard box, no goals came from them.
And it's costing them points. Because there has been a pattern in Arsenal's last two matches. Dominate the first half, only take a 1-0 lead, start the second half slowly and then end up drawing the game.
Out of the 2.2 worth of Expected Goals Arsenal missed in the game, 0.96 of that tally came in the first half. From their 13 shots that didn't lead to a goal, they should have taken a bigger advantage.
It invited Dortmund back into the contest when there shouldn't have been one in the first place. Like Newcastle did at the weekend, the Bundesliga leaders sorted their game plan out in the half-time break and came out firing.
Arteta is right that the Newcastle and Dortmund games are different because Arsenal rallied to seize dominance of the game right after the German side's equaliser.
But once again, the conversation sits around the holes in Arsenal's attacking quality, particularly at left wing and up front. After Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus left the club this summer without being replaced, Arsenal are still searching for attacking inspiration at left wing, with neither centre-forward in a goalscoring run of form.
Christos Tzolis is still waiting for his first Arsenal goal, Eberechi Eze is lacking consistency and Viktor Gyokeres backed up his early strike and impressive all-round display by creating doubts again by missing a late sitter.
At the start of the season, Gary Neville questioned whether Arsenal had the attacking player capable of delivering the Champions League. The draw to Dortmund backed that claim up.
Arteta struck a calm and positive tone after the Dortmund draw. It was a figure who knows his team have a six-point lead at the top of the Premier League, and will go on to qualify for the knockout stages of the Champions League.
But if these traits continue, it can all slip away quickly in this busy part of the season. If Arsenal don't beat Real Madrid, their top eight spot will be under threat.
Last season, they also benefited hugely from getting a top two spot that meant the second legs of their entire knockout stages were at the Emirates. PSG and Real can open up a bit of a gap on Arsenal in the coming weeks.
And up next, it's Manchester City at the Emirates. Enzo Maresca's side tend to score in most games. A 1-0 lead may not be enough.
Maresca still searching for the Man City solutions
Sky Sports' Adam Bate at the Etihad Stadium:
Move the ball quicker, yelled one fan from behind the press box. Press them, screamed a youngster in front. They were not wrong. Manchester City still have the individual quality to entertain the Etihad Stadium but they are also a frustrating watch at present.
City have picked up just one point from their last four Premier League games and while they did defeat RB Leipzig 3-2 in their previous Champions League outing, they let in two more in this draw with Napoli. It is 10 games now without keeping a clean sheet.
"Off the ball, the team was good from my point of view," said Enzo Maresca in the press conference afterwards, presenting a positive spin. "We did not concede a lot. The problem is that they were clinical. We created many chances." Not everyone agreed.
"It is not good enough," City captain Erling Haaland had told TNT Sports just before. "We let them in too easily and were unable to control or attack the game as we want." Tellingly, the striker then added: "When you do not win you start to question everything."
Maresca is being questioned. He has stressed that he is months into his time here not years and it is evident that he is still searching for the solutions. Finding the best role for new signings

items.title: Championship roundup: Boro edge Swansea, West Ham lose at Portsmouth
items.summary:
Will Lankshear was back among the goals as Middlesbrough cemented their position at the top of the Championship with a 2-1 win over Swansea.
Lankshear had missed the final two games before the international break because of a hamstring injury, and was only afforded a late substitute appearance in Sa
items.text:
Will Lankshear was back among the goals as Middlesbrough cemented their position at the top of the Championship with a 2-1 win over Swansea.
Lankshear had missed the final two games before the international break because of a hamstring injury, and was only afforded a late substitute appearance in Saturday’s win over Bristol City. Having been restored to the starting lineup at the Riverside, the Championship’s leading scorer claimed his 14th league goal of the season to re-establish his side’s lead in the second half after Joseph Opoku’s driven finish had cancelled out Myles Peart-Harris’ opener.
At the other end, Preston’s revival under Graham Alexander picked up more pace as they took Cardiff’s unbeaten home league record with a 4-0 triumph in the Welsh capital that moved them off the bottom of the Championship. It was their first win on the road this season and made it seven points from their last three games after a win over Southampton and a draw at West Ham.
Thierry Small scored in the 25th minute, Alfie Devine fired home in the 33rd, Andy Moran joined them on the scoresheet in the 62nd and then the captain Andrew Hughes headed home in the 69th. It was a tactical masterclass from Alexander’s men as they completely nullified Cardiff’s usual free-flowing approach and forced the home side into error after error.
Back at the top, Adam Armstrong’s double made it six goals in six games to give dominant Wolves a 3-0 win over Derby at Molineux that took them up to second. Armstrong’s double sandwiched Mateus Mané’s first of the season as Wolves’ fourth straight win stretched their unbeaten run to eight games to climb a place to second in the table. Despite a couple of first-half scares from Derby, Wolves could have had several more goals, while Derby are now bottom after one win in 13.
Scott Parker’s winless start to life as West Ham manager continued as Odin Bailey netted his first Portsmouth goal in a 1-0 victory at Fratton Park. Parker has lost two and drawn two since replacing Nuno Espírito Santo in the Hammers dugout, with the east Londoners without victory in six and 11 points off the top of the table. The Championship’s top scorers failed to scored for the first time this season, despite hitting the woodwork twice, as Bailey’s first-half strike was enough for Portsmouth to rise to 10th.
Sydie Peck equalised in the 90th minute as Sheffield United came from behind to secure a 1-1 Championship draw with Southampton at Bramall Lane. Lewis Dobbin had given the visitors an early lead but the Blades stepped up a gear after the break and finally found a way past the goalkeeper Daniel Peretz through Peck. The equaliser saw Sheffield United move within a point of the top eight and remain two behind their sixth-placed opponents.
Charlton swept Lincoln aside at the Valley with an impressive 4-0 victory. Joe Rankin-Costello’s first goal of the season quickly broke the deadlock with Ivan Mesik doubling the advantage inside the opening quarter of an hour. Tyreece Campbell’s finish early in the second half ended any lingering doubts that the Imps were heading for a fifth straight Championship loss. Miles Leaburn’s stoppage-time goal was nothing less than the utterly dominant home team deserved.
Bristol City stopped the rot at home by claiming a welcome point in a 1-1 draw with Wrexham. Michael Skubala, the home manager, had to endure chants about his employment prospects from the Ashton Gate faithful after Joe Worrall had given Wrexham a seventh-minute lead.
But City – who had lost their previous four home games – lifted mounting pressure on Skubala with a spirited display that took them up two places to 16th. Cameron Pring rewarded their endeavour with a rare goal after 51 minutes, the full-back on target for the first time since December 2023.
Norwich’s impressive run of victories came to an end as QPR held them to a 1-1 draw at Carrow Road. The Canaries had won their previous five Championship fixtures but had to come from behind to pick up a point this time around after Harvey Vale had fired the visitors in front just before the break.
Philippe Clement’s side were quickly back on level terms in the second half through a well-taken Anthony Musaba effort, but were well contained after that as Rangers registered a well-deserved point.

items.title: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
items.summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media.
The topic of succession planning also came up — a p
items.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media.
The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported, citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy.
Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy.
Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings.
Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman.
“When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.”
Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however.
